$k$  marbles are placed onto the cells of a  $2024 \times 2024$  grid such that each cell has at most one marble and there are no two marbles are placed onto two neighboring cells (neighboring cells are defined as cells having an edge in common).

a) Assume that  $k=2024$ . Find a way to place the marbles satisfying the conditions above, such that moving any placed marble to any of its neighboring cells will give an arrangement that does not satisfy both the conditions.
b) Determine the largest value of  $k$  such that for all arrangements of  $k$  marbles satisfying the conditions above, we can move one of the placed marble onto one of its neighboring cells and the new arrangement satisfies the conditions above.
solution_md: Here's a full classification of which $k$ work for part (b). We claim that $k \le 2023, 2025 \le k \le 4045$ work. ------------------- **Proof that $k = 2024$ does not work.** This is part (a). Fill in the main diagonal lol. ------------------- **Proof that $k \ge 4046$ do not work.** Note that $k \le \frac{2024^2}{2}$ by constraints. Take a $4046$ token configuration which is a diagonal rectangle which is one off the main diagonal. Then greedily fill largest diagonals of the same parity, place excess in the middle of the diagonal rectangle. [asy] size(10cm); int N = 10; for (int i = 0; i <= N; ++i) { draw((0,i)--(N,i)); draw((i,0)--(i,N)); } for (int i = 0; i <= N-1; ++i) { for (int j = 0; j <= N-1; ++j) { if ((i + j) % 2 == 0) { if (((i - j) * (i - j) == 4) || (i + j) == 2 || (i + j) == 2*N-4) { fill(shift(i,j)*unitsquare, white+blue); } else if (i == j) { fill(shift(i,j)*unitsquare, white+red); } else { fill(shift(i,j)*unitsquare, white+green); } } } } [/asy] In order, fill blue, then green, then red. ------------------- **Proof $k \le 2023$ work.** FTSOC suppose not. Take the convex hull of tokens. By extremal it follows that the edges of the convex hull consist of entire diagonals $A_1A_2, A_3A_4, A_5A_6, A_7A_8$ such that $A_2A_3$ is the opposite border of the board as $A_6A_7$ . Note that these diagonals are disjoint else we get a path of length $2024$ .**Claim:** There exists a path between any two tokens $a, b$ such that $t_0 = a, t_n = b$ and the taxicab distance between $t_i, t_{i+1}$ is $2$ . *Proof.* Suppose not, then spam along both tokens up and down to get two disjoint chains of length $1012$ , contradictions. $\blacksquare$ **Claim:** There exists a path between $A_2$ and $A_3$ such that each move between adjacent $A_2$ and $A_3$ has nonzero vertical component in direction $A_2$ , $A_3$ . *Proof.* Spam going towards $A_3$ from $A_2$ and spam going towards $A_2$ from $A_3$ . These paths then must intersect. $\blacksquare$ Then the path from $A_1$ to $A_2$ and $A_5$ to $A_6$ can't intersect else that implies a path of length $2024$ . Now take paths $A_8-A_1-A_2-A_3$ , $A_4-A_5-A_6-A_7$ which are disjoint, and both have length at least $1012$ , for a total at least $2024$ , contradiction. [asy] draw(unitsquare); draw((0.3,0)--(0,0.3), blue); draw((0.8,0)--(1,1-0.8), blue); draw((0.7,1)--(1,0.7), blue); draw((0.4,1)--(0,1-0.4), blue); draw((0,1-0.4)..(0.2,0.5)..(0,0.3), green); draw((1,0.7)..(0.8,0.5)..(1,1-0.8), green); dot(" $A_1$ ", (0, 1-0.4), W); dot(" $A_2$ ", (0, 0.3), W); dot(" $A_3$ ", (0.3, 0), S); dot(" $A_4$ ", (0.8, 0), S); dot(" $A_5$ ", (1, 1-0.8), E); dot(" $A_6$ ", (1, 0.7), E); dot(" $A_7$ ", (0.7, 1), N); dot(" $A_8$ ", (0.4, 1), N); [/asy] ------------------- **Proof $2025 \le k \le 4045$ work.** FTSOC suppose this is possible. We show that $k \ge 4046$ , contradiction. We also give a diagram for the $n = 10$ case. As above, all squares must be a subset of the checkerboard pattern, else you can force two edges to touch by taking a vertical line through one of them and a horizontal one of an opposite parity. Consider the diagonals from top left to bottom right of the same parity as the checkerboard and WLOG let the bottom left square be part of the checkerboard. Call the diagonal from top left to bottom right the *divider* and the other main diagonal the *snake*. We once again get two distinct minimal diagonals (draw in blue and potentially corners) such that one lies below the divider and one lies above the divider.**Claim:** For each diagonal between these two diagonals, at least two squares are filled in. *Proof.* If the minimal diagonals isn't a single corner block, then inductively fill in diagonals starting from that diagonal to get the result (consider the extremal pieces in the diagonal). Else, WLOG suppose the bottom right minimal diagonal is a single corner. If the diagonal above this one has two or three elements, we induct as before. Else, it follows that the next square in the snake is the only square filled in. This must keep occuring until either we get that all the squares directly below the divider are empty, which forces only the snake to be filled in, contradiction, or we get a case where for some diagonal below the divider, all squares in it but at most one are filled. Then clear everything below this diagonal and move one token if necessary to fill in the diagonal, and repeat the process. $\blacksquare$ We draw in the relevant squares in light blue. As such, if we project the minimal diagonals to the edge (draw in red), then all diagonals but the corners have $2$ , and the corners have $1$ . This gives at least $2 \cdot 2024 - 2 = 4046$ squares, contradiction. [asy] size(10cm); int N = 10; for (int i = 0; i <= N; ++i) { draw((0,i)--(N,i)); draw((i,0)--(i,N)); } for (int i = 0; i <= N-1; ++i) { for (int j = 0; j <= N-1; ++j) { if ((i + j) == 4 || (i + j) == 2*N-6) { fill(shift(i,j)*unitsquare, white+blue); } else if ((i - j) == -6 | (i - j) == 6) { fill(shift(i,j)*unitsquare, white+lightblue); } } } pen gr = lightgray; fill(shift(7,5)*unitsquare, gr); fill(shift(5,7)*unitsquare, gr); fill(shift(5,3)*unitsquare, gr); fill(shift(5,5)*unitsquare, gr); fill(shift(7,3)*unitsquare, gr); fill(shift(5,1)*unitsquare, gr); fill(shift(3,3)*unitsquare, gr); fill(shift(2,4)*unitsquare, gr); fill(shift(2,6)*unitsquare, gr); fill(shift(1,5)*unitsquare, gr); fill(shift(3,7)*unitsquare, gr); fill(shift(4,4)*unitsquare, gr); pen lr = white+red; fill(shift(0,0)*unitsquare, lr); fill(shift(2,0)*unitsquare, lr); fill(shift(0,2)*unitsquare, lr); fill(shift(N-0-1,N-0-1)*unitsquare, lr); fill(shift(N-2-1,N-0-1)*unitsquare, lr); fill(shift(N-0-1,N-2-1)*unitsquare, lr); [/asy]

<details><summary>Solution to a)</summary>Simply arrange all marbles along one of the two main diagonals.</details>
<details><summary>Solution to b)</summary>We claim that  $k=2023$  is the largest such value. Part a) shows that  $k\leq 2023$ . We have to show that there is a way to move a marble if  $k<2024$ . stem_md: For each polynomial  $P(x)$ , define   $$ P_1(x)=P(x), \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, $$     $$ P_2(x)=P(P_1(x)),  \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, $$     $$ ... $$     $$ P_{2024}(x)=P(P_{2023}(x)), \forall x \in \mathbb{R}. $$   Let  $a>2$  be a real number. Is there a polynomial  $P$  with real coefficients such that for all  $t \in (-a, a)$ , the equation  $P_{2024}(x)=t$  has  $2^{2024}$  distinct real roots?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Answer</summary>The answer to this is  $\boxed{\text{Yes}}$ .</details>

<details><summary>Solution</summary>First, let's extend the definition of  $P_n(x)$  to any positive integer  $n$ .
Consider the polynomial  $P(x)=Cx(x-1)$  for  $C \geq 4a$  and  $C+2>2\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4a}{C}}$ . This choice of  $C$  is possible, since when  $C$  tends to go to infinity,  $C+2$  tends to go to  $\infty$  while  $2\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4a}{C}}$  tends to go to  $2$ .
We claim that the equation  $P_n(x)=t$  has all  $2^n$  real roots for all  $t \in (-a, a)$ .
We prove this by induction.
For  $n=1$ , the equation  $x(x-1)=\frac{t}{C}$  has the discriminant  $\Delta = 1+ \frac{4t}{C}=\frac{C+4t}{C}>0$  (since  $C \geq 4a$ ,  $C+4t>4a-4a=0$ ), so the equation  $P_1(x)=0$  has two roots, namely  $x_1 = \frac{1-\sqrt{1+ \dfrac{4t}{C}}}{2}$  and  $x_2 = \frac{1+\sqrt{1+ \dfrac{4t}{C}}}{2}$ .
Now assume that our claim holds true for  $1, 2, \ldots, n$ .
Define a sequence  $(u_n)$  as  $u_0=t$  and for each  $1 \leq i \leq n-1$ , let  $u_i$  denote the greatest root, among the  $2^{i-1}$  roots of the equation  $P_i(x)=0$ . It is trivial that  $u_n>0$  for all  $n>1$ .
The equation  $Cx(x-1)=k$ , for some real number  $k>-\frac{C}{4}$ , has two solutions, namely  $x=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4k}{C}}}{2}$  and  $x=\frac{1-\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4k}{C}}}{2}$ . So when  $k$  increases, the larger roots also increases, and the smaller root decreases. (1)
This means  $u_{n+1} = \frac{1+\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4u_n}{C}}}{2}$  for all non-negative integers  $n$ .
Since  $t<a$  and  $C>4a$ , it follows that  $u_1 = \frac{1+\sqrt{1+ \dfrac{4t}{C}}}{2} < \frac{1+\sqrt{1+ \dfrac{4a}{4a}}}{2}<a.$ We then induct, with base case  $n=0, 1$ , to prove that  $u_n<a$  for all positive integers  $n$ .

Now, the equation  $Cx(x-1)=u_{n-1}$  has two roots, which are  $x_1=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4u_{n-1}}{C}}}{2}$  and   $x_2=\frac{1-\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4u_{n-1}}{C}}}{2}$ . Since  $u_{n-1}$  is the largest root among the  $2^{n-1}$  root, with (1) it follows that  $x_1, x_2$  are the largest and smallest root among the  $2^{n}$  roots of the equation  $P_n(x)=t$  respectively.

Now consider the equation  $Cx(x-1)=x_2$ , equivalently  $x(x-1)=\frac{x_2}{C}$ . The discriminant of this is then  $1+\frac{4x_2}{C} = \frac{1}{C} \left( C+2 \left( 1-\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4u_{n-1}}{C}} \right) \right) > \frac{1}{C} \left( C+2-2\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4a}{C}} \right)>0.$ This means the equation  $Cx(x-1)=x_2$  has two distinct roots. And since  $x_2$  is the smallest root among the  $2^n$  roots of  $P_n(x)=t$ , it follows that for each of these  $2^n$  roots, let's say  $y$ , the equation  $Cx(x-1)=y$  has two distinct roots. So there are a total of  $2 \cdot 2^n = 2^{n+1}$  roots, and so the equation  $P_{n+1}(x)=t$  has  $2^{n+1}$  roots. In addition, since the degree of  $P_{n+1}(x)$  is  $2^{n+1}$ , it follows that the equation has exactly  $2^{n+1}$  roots.

So the induction is complete, and the problem is solved.</details>

The idea is to consider a transformation of Chebyshev polynomials in general:
Let  $T_{n}(x)$  be the n-th chebyshev polynomial with coefficients  $(a_{i_{1}},a_{i_{2}},...,a_{i_{k}})$  where we have   $[x^{i_{t}}]=a_{i_{t}}$ .

Consider the polynomial  $P(x) = \frac{2x^2 - a^2}{a}$ . stem_md:
For each positive integer  $n$ , let  $\tau (n)$  be the number of positive divisors of  $n$ .

a) Find all positive integers  $n$  such that  $\tau(n)+2023=n$ .
b) Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers  $k$  such that there are exactly two positive integers  $n$  satisfying  $\tau(kn)+2023=n$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Part a sketch</summary>We first use the lemma  $\tau(n)<2\sqrt{n}$  to get  $n=\tau(n)+2023<2\sqrt{n}+2023$ .
This gives  $n<46^2=2116$ .
The problem condition implies  $n > 2023$ , hence  $n \geq 2+2023=2025$ .
In addition,  $n= 2025$  fails so  $2026 \leq n \leq 2115$ . But this means  $n$  is not a perfect square, so  $\tau(n)$  is even, implying that  $n$  is odd.
Considering all odd  $n$ 's varying from  $2026$  to  $2115$ , we can use the  $\tau(n)$  formula to get that  $\tau(n) \leq 16$ .
This gives  $n \geq 2023+16 = 2039$ .
Now, directly checking all odd  $n$ 's from  $2027$  to  $2039$  gives no such  $n$ .
Hence, there are no positive integers  $n$  such that  $\tau(n)+2023=n$ .</details>

<details><summary>Part b sketch</summary>We claim all primes  $k>2040$  work.
First, if  $k \mid n$ , write  $n = k^a \cdot l$  for some positive integers  $a, l$  with  $(l, k)=1$ .
Then the equation is equivalent to  $(a+1) \tau(l) + 2023 = k^a \cdot l$ .
We use the lemma  $\tau(l)<2\sqrt{l}$  to get  $k^a \cdot l < 2(a+1) \sqrt{l} + 2023$ .
Now, consider the function  $f(x)=k^ax^2-2(a+1)x-2023$  for  $x \geq 1$ . We get that  $f'(x)=2(k^ax-(a+1)) \geq 2(k^a-(a+1))>0,$  so the function is increasing on  $[1, \infty)$ . This means  $f(\sqrt{l}) \geq f(1)=k^a-(2a+2025)>0,$  absurd.
This means  $(n, k)=1$ . The equation is now  $2\tau(n)+2023=n$ .

The condition implies  $n > 2023$ , hence  $n \geq 2+2023=2025$ .
We now use the lemma  $\tau(n)<2\sqrt{n}$  to get  $n<4\sqrt{n}+2023$ , so  $n \leq 2218$ .
In addition,  $n= 2025$  fails and  $n$  is odd, so  $2027 \leq n \leq 2218$ .
Considering all odd  $n$ 's varying from  $2026$  to  $2218$ , we can use the  $\tau(n)$  formula to get that  $\tau(n) \leq 16$ .
This gives  $n \geq 2023+16 = 2039$ .
Now, directly checking all odd  $n$ 's from  $2027$  to  $2039$  gives  $n=2027$  and  $n=2031$ .
Our claim is proved, the problem is solved.</details>

stem_md: In the space, there is a convex polyhedron  $D$  such that for every vertex of  $D$ , there are an even number of edges passing through that vertex. We choose a face  $F$  of  $D$ . Then we assign each edge of  $D$  a positive integer such that for all faces of  $D$  different from  $F$ , the sum of the numbers assigned on the edges of that face is a positive integer divisible by  $2024$ . Prove that the sum of the numbers assigned on the edges of  $F$  is also a positive integer divisible by  $2024$ .
solution_md:
Here is one approach for this problem.
Edit: After reading post #3, I find that I use the same idea as @rtyu852, so I will let this post as a more detail version.

<details><summary>A more detail version of post #3</summary>Because the polyhedron  $D$  is convex, it can be considered as a planar graph  $G$  where the vectices of graph are corresponding to the vertices of  $D$ , and two vertices in  $G$  are connected if and only if two corresponding vertices in  $D$  are connected.

Let  $G'$  be the dual graph of  $G$ . Apparently, each vertex of  $G$  is corresponding to a face of  $G'$ , and each face of  $G$  is corresponding to a vertex in  $G'$ . Because for every vertex of  $G$ , there are an even number of edges passing through it, each face of  $G'$  surrounded by an even number of edges. In other words, each face of  $G'$  is formed by an even cycle.

Suppose that there exists an odd cycle  $C=v_{1}v_{2}\ldots v_{k}v_1$  in  $G'$ . WLOG, suppose that the area of the interior region of  $C$  is minimal. From the claim above,  $C$  can not form a face in  $G'$ , so there exists to vertex  $v_{i},v_{j}\in C$  and a path  $P$  connecting  $v_{i}$  and  $v_{j}$  which does not share any edge with  $C$  and lies inside  $C$ .

Because  $C$  is an odd cycle, the lengths of two paths  $P_1=v_{i}v_{i+1}\ldots v_{j}$  and  $P_2=v_{j}v_{j+1}...v_{i}$  in  $C$  have different parities.

Because  $P$  does not share any edge with  $C$ , or, in other words,  $P_1$  and  $P_2$ , the pairs  $(P,P_1)$  and  $(P,P_2)$  make two new cycles  $C_1$  and  $C_2$  respectively. The lengths of  $P_1$  and  $P_2$  have the different parities, and so do  $C_1$  and  $C_2$ . Without loss of generality, assume that  $C_1$  is an odd cycle.

However, the area the interior region of  $C_1$  is apparently smaller than  $C$ 's, which contradicts our assumption about  $C$ .

Thus, there is no odd cycle in  $G'$ , which implies that  $G'$  is a bipartite graph. Let  $A$  and  $B$  be two part of the graph  $G'$ . We color all the vertices of  $A$  and  $B$  by red and green respectively.

Now, we color all the face of  $G$ : a face is red if it is corresponding to a red vertex of  $G'$ , and vice versa. Without loss of generality, assume that  $F$  is red. Since then, we choose all the green faces of  $G$ .

Because every edge in  $G$  belongs to one red face and one green face, it must be chosen exactly once. Therefore, if we take the sum of all numbers assigned to all the chosen edges, we will obtain the sum of numbers assigned to all edges of  $G$ . We denote that sum by  $s$ . Additionally, according to the hypothesis, the sum of all the edges of a face other than  $F$  is divisible by  $2024$ , so  $s$  is divisible by  $2024$ .

Notice that if the take the sum of all edges assign to each face, and take the sum of all obtained values, we will get  $2s$ , which is divisible by  $2024$ . Hence, the sum of all numbers assigned to the edges of  $F$  is divisible by  $2024$ .</details>

Let  $X,Y,Z$  be feet the altitudes of from  $A,B,C$  to the sides  $BC,CA,AB$  respectively. Let  $A',B',C'$  be the reflections of  $X,Y,Z$  in  $EF,FD,DE$  respectively. Prove that triangles  $ABC$  and  $A'B'C'$  are similar.
solution_md:
Let  $ I, O, H $  be the incenter, circumcenter, orthocenter of  $ \triangle ABC $ , respectively, and let  $ I' $  be the image of  $ I $  under the inversion WRT  $ \odot (ABC) $ . Let  $ M $  be the midpoint of  $ IH $  and let  $ I_A $  be the  $ \angle A $  - excenter WRT  $ \triangle ABC $ . Let  $ T $  be the midpoint of  $ AH $  and let  $ J $  be the reflection of  $ I $  in  $ EF $ . Since  $ J $  is the incenter of  $ \triangle AYZ$ , it follows that  $ J, H, X, I_A $  are concyclic, hence  $ \triangle ATJ \sim \triangle AOI $ . Let  $ AI $  intersect  $ \odot (ABC) $  again at  $ N $  and let  $ K $  be the reflection of  $ A $  in  $OI $ . Note that the reflection point of  $ T $  in  $ EF $  lies on  $ OI $  and  $K, N, I' $  are collinear, 
\begin{align*}
\measuredangle (NI', NM) 
 &= \measuredangle (NK, I_AH) 
 &= \measuredangle (NK, NI_A) + \measuredangle (NI_A, I_AH) 
 &= \measuredangle (OI, OA) + \measuredangle (JX, XH) 
 &= \measuredangle (TX, TJ) + \measuredangle (JX, XH) 
 &= \measuredangle (JX, JT) 
 &= \measuredangle (II', IA'). 
\end{align*} 
Thus, by combining  $ MN : A'I = HI_A : 2XJ = AO : AI = NI' : II' $ , we get  $ \triangle I'MN \sim \triangle I'A'I \Longrightarrow \triangle I'OA \sim \triangle I'MA' $ . Similarly,  $ \triangle I'OB \sim \triangle I'MB', \triangle I'OC \sim \triangle I'MC' $ , so it is easy to see  $ \triangle ABC \cup O \cup I' \sim \triangle A'B'C' \cup M \cup I' $ .  $ \blacksquare $

stem_md: Let  $P(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$  be a monic, non-constant polynomial. Determine all continuous functions  $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$  such that  $$ f(f(P(x))+y+2023f(y))=P(x)+2024f(y), $$  for all reals  $x,y$ .
solution_md:
Let $P(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ be a monic, non-constant polynomial. Determine all continuous functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $$ f(f(P(x))+y+2023f(y))=P(x)+2024f(y), $$ for all reals $x,y$ .
Let $Q(x,y)$ be the assertion $f(f(P(x))+y+2023f(y))=P(x)+2024f(y)$ Since $P(x)$ is monic, RHS is not upperbounded, and so $f(x)$ is not upperbounded 1) Claim : $f(P(x))=P(x)$ $\forall x\in\mathbb R$ 1.1) If $f(x)$ is not lowerbounded Since neither upperbounded, neither lowerbounded and continuous, $f(x)$ is surjective. Let then $x\in\mathbb R$ and $y$ such that $f(y)=-\frac{f(P(x))}{2023}$ So $f(P(x))+y+2023f(y)=y$ and $Q(x,y)$ becomes $-\frac{f(P(x))}{2023}=P(x)-2024\frac{f(P(x))}{2023}$ Q.E.D. 1.2) If $f(x)$ is lowerbounded Then $x+2024f(x)$ is continuous not upperbounded. And $Q(x,P(x))$ $\implies$ $f(P(x)+2024f(P(x)))=P(x)+2024f(P(x))$ and so $f(x+2024f(x))=x+2024f(x))$ for all $ x$ great enough. And since $x+2024f(x)$ is continuous not upperbounded, this is $f(x)=x$ for all $x>A$ for some $ A$ Let any $x\in\mathbb R$ , choosing $y>\max(A,\frac{A-f(P(x))}{2024})$ , we have : $y>A$ implies $f(y)=y$ and $Q(x,y)$ becomes $f(f(P(x))+2024y)=P(x)+2024y$ $f(P(x))+2024y>A$ implies $f(f(P(x))+2024y)=f(P(x))+2024y$ and previous line implies then $f(P(x))=P(x)$ $\forall x$ Q.E.D. 2) $f(x)=x$ $\forall x$ Let $y\in\mathbb R$ Since $P(x)$ is nonconstant $P(x)-P(y)$ covers $\mathbb R$ and so $\exists u,v$ such that $P(u)-P(v)=y+2023f(y)$ So LHS of $P(v,y)$ becomes $f(f(P(v))+y+2023f(y))=f(P(v)+y+2023f(y))=f(P(u))=P(u)=P(v)+y+2023f(y)$ And RHS is $P(v)+2024f(y)$ And so $2024f(y)=y+2023f(y)$ And $\boxed{f(x)=x\quad\forall x\in\mathbb R}$ , which indeed fits

In a garden, which is organized as a  $2024\times 2024$  board, we plant three types of flowers: roses, daisies, and orchids. We want to plant flowers such that the following conditions are satisfied:

(i) Each grid is planted with at most one type of flower. Some grids can be left blank and not planted.
(ii) For each planted grid  $A$ , there exist exactly  $3$  other planted grids in the same column or row such that those  $3$  grids are planted with flowers of different types from  $A$ 's.
(iii) Each flower is planted in at least  $1$  grid. 

What is the maximal number of the grids that can be planted with flowers?
solution_md:
Solved with**erkosfobiladol**.**Answer:**  $12\times 2018$ .**Example:**
The  $6\times 2018$  rectangle satisifies the condition. After rotating this and replacing  $B$  with  $C$ , we get  $2$  rectangles where both have  $6\times 2018$  squares.  $$ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline
A&A&A&B&B&B\hline
A&A&A&B&B&B\hline
.&.&.&.&.&.\hline
A&A&A&B&B&B\hline
\end{array} $$  **Proof:** Assume that it's possible to choose more filled squares.

Assume that there exists a row with  $\geq 2018$  filled squares.
Swapping the positions of rows and columns doesnot affect the conditions. 
Let  $l$  be the number of the filled squares in the row or column with maximum filled squares.
If there exists a row with  $l\geq 2018$  filled squares,  $$ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline
A&A&A&A&...&A&&&&&\hline
&&&&&&&&&&\hline
&&&&&&&&&&\hline
&&&&&&&&&&\hline
\end{array} $$  The row must be filled by exactly  $1$  letter. WLOG let it be  $A$ .
In  $i.$  column where  $1\leq i\leq l$ , there are at most  $6$  letters because  $A$  in  $i.$  column must see  $3$  others. So there are at most  $6l$  filled squares in the  $l\times 2024$  rectangle. Also there can be at most  $(2024-l)l$  filled squares in the  $(2024-l)\times 2024$  rectangle.
Thus there can be at most  $6l+(2024-l)l=l(2030-l)$  filled squares. For  $l\geq 2018,$  we have  $l(2030-l)\leq 2018.12$ . In this case, there can be at most  $12. 2018$  filled squares.

Therefore  $l\leq 2017$ .**Claim:**There are at least  $7$  rows which have  $\geq 7$  filled squares.**Proof:** Let the rows with  $\geq 7$  filled squares be good rows. Denote  $m$  as the number of good rows. There can be at most  $2017m+(2024-m)6=2011m+2024.6$  filled squares.
If  $6\geq m\implies 2011.6\geq 2011m\geq 12.2018-6.2024+1\implies 6.4035>12.2018\implies 4035>4036$  which gives a contradiction.

The intersection of a good row and a good column must be empty.
Denote  $g_i$  as the number of filled squares in  $i.$  good row.
\[\sum{g_i}\geq 12.2018-6.2017+1=6.2019+1\]
Intersection of good rows and a column can have at most  $6$  filled squares hence 
\[\sum{g_i}\leq 6.2017\]
\[6.2017\geq \sum{g_i}\geq 6.2019+1\]
Gives a contradiction.

stem_md:
Let  $\alpha \in (1, +\infty)$  be a real number, and let  $P(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$  be a monic polynomial with degree  $24$ , such that 

(i)  $P(0) = 1$ .
(ii)  $P(x)$  has exactly  $24$  positive real roots that are all less than or equal to  $\alpha$ . 

Show that  $|P(1)| \le \left( \frac{19}{5}\right)^5 (\alpha-1)^{24}$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Letting  $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{24} \in (0,\alpha]$  be the roots, we have  $\prod_i \alpha_i=1$  and we want to maximize  $\prod_i \vert 1-\alpha_i\vert$ .
It' easy to see that if we have  $0<\alpha<1<\beta<\alpha$ , then we increase the expression by increasing  $\beta$  and decreasing  $\alpha$ , keeping the product constant.
So we can assume that all variables that are bigger than  $1$  are equal to  $\alpha$ .
Moreover, it is easy to see that the expression is maximal when all of the variables that are smaller than  $1$  are equal (otherwise again replace two of them by their geometric mean and just use AM-GM, only two factors change).
So we are left with the situation of  $24-k$  of the variables being equal to  $\alpha$  and the remaining  $k$  ones being equal to  $\beta<1$  where  $\beta^{k}\alpha^{24-k}=1$  and we need to prove that  $\left(\frac{1-\beta}{\alpha-1}\right)^k \le \left(\frac{19}{5}\right)^5$ .
Let us first show that for fixed  $k$ , the expression is at most  $\left(\frac{24-k}{k}\right)^k$ .
Indeed, we will show that if  $t \in [0,1]$  and  $\alpha^{1-t}\beta^t=1$ , then  $\frac{1-\beta}{\alpha-1} \le \frac{1-t}{t}$  (we can then choose  $t=\frac{k}{24}$  to finish). But this is equivalent to  $t\beta+(1-t)\alpha \ge 1$  which immediately follows from the condition by weighted AM-GM.

Finally, we are only left to maximize  $f(k)=\left(\frac{24-k}{k}\right)^k$  over all choices of  $k \in \{1,2,\dots,23\}$ .
In general, the function  $g(t)=\left(\frac{1-t}{t}\right)^t$  takes its maximum when  $t \in (0,1)$  is the unique root of  $\log \frac{1-t}{t}=\frac{1}{1-t}$ , which happens to be  $t_0 \approx 0.2178$ , and  $g$  is increasing for  $t<t_0$  and decreasing for  $t>t_0$ .
So it suffices to check that  $f(4)<f(5)$  and  $f(6)<f(5)$  i.e. that  $\left(\frac{19}{5}\right)^5$  is bigger than both  $5^4=625$  and  $3^6=729$  which can be done by hand: It suffices to prove  $\left(\frac{19}{15}\right)^5>3$ . But the LHS is bigger than  $\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)^5$  and the claim follows by noting that  $5^5=3125>3072=3 \cdot 4^5$ . In general, the maximum will occur when  $k \approx t_0n$  where we replace  $24$  by  $n$ .</details>

stem_md: Let incircle  $(I)$  of triangle  $ABC$  touch the sides  $BC,CA,AB$  at  $D,E,F$  respectively. Let  $(O)$  be the circumcircle of  $ABC$ . Ray  $EF$  meets  $(O)$  at  $M$ . Tangents at  $M$  and  $A$  of  $(O)$  meet at  $S$ . Tangents at  $B$  and  $C$  of  $(O)$  meet at  $T$ . Line  $TI$  meets  $OA$  at  $J$ . Prove that  $\angle ASJ=\angle IST$ .
solution_md:
Here is a synthetic solution.**Lemma:** Given points  $A,B,C,D$  lying on a circle. The tangents from  $A$  and  $B$  intersect at  $K$  and the tangents from  $C$  and  $D$  intersect at  $L$ . Then, the points  $K, L, AC\cap BD, AD\cap BC$  are collinear.

<details><summary>Proof</summary>Pascal on  $AACBBD$  and  $CCBDDA$</details>

Let  $EF\cap (ABC)=\{M,N\}$ . Let the tangents from  $A$  and  $N$  to  $(ABC)$  intersect at  $V$ . Let  $X$  and  $Y$  be the intersection of  $MD$  and  $ND$  with  $(I)$ . Let  $BN\cap AC=K, CM\cap AB=L$ . 

Using our *lemma* on the quadrilateral  $FEDX$  gives us that  $LX$  is tangent to  $(I)$ . Let  $AC\cap MB=U$ . Using the *lemma* on  $AMBC$ , one can show that  $U, L\in ST$ . Now, let's do something different and use our *lemma* on  $EXDF$  to show that the tangent from  $X$  to  $(I)$  (so the line  $LX$ ) is also passing through  $U$ . Hence, the line  $ST$  is tangent to  $(I)$  at  $X$ . Similarly, the line  $UT$  is tangent to incircle at  $Y$ .

Let  $H$  be the foot of the altitude from  $I$  to  $SV$ . We want to show that  $I$  and  $J$  are isogonal conjugates in  $\triangle TSV$ . We know that  $TI$  is the angle bisector of  $\angle STV$  so proving  $AHXY$  is cyclic is sufficient.

Applying Pascal on  $AACMNB$  gives us that  $P=KL\cap EF$  lies on  $AH$ . We know that  $EFHA$  and  $EFXY$  are cyclic, hence it suffices to show that  $AH, EF$  and  $XY$  are concurrent (or  $P\in XY$ ). Just notice that this is a result of using the *lemma* on  $EFXY$ .


<details><summary>Remark</summary>Since the lemma can be proven using Pascal twice, one can solve this problem just by using Pascal 15 times  :ewpu:</details>

stem_md: Let's call a power of two *compact* if it can be represented as the sum of no more than  $10^9$  not necessarily distinct factorials of positive integer numbers. Prove that the set of compact powers of two is finite.
solution_md:
We prove the following stronger result:

For any integers  $m, n \ge 0$ , the equation  $a_1! + \cdots + a_m! = 2^b - n$  has only finitely many integer solutions  $(a_1, \dots, a_m, b)$  with  $1 \le a_1 \le \cdots \le a_m$ .

We prove by induction on  $m$ . For  $m = 0$ , the equation reduces to  $2^b = n$  so for any  $n$  there is at most one solution.
Suppose that the result is true for  $m - 1$ . We prove it for  $m$ .

Given a fixed  $n$ , we show that there are only finitely many possible values of  $a_1$ . There are two cases.

First case:  $n = 0$ . In this case, we must have  $a_1 \le 2$ , otherwise  $2^b$  would be a multiple of  $3$ .
Second case:  $n > 0$ . We have  $2^b > n$ , which implies  $b > v_2(n)$  where  $v_2$  is the  $2$ -adic valuation.
Therefore we get  $v_2(n) = v_2(2^b - n) = v_2(a_1! + \cdots + a_m!) \ge v_2(a_1!)$ , which holds only for finitely many  $a_1$ .

Now for each possible value of  $a_1$ , the equation reduces to  $a_2! + \cdots + a_m! = 2^b - (n + a_1!)$ , thus the induction hypothesis tells us that there are only finitely many solutions.
Since there are only finitely many possible  $a_1$ , the total number of solutions is finite.

stem_md:
Given a  $2025 \times 2025$  board and  $k$  chips lying on the table. Initially, the board is empty. It is allowed to place a chip from the table on any free square  $A$  if two conditions are met simultaneously:
– the cell next to  $A$  from below has a chip (or  $A$  is on the bottom edge of the board);
– the cell next to  $A$  on the left has a chip (or  $A$  is on the left edge of the board).
In addition, it is allowed to remove any chip from the board and put it on the table. At what minimum  $k$  can a chip appear in the upper-right corner of the board?
solution_md:
Let  $n = 2025$ . We claim that  $k = n$  is minimal. This can be constructed by repeatedly constructing larger and larger diagonals until you get  $n$  chips on the top left and bottom right diagonal, and then merge them until you get the upper right corner.

To show  $k = n-1$ , we first can delete the bottom half of the grid so that we have a triangular grid with rows of length  $n, n-1, \dots, 1$  connecting each to higher elements, and we place chips on the bottom row of size  $n$  at no cost. Then the idea is that we can show inductively that we can have at most  $(n-1)-i$  chips above the  $i$ th row from the bottom, so there's at most one chip in the penultimate row, and thus it isn't possible to fill the upper right corner.

stem_md: The numbers from  $1$  to  $2025$  are arranged in some order in the cells of the  $1 \times 2025$  strip. Let's call a *flip* an operation that takes two arbitrary cells of a strip and swaps the numbers written in them, but only if the larger of these numbers is located to the left of the smaller one. A *flop* is a set of several flips that do not contain common cells that are executed simultaneously. (For example, a simultaneous flip between the 2nd and 8th cells and a flip between the 5th and 101st cells.) Prove that there exists a sequence of  $66$  flops such that for any initial arrangement, applying this sequence of flops to it will result in the numbers being ordered from left to right in ascending order.
solution_md: Of course the solution is basically mergesort. It suffices to merge two sequences with size  $\frac n2$  in  $\log n$  flops. Index starting from  $0$ . Assume without loss of generality  $n$  is a power of  $2$ , otherwise if some flip requires an index which is too large, ignore it and pretend that the rest of the strip is filled with infinity. Call a sequence good if when it is turned into a cyclic sequence, there are exactly two direction changes. Let the sequences be  $a$  and  $b$ . For the first flop, pair the  $i$ th largest element of  $a$  with the  $i$ th smallest element of  $b$ . Then, the elements of  $a$  are now all less than the elements of  $b$ . Both sequences are now good. In the  $k$ th flop for  $2\leq k\leq\log n$ , pair  $i$  with  $i\oplus\frac n{2^k}$ . For any good sequence, either the smaller half or the larger half is contiguous, so if all  $2^{k-1}$  subsequences of length  $\frac n{2^{k-1}}$  are good, this flop makes each of the  $2^k$  subsequences of length  $\frac n{2^k}$  good, and every element in a subsequence is smaller than every element in every successive subsequence. At the end, all  $n$  subsequences have size  $1$  and are sorted.

stem_md: The real number  $a>1$  is given. Suppose that  $r$ ,  $s$  and  $t$  are different positive integer numbers such that  $\{a^r\}=\{a^s\}=\{a^t\}$ . Prove that  $\{a^r\}=\{a^s\}=\{a^t\}=0$ .
solution_md:
This solution is credited to my friend's friend.

Without loss of generality, suppose  $\text{gcd}(r,s,t)=1$  and  $r > s > t$ .

Lemma 1.  $g(x)=\frac {x^r-x^s}{x^s-x^t}$  is a monotonically increasing function for  $x > 0$ .

Proof:  $x(x^s-x^t)^2 g'(x) = (r-s)x^{r+s} - (r-t)x^{r+t} + (s-t)x^{s+t} \geq 0$ . (The last inequality is by AM-GM)

Back to the original problem:

Let  $a^r-a^s-m=0$  and  $a^s-a^t-n=0$  where  $m,n$  positive integers. Use  $f(x)$  to denote the greatest common factor of  $x^r-x^s-m$  and  $x^s-x^t-n$ , which turns out to be a monic polynomial as well (The gcd of two monic polynomials with integer coefficients is also a monic polynomial with integer coefficients.) It easy to see  $f(a)=0$ . If we can prove that the degree of  $f(x)$  is exactly 1, then  $a$  must be an integer, concluding  $\{a^r\}=\{a^s\}=\{a^t\}=0$ .

Let's prove it by contradiction. If  $f(x)$  has another root  $b\neq a$  (which could be a complex number), it derives  $$ \begin{cases}
b^r-b^s-m=0 &\quad (1)
b^s-b^t-n=0 &\quad (2)
\end{cases} $$   $n\cdot(1)-m\cdot (2)$  gives  $nb^r+mb^t=(m+n)b^s$  which follows  $(m+n)|b|^s \leq n|b|^r +m|b|^t$ , that is   $$ \frac mn \leq \frac {|b|^r - |b|^s}{|b|^s-|b|^t} \quad (3) $$  On the other hand,  $2\leq m+n = a^r-a^t = b^r-b^t \leq |b|^r + |b|^t$ , showing  $|b|\geq 1$ . Moreover,  $a^r-a^t = b^r-b^t\geq |b|^r-|b|^t$ . Since  $x^r-x^t$  is monotonically increasing for  $x\geq0$ , it derives  $a \geq |b|$ . Therefore, it follows that  $$ \frac m n = \frac {a^r-a^s}{a^s-a^t}\geq \frac {|b|^r - |b|^s}{|b|^s-|b|^t} \quad (4) $$  according to Lemma 1.

Combining  $(3)$  and  $(4)$  holds the equality which means  $a\geq |b|$  also achieves equality, that is  $a=|b|$ .

If  $a=-b$ , it must be that  $r,s,t$  are all even numbers which contradicts our supposition of coprimality. If  $a = b$ , it also contradicts our hypothesis of different roots.

In summary,  $f(x)$  is a linear polynomial, which finishes this problem.

stem_md: Peer and Solveig are playing a game with  $n$  coins, all of which show  $M$  on one side and  $K$  on the opposite side. The coins are laid out in a row on the table. Peer and Solveig alternate taking turns. On his turn, Peer may turn over one or more coins, so long as he does not turn over two adjacent coins. On her turn, Solveig picks precisely two adjacent coins and turns them over. When the game begins, all the coins are showing  $M$ . Peer plays first, and he wins if all the coins show  $K$  simultaneously at any time. Find all  $n\geqslant 2$  for which Solveig can keep Peer from winning.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We claim Solvieg stops Peer for all  $n \ge 5$ .

First, we show Peer wins for  $2 \le n \le 4$ . For  $n = 2$ , Peer flips coin  $1$ , then Solvieg must flip coin  $1$  and  $2$ , and Peer wins by flipping coin  $1$ . For  $n = 3$ , Peer flips coin  $1$ , then to not lose Solvieg must flip coins  $1$  and  $2$ , and finally Peer flips coins  $1$  and  $3$ . For  $n = 4$ , Peer flips coins  $1$  and  $4$ . Note Solvieg cannot flip coins  $2$  and  $3$ , so WLOG say it's  $1$  and  $2$  flipped, then Peer wins by flipping  $1$  and  $3$ .

Now, we show Solvieg wins for  $n \ge 5$ . In particular, we show that at the start of any of Peer's turns, both coins  $2$  and  $3$  show  $M$ . This works, as Peer cannot flip both  $2$  and  $3$ , so at least one coin shows  $M$  after Peer's turn. Now, suppose it's Solvieg's turn. If both  $2$  and  $3$  show  $M$ , flip coins  $4$  and  $5$ . If  $2$  shows  $K$  and  $3$  shows  $M$ , flip coins  $1$  and  $2$ . If  $2$  shows  $M$  and  $3$  shows  $K$ , flip coins  $3$  and  $4$ . This also prevents the case from both  $2$  and  $3$  showing  $K$ , so we're done.</details>

stem_md:
In Duckville there is a perpetual trophy with the words “Best child of Duckville” engraved on it. Each inhabitant of Duckville has a non-empty list (which never changes) of other inhabitants of Duckville. Whoever receives the trophy
gets to keep it for one day, and then passes it on to someone on their list the next day. Gregers has previously received the trophy. It turns out that each time he does receive it, he is guaranteed to receive it again exactly  $2025$  days later (but perhaps earlier, as well). Hedvig received the trophy today. Determine all integers  $n>0$  for which we can be absolutely certain that she cannot receive the trophy again in  $n$  days, given the above information.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We claim that all integers  $n$  with  $\gcd(n,2025) = 1$  can never happen. We first show that all integers with  $\gcd(n,2025) = d > 1$  could happen. Take  $d$  people  $P_1,P_2,\dots,P_d$  (with  $P_1$  being Gregers), and only  $P_{i+1}$  being on  $P_i$ 's list (indices are mod  $d$ ). Then, Gregers gets the trophy exactly on the days which are multiple of  $d$ 's. As  $d \mid n,2025$ , Gregers can get it in  $n$  days.

Now, we show that if  $\gcd(n,2025) = 1$ , then Gregers cannot get it in  $n$  days. Assume to the contrary, and that we can reach Gregers in  $n$  days. Define a trophy cycle  $C$  as a set of people  $P_1,P_2,\dots,P_j$ , where  $P_1$  is Gregers, and the trophy is passed from  $P_i$  to  $P_{i+1}$  for all  $i$  (indices mod  $j$ ). Call  $C$  minimal if the only time Gregers appears in the cycle  $C$  is as  $P_1$ . Then, every trophy cycle is composed of minimal trophy cycles. Suppose the length of some minimal cycle is  $a$ , from cycle  $C$ .  Note  $a \ge 2$ , as nobody has themself on their list. Say that minimal trophy cycle  $C$  reaches Gregers in  $a$  days, and trophy cycle  $D$  reaches Gregers in  $n$  days. Consider first running cycle  $D$ , then cycle  $C$  repeatedly. Then, from day  $n$  and onwards, Gregers recieves the trophy only on day  $n, n+a, n+2a, \dots$ . However, Gregers recieves the trophy every  $2025$  days. So, for  $2025m \ge n$ , there exists an integer  $k$  such that  $2025m = n + ka$ . Similarly, there exists  $k' > k$  such tthat  $2025(m+1) = n + k' \cdot a$ , and so  $a(k' - k) = 2025$ . This implies that  $a \mid 2025$ , and so  $a \mid 2025m - ka = n$ . Then,  $\gcd(2025,n) \ge a > 1$ , a contradiction.</details>

stem_md: A teacher asks each of eleven pupils to write a positive integer with at most four digits, each on a separate yellow sticky note. Show that if all the numbers are different, the teacher can always submit two or more of the eleven stickers so that the average of the numbers on the selected notes are not an integer.
solution_md: Let us assume the opposite is true, that is, there exists a set \( A \) such that the average of any nonempty subset is an integer. **Claim:** All 11 numbers must be congruent modulo \( m \), where \( 1 \leq m < 11 \). Let \( a \) and \( b \) be any two numbers in \( A \). Consider a subset \( S \) of \( A \) of size \( m - 1 \) that excludes both \( a \) and \( b \). Such a subset exists since \( m < 11 \). Let \( X \) be the sum of the elements in \( S \). Since the average of any subset is an integer, it follows that the sum of numbers in \( S \cup \{a\} \) and \( S \cup \{b\} \) must be divisible by \( m \). That is, \[ X + a \equiv 0 \pmod{m} \quad \text{and} \quad X + b \equiv 0 \pmod{m} \implies a \equiv b \pmod{m} \] Applying this argument to all pairs \( a, b \) in \( A \), we conclude that all 11 numbers are congruent modulo \( m \). $\square$ Now, observe that this result immediately implies that all the numbers are congruent modulo \( 5, 7, 8, 9 \). By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, since these moduli are pairwise coprime, there exists a unique solution modulo $5 \cdot 7 \cdot 8 \cdot 9 = 2520$ . Since there are 11 numbers in \( A \), the largest must be at least $2520 \cdot 10 \geq 10^4$ . However, all numbers in \( A \) must be at most four digits long, leading to a contradiction! \(\blacksquare\)

stem_md: Which positive integers  $a$  have the property that \(n!-a\) is a perfect square for infinitely many positive integers \(n\)?
solution_md:
Claim:  $a$  is a perfect square. 
Proof: Suppose not. Let  $p$  be a prime with  $
u_p(a)$  odd. Setting  $n$  large enough (with  $n! - a$  being a square) so that  $p^{
u_p(a) + 1}$  divides  $n!$  gives that  $
u_p(n! - a) = 
u_p(a)$ , a contradiction.  $\square$ Now, let  $a =b^2$  and  $p$  be any  $3 \pmod 4$  prime greater than  $b$  (exists by Dirichlet). Choose  $n > p$  where  $n! - a$  is a square. Note that  $n! - a \equiv -b^2\pmod p$ , so  $-b^2$  is a QR modulo  $p$ , implying  $-1$  is a QR modulo  $p$  (as  $p$  doesn't divide  $b$ ), which is absurd since  $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ .

stem_md: Let \(ABC\) be a triangle. Let \(E,F\) be the feet of the altitudes from \(B,C\) respectively. Let \(P,Q\) be the projections of \(B,C\) onto line \(EF\). Show that \(PE=QF\).
solution_md: good one. Of course we have to use DDIT. Let  $H=BE\cap CF$  be the orthocenter,  $\infty$  be the point at infinity along the direction perpendicular to  $EF$ , and  $M$  the midpoint of  $EF$ . The projections from  $A$  and  $H$  to  $EF$  are  $A’$  and  $H’$ , respectively.  As  $AH$  is a diameter of  $(AEFH)$ ,  $M$  is also the midpoint of  $A’H’$ . stem_md: Find all polynomials \(P\) with real coefficients satisfying   $$ P(\frac{1}{1+x})=\frac{1}{1+P(x)} $$  for all real numbers \(x\neq -1\)
solution_md:
Consider  $Q(x)=(x+1)^{\deg P} P \left(\frac{1}{x+1} \right)$  and notice that if  $P$  was constant  $c$  then it satisfies that  $c^2+c-1=0$  and from quadratic formula  $c=\frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$  happen to work.
So if  $\deg P \ge 1$  then we have  $(P(x)+1)Q(x)=(x+1)^{\deg P}$  and this shows that  $\deg Q+\deg P=\deg P$  so  $\deg Q=0$  and this means that all coeffs but the leading one are all zero and thus  $P(x)=c \cdot x^n$  for some positive integer  $n$  and thus we have that  $c(c \cdot x^n+1)=(x+1)^n$  and checking constant coeff this gives  $c=1$  and thus  $x^n+1=(x+1)^n$  which is true only when  $n=1$  therefore only  $P(x)=x$  works on this case, and since all solutions have been found we are done :cool:.

stem_md: Determine the largest real number \(C\) such that   $$ \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{2y}+\frac{1}{3z}\geqslant C $$  for all real numbers \(x,y,z\neq 0\) satisfying the equation  $$ \frac{x}{yz}+\frac{4y}{xz}+\frac{9z}{xy}=24 $$
solution_md:
The answer is \(C=-2\).
Multiply both sides of the equality by \(xyz\). Then we have  $$ x^2+4y^2+9z^2=24xyz $$  let \(a=x, b=2y, c=3z\). Then the equation rewrites to  $$ a^2+b^2+c^2=4abc $$  Now note that  $$ \frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}\geqslant C $$  rewrites as  $$  bc+ca+ab\geqslant Cabc $$    $$ 2(bc+ca+ab)\geqslant 2Cabc $$    $$ a^2+b^2+c^2+2(bc+ca+ab)\geqslant (2C+4)abc $$    $$ (a+b+c)^2\geqslant (2C+4)abc $$   
Which is trivial if \(C=-2\). Equality holds at \(a,b,c=\frac{3}{2},-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{3}{4}\) or \(x,y,z=\frac{3}{2},-\frac{3}{8},-\frac{1}{4}\)

stem_md: Let  $ABCDE$  be a convex pentagon with  $AB=14,$   $BC=7,$   $CD=24,$   $DE=13,$   $EA=26,$  and  $\angle B=\angle E=60^{\circ}.$  For each point  $X$  in the plane, define  $f(X)=AX+BX+CX+DX+EX.$  The least possible value of  $f(X)$  can be expressed as  $m+n\sqrt{p},$  where  $m$  and  $n$  are positive integers and  $p$  is not divisible by the square of any prime. Find  $m+n+p.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>best problem on the test by far</summary>[asy]

import olympiad;
pair D=(0,0), C=(24,0), A=(39/2, 13sqrt(3)/2), E=(-13/2, 13sqrt(3)/2), B=(24+13/2, 3sqrt(3)/2);
draw(A--B--C--D--E--A);
draw(D--A--C);
label(" $A$ ", A, N);
label(" $B$ ", B, dir(1));
label(" $C$ ", C, SE);
label(" $D$ ", D, SW);
label(" $E$ ", E, W);
draw(rightanglemark(A,D,E,32));
draw(rightanglemark(A,C,B, 32));
[/asy]

Firstly, note that both  $DEA$  and  $CBA$  are similar to  $30$ - $60$ - $90$  triangles, so  $\angle EDA=\angle ACB=90^{\circ}.$  Thus,  $AD=13\sqrt{3}$  and  $AC=7\sqrt{3}.$ Motivated by wishful thinking, we now prove the following claim:

Claim: The foot of the perpendicular from  $A$  to  $BE$  is the fermat point of  $\triangle ACD.$ Proof:

[asy]
import olympiad;
pair D=(0,0), C=(24,0), A=(39/2, 13sqrt(3)/2), E=(-13/2, 13sqrt(3)/2), B=(24+13/2, 3sqrt(3)/2);
draw(A--B--C--D--E--A);
draw(D--A--C);
label(" $A$ ", A, N);
label(" $B$ ", B, dir(1));
label(" $C$ ", C, SE);
label(" $D$ ", D, SW);
label(" $E$ ", E, W);
draw(rightanglemark(A,D,E,32));
draw(rightanglemark(A,C,B, 32));
pair P=foot(A, B, E);
draw(B--E);
draw(D--P--A--P--C);
draw(rightanglemark(E,P, A, 32));
draw(rightanglemark(B,P, A, 32));
label(" $P$ ", P, dir(260));
[/asy]

Let  $P$  be the foot of the altitude from  $A$  to  $BE.$ Note that  $\angle ADE=90^{\circ}=\angle APE$  and  $\angle ACB=90^{\circ}=\angle APB,$  so  $APDE$  and  $APCB$  are cyclic.

Then,  $\angle APD=180^{\circ}-\angle AED=180^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=120^{\circ}$  and  $\angle APC=180^{\circ}-\angle ABC=180^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=120^{\circ},$  so  $P$  is the fermat point of  $ACD,$  as desired.

Now, for all  $X,$   $f(X)=(AX+CX+DX)+(BX+EX)\geq (AP+CP+DP)+(BP+EP)=f(P),$  so  $f(X)$  is minimized at  $P.$  We just need to evaluate  $f(P)$  now.

By the law of cosines,  $576=DC^2=AD^2+AC^2-2AD\cdot AC\cdot \cos(\angle CAD)=507+147-2\cdot 13\sqrt{3}\cdot 7\sqrt{3}\cdot \cos(\angle CAD)=654-6\cdot13\cdot7\cos(\angle CAD),$  so  $6\cdot 13\cdot 7\cos(\angle CAD)=654-576=78,$  so  $\cos(\angle CAD)=\dfrac{1}{7}.$  Now,  $\sin(\angle CAD)=\dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{7},$  so  $\cos(\angle BAE)=\cos(60^{\circ}+\angle CAD)=\cos(60^{\circ})\cos(\angle CAD)-\sin(60^{\circ})\sin(\angle CAD)=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot \dfrac{1}{7}-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{7}=\dfrac{1}{14}-\dfrac{12}{14}=-\dfrac{11}{14}.$  As such, by the law of cosines,  $BE^2=AE^2+AB^2-2\cdot AE\cdot AB\cdot\cos(\angle BAE)=676+196-2\cdot 26\cdot 14\cdot -\dfrac{11}{14}=872+52\cdot11=872+572=1444,$  so  $BE=38.$  

Let  $AP=a,$   $CP=b,$   $DP=c.$  It now suffices to find  $a+b+c.$ First, by the law of cosines on  $\triangle APC,$   $\triangle APD,$  and  $\triangle CPD,$  we have  $a^2+ab+b^2=147,$   $a^2+ac+c^2=507,$  and  $b^2+bc+c^2=576,$  so  $(a^2+ab+b^2)+(a^2+ac+c^2)+(b^2+bc+c^2)=2(a^2+b^2+c^2)+(ab+bc+ac)=147+507+576=1230.$  Also,  $[ACD]=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot AD\cdot AC\sin(\angle CAD)=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 13\sqrt{3}\cdot 7\sqrt{3}\cdot \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{7}=78\sqrt{3},$  and  $78\sqrt{3}=[ACD]=[APC]+[CPD]+[APD]=\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot ab\cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot bc\cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot ca\cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot ca=(ab+bc+ca)\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4},$  so  $ab+bc+ac=312.$  

Now,  $2(a+b+c)^2=2(a^2+b^2+c^2+2ab+2bc+2ac)=(2(a^2+b^2+c^2)+(ab+bc+ac))+3(ab+bc+ac)=1230+3\cdot 312=1230+936=2166,$  so  $(a+b+c)^2=1083=3\cdot361.$  

As such,  $a+b+c=19\sqrt{3},$  so  $f(P)=(BP+EP)+(AP+CP+DP)=BE+(a+b+c)=38+19\sqrt{3},$  and  $m+n+p=38+19+3=\boxed{060}.$</details>

For the former, we need  $X$  to lie on  $BE$ , and for the latter,  $X$  must be the format point of  $\triangle ACD$ , so we need to show that the format point  $X$  does indeed lie on  $BE$ .

Draw circles  $(AE)$  and  $(AB)$  and consider their intersection point  $X'$ . By cyclic quad angle properties, we immediately have  $\angle AX'D = \angle AX'C = 120^\circ$ , so  $X' = X$  is the format point. However, we also have  $\angle EXA + \angle AXB = 90 + 90 = 180^\circ$ , so  $X$  is on  $EB$ !

Now just do some Lock of Cosign bashing to find  $BX + EX  = BE = 38$ , which also gives us the length of  $AX$ . Some usage of Tolomy's Theorem on  $(AE)$  and  $(AB)$  gives us  $CX$  and  $DX$ , and adding  $AX+CX+DX$  yields  $19\sqrt3$ . Thus, our final answer is  $\boxed{38+19\sqrt3}$  (yielding  $60$  for the answer extraction)</details>

By Ptolemy's Inequality on  $ABCX$  and  $AXDE$ ,  $$ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}AX + \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}CX \geq BX, $$   and   $$ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}AX + \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}DX \geq EX. $$  Adding,  $BX + EX \leq \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}(AX + CX + DX)$ , so  $f(X) \leq \frac{\sqrt{3}+2}{\sqrt{3}}(AX+CX+DX)$ , with equality iff the aforementioned quadrilaterals are cyclic -- but, by  $120^{\circ}$  angles, this means  $X$  is the Fermat point of  $\triangle{ACD}$ . Since that point minimizes  $AX + CX + DX$ , it must be the minimum.

Now compute the sum of the lengths of the distances to the Fermat point using Law of Cosines and sine area. This gives  $38 + 19\sqrt{3} \implies \boxed{060}$ .

Rephrase the problem as follows.

Let  $\triangle ACD$  be a triangle with  $AC=7\sqrt{3}$ ,  $AD=13\sqrt{3}$ , and  $CD=24$ . Let  $B$  be such that  $\angle CBA=60$  and  $\angle BCA=90$ , and define  $E$  similarly.

Let  $X_{13}$  denote the Fermat point of  $\triangle ACD$ . This point satisfies  $\angle CX_{13}D=\angle AX_{13}C=\angle AX_{13}D=120$ , and it is well known that it minimizes  $AX+CX+DX$  (proof: smoothing). The main claim is the following.

Claim:  $X_{13}$  lies on  $BE$ , and thus also minimizes  $BX+XE$ . Note that  $AX_{13}BC$  and  $AX_{13}DE$  are cyclic due to the  $60$  and  $120$  angles. Thus,  $$ \angle AX_{13}B=\angle ACB=90 $$  and similarly for  $\angle AX_{13}E$  so  $B,X_{13},E$  are collinear.

Let  $P$  be the point on the other side of  $CD$  as  $A$  such that  $PCD$  is equilateral. Let   $$ AX_{13}=a,CX_{13}=c,DX_{13}=d. $$  However, by Ptolemy on  $CPDX_{13}$ ,  $$ c+d=X_{13}P \rightarrow a+c+d=AP. $$  By Ptolemy on  $AX_{13}CB$  and  $AX_{13}DE$ ,  $$ BX_{13}+EX_{13}=\frac{7a+14c}{7\sqrt{3}}+\frac{13a+26d}{13\sqrt{3}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}(a+c+d), $$  which means the answer is   $$ (a+c+d)(1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}). $$  We know that  $a+c+d=AP$ , so coordinate bash to find that  $AP=19\sqrt{3}$ , so the answer is  ${38+19\sqrt{3}}$ .

Let  $X$  be the Fermat point of  $ACD$ . Then,  $\angle AXE+\angle AXB=\angle ADE+\angle ACB=180^\circ$ , so  $X$  lies on  $BE$ . Therefore, we need to find  $AX+CX+DX+BE$ . Since  $\angle ADC=30^\circ$ , the point  $A'$  such that  $A'CD$  is an equilateral triangle satisfies  $\angle ADA'=90^\circ$ , so  $AX+CX+DX=AA'=\sqrt{(13\sqrt3)^2+24^2}=19\sqrt3$ . By Ptolemy,  $XE\sqrt3=AX+2DX$  and  $XB\sqrt3=AX+2CX$ , so  $BE\sqrt3=2(AX+CX+DX)=38\sqrt3$ , implying  $BE=38$ . Therefore, the minimum is  $\boxed{38+19\sqrt3}$ .

Some intuition here - in general, finding the minimum total distance to a set of (5 or more) points in general position is very difficult. so the only way really the problem can be doable is if five lengths can be split into groups where some point minimizes each group at the same time.

This is what motivated the solution for me in test, {A,C,D} {B,E} is probably the most natural partition which then leads you to guess that the Fermat point lies on BE. Once you guess this, it is in fact easy to prove by cyclic quads and two perpendiculars.

Note that  $\triangle ACB$  and  $\triangle ADE$  are both 30-60-90 triangles, and  $AC = 7\sqrt{3}$  and  $AD = 13\sqrt{3}$ .

Let  $F$  be the fermat point of  $\triangle ACD$ . Then  $AX + CX + DX$  is minimized for  $X = F$ . Moreover, since  $\angle AXD = \angle AXC = 120^{\circ}$ , we find that  $ABFC$  and  $AEDF$  are cyclic. Thus,  $90^{\circ} = \angle ACB = \angle AFB = \angle ADE = \angle AFE$ , so  $F$  lies on  $\overline{BE}$  and thus  $f(X)$  is minimized for  $X = F$ .

Now, let  $a = AF, c = CF$ , and  $d = DF$ . By the law of cosines on  $\triangle AFC$ ,  $\triangle AFD$ , and  $\triangle CFD$ , we find that
\begin{align*}
a^2 + c^2 + ac &= 147 
c^2 + d^2 + cd &= 576 
d^2 + a^2 + da &= 507.
\end{align*}
Summing all three equations yields  $2(a^2 + c^2 + d^2) + ac + cd + da = 1230$ . Additionally, from computing the area of  $\triangle ACD$  in two ways, we find that  $\tfrac{ac\sqrt{3} + cd\sqrt{3} + da\sqrt{3}}{4} = 78\sqrt{3}$ , so  $ac + cd + da = 312$ . We then find that  $(a + b + c)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + 2ac + 2cd + 2da = 1083$ , so  $a + b + c = 19\sqrt{3}$ .

Now, we find  $BF + DF$ . From Ptolemy's theorem on  $ABCF$ , we have  $BF \cdot 7\sqrt{3} = 7a + 14c$ , so  $BF\sqrt{3} = a + 2c$ . Similarly,  $DF\sqrt{3} = a + 2b$ , so  $BF + DF = \tfrac{2a + 2b + 2c}{\sqrt{3}} = 38$ . Thus,  $f(F) = 38 + 19\sqrt{3} \implies \boxed{060}$ .

stem_md: The set of points in  $3$ -dimensional coordinate space that lie in the plane  $x+y+z=75$  whose coordinates satisfy the inequalities   $$ x-yz<y-zx<z-xy $$  forms three disjoint convex regions. Exactly one of those regions has finite area. The area of this finite region can be expressed in the form  $a\sqrt{b},$  where  $a$  and  $b$  are positive integers and  $b$  is not divisible by the square of any prime. Find  $a+b.$
solution_md:
Direct bash

Notice we have  $z = 75 - x - y$ . From the first inequality, we have
\begin{align*}
	x - yz < y - zx &\implies x - y(75 - x - y) < y - (75 - x - y)x 
    &\implies x - 75y + xy + y^2 < y - 75x + x^2 + xy 
    &\implies 76x - 76y + y^2 - x^2 < 0 
    &\implies (x - y)(76 - x - y) < 0
\end{align*}
This means that either  $x < y$  and  $x + y < 76$  or  $x > y$  and  $x + y > 76$ . From the second inequality, we have
\begin{align*}
	y - zx < z - xy &\implies y - (75 - x - y)x < 75 - x - y - xy 
    &\implies y - 75x + x^2 + xy < 75 - x - y - xy 
    &\implies 2y + 2xy + x^2 - 74x - 75 < 0 
    &\implies (x + 1)(2y + x - 75) < 0
\end{align*}
This means we either have  $x < -1$  and  $2y + x > 75$  or  $x > -1$  and  $2y + x < 75$ . Now we can graph these on the  $xy$ -plane. It turns out the region is bounded by  $(-1, -1)$ ,  $(-1, 38)$ , and  $(25, 25)$ . Thus, our desired region is a triangle with vertices  $A(-1, -1, 77)$ ,  $B(-1, 38, 38)$ , and  $C(25, 25, 25)$ .

Notice that  $AB = 39\sqrt2$ ,  $AC = 26\sqrt6$ , and  $BC = 13\sqrt6$ . This is a right triangle with a right angle at  $B$ . The answer is thus \[\frac12 \cdot 13\sqrt6 \cdot 39\sqrt2 = 507\sqrt3 \implies \boxed{510}.\]

stem_md: Let  $k$  be a real number such that the system \begin{align*} &|25+20i-z|=5 &|z-4-k|=|z-3i-k|  \end{align*} has exactly one complex solution  $z.$  The sum of all possible values of  $k$  can be written as  $\dfrac{m}{n},$  where  $m$  and  $n$  are relatively prime positive integers. Find  $m+n.$  Here  $i=\sqrt{-1}.$
solution_md:
Let $k$ be a real number such that the system \begin{align*} |25+20i-z|&=5 |z-4-k|&=|z-3i-k| \end{align*} has exactly one complex solution $z.$ The sum of all possible values of $k$ can be written as $\dfrac{m}{n},$ where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m+n.$ Here $i=\sqrt{-1}.$
Write $z=x+yi$ . We have: $$ 5^2=|(25-x)+(20-y)i|^2=(25-x)^2+(20-y)^2=(x-25)^2+(y-20)^2 $$ and $$ |(x-4-k)+yi|^2=|(x-k)+(y-3)i|^2\Rightarrow(x-4-k)^2+y^2=(x-k)^2+(y-3)^2. $$ Rearranging the second equation, we have $y=\frac43x-\frac{8k+7}6$ . -8k-7)/6 The equation $(x-25)^2+(y-20)^2=5^2$ can be interpreted geometrically to mean that $(x,y)$ lies on a circle in the Cartesian plane with center $(25,20)$ and radius $5$ , while the equation $y=\frac43x-\frac43k-\frac76$ can be interpreted to mean that $(x,y)$ lies on a line in the Cartesian plane with slope $\frac43$ and a height that is based on $k$ . For this system to have exactly one solution, the line must intersect the circle at exactly one point, i.e. the line must be tangent to the circle.**Solution 1:** The radius that intersects the point of tangency must then be perpendicular to the line $y=\frac43x-\frac43k-\frac76$ , so it must have slope $-\frac34$ . Since the radius goes through the center of the circle, it lies on $y=-\frac34x+\frac{155}4$ . The intersection of the line $y=-\frac34x+\frac{155}4$ with the circle yields the two possible points of tangency. To find these, we substitute into the equation of the circle: \begin{align*} (x-25)^2+\left(-\frac34x+\frac{155}4-20\right)^2&=25 (4x-100)^2+(-3x+75)^2&=400 16x^2-800x+10000+9x^2-450x+5625&=400 x^2-50x+609&=0 x&=25\pm4 y&=-\frac34x+\frac{155}4=20\mp3 \end{align*} Therefore, after rearranging $y=\frac43x-\frac43k-\frac76$ into $k=x-\frac34y-\frac78$ , we get that $k$ is either: $$ k=29-\frac34\cdot17-\frac78=\frac{123}8 $$ or $$ k=21-\frac34\cdot23-\frac78=\frac{23}8 $$ so the sum of these is $\frac{146}8=\frac{73}4\Rightarrow\boxed{077}$ .
alternate finishFrom $x^2-50x+609=0$ we know that the sum of possibilities for $x$ is $50$ . Then using $y=-\frac34x+\frac{155}4$ , the sum of possibilities for $y$ is $-\frac34\cdot50+\frac{155}4\cdot2=40$ (multiplying the constant term by $2$ since there are two possibilities here). Then since $k=x-\frac34y-\frac78$ the sum of possibilities for $k$ is $50-\frac34\cdot40-\frac78\cdot2=\frac{73}4$ .

Note that the midpoint of these is the center of the circle, $(25,20)$ , so $\left(\frac{x_1+y_1}2,\frac{x_2+y_2}2\right)=(25,20)$ , that is, $x_1+x_2=50$ and $y_1+y_2=40$ . Then the sum of the possible values for $k$ will be: \begin{align*} k_1+k_2&=x_1-\frac34y_1-\frac78+x_2-\frac34y_2-\frac78 &=(x_1+x_2)-\frac34(y_1+y_2)-\frac74 &=\frac{73}4\Rightarrow\boxed{077} \end{align*}

<details><summary>Clean solution that requires next to no insight</summary>First, note that \( z \) lies on the circle centered at \( 25+20i \) with radius \( 5 \) in the complex plane.

We then note that \( z - 4 - k \) lies on another circle of radius 5 centered at \( 21 - k + 20i \), and \( z - 3i - k \) lies on a different circle of the same radius centered at \( 25 - k + 17i \).

Let   $$ 25+20i - z = a+bi, $$   
where   $$ a = 5\cos\theta, \quad b = 5\sin\theta. $$  Then we must have  $$ (21-k-a)^2 + (20-b)^2 = (25-k-a)^2 + (17-b)^2. $$  Applying difference of squares gives us   $$ 4(46 - 2(a+k)) = 3(37 - 2b). $$  Expanding, we get:  $$ 184 - 8a - 8k = 111 - 6b $$  which simplifies to  $$ 73 - 8k = 8a - 6b. $$  Thus,   $$ 73 - 8k = 40\cos\theta - 30\sin\theta. $$  Clearly, the only \( k \) that gives only one possible value of \(\theta\) is when \( 40\cos\theta - 30\sin\theta \) is maximized or minimized, which by Cauchy-Schwarz is \( \pm 50 \).

Computing, we have   $$ 73 - 8k = 50 \Rightarrow k = \frac{23}{8}, $$   
and   $$ 73 - 8k = -50 \Rightarrow k = \frac{123}{8}. $$  Summing these two possible values gives   $$ \frac{146}{8} = \frac{73}{4}, $$   
giving us a final answer of   $$ \boxed{077}. $$</details>

Bashing time

Let  $z = a + bi$ . Then our equations become

\[(25 - a)^2 + (20 - b)^2 = 25\]
\[(a - 4 - k)^2 + b^2 = (a - k)^2 + (b - 3)^2\]

We expand out the second equation:

\[a^2 + 16 + k^2 - 8a - 2ak + 8k + b^2 = a^2 - 2ak + k^2 + b^2 - 6b + 9\]
\[16 - 8a  + 8k = -6b + 9\]
\[a = \frac{8k + 7 + 6b}{8}\]

We now plug this into the first equation:

\[\left(25 - \frac{8k + 7 + 6b}{8}\right)^2 + (20 - b)^2 = 25\]
\[\left(\frac{193}{8} - k - \frac{3}{4}b\right)^2 + (20 - b)^2 = 25\]

Let  $v = \frac{193}{8} - k$  to simplify calculations. 

\[\left(v - \frac{3}{4}b\right)^2 + (20 - b)^2 = 25\]
\[v^2 - \frac{3}{2}bv + \frac{9}{16}b^2 + 400 - 40b + b^2 = 25\]
\[\frac{25}{16}b^2 - b\left(\frac{3}{2}v + 40\right) + (v^2 + 375)\]

In order for there to be exactly one solution for  $z$ , the discriminant of this quadratic must be  $0$ :

\[\left(\frac{3}{2}v + 40\right)^2 - 4\left(\frac{25}{16}\right)\left(v^2 + 375\right) = 0\]

 Since we are asked for the sum of all  $k$ , we just use Vieta's relations on this quadratic.

\[\frac{9}{4}v^2 + 120v + 1600 - \frac{25}{4}v^2 - 4\left(\frac{25}{16}\right)\left(375\right) = 0\]
\[-4v^2 + 120v + c = 0\]

We can ignore the constant term because it's irrelevant to the sum of the roots. Since we have  $v_1 + v_2 = 30$ , we conclude that

\[2\left(\frac{193}{8}\right) - (k_1 + k_2) = 30\]
\[k_1 + k_2 = \frac{73}{4}\]

So the answer is  $73 + 4 = \boxed{77}$ .

Algebraic non-bash solution

The first equation implies  $$ z-k=(25-5\cos(a)-k)+(20-5\sin(a))i $$  for some real  $a.$  Then, let  $z-k=x+yi.$  By the second equation,  $$ (x-4)^2+y^2=x^2+(y-3)^2 $$  which simplifies to  $$ 8x=6y+7. $$  Plugging in the real parts for  $x$  and  $y,$  we have  $$ 200-40\cos(a)-8k=127+7-30\sin(a). $$  This means that  $$ 73-8k=40\cos(a)-30\sin(a). $$  Dividing both sides by  $50,$  we have  $$ \dfrac{73-8k}{50}=\dfrac{4}{5}\cos(a)-\dfrac{3}{5}\sin(a). $$  Let  $m$  be an angle such that  $\cos(m)=\frac{4}{5}$  and  $\sin(m)=\frac{3}{5}.$  Recognizing the cosine angle addition formula, we have  $$ \dfrac{73-8k}{50}=\cos(a+m). $$  This has one solution for  $a$  precisely when  $$ \dfrac{73-8k}{50}=\pm 1, $$  and simple algebra gets the answer  $$ k=\dfrac{73\pm 50}{8}\implies \dfrac{73-50+73+50}{8}=\dfrac{73}{4}\implies\boxed{077}. $$

stem_md: Find the sum of all integer bases  $b>9$  for which  $17_b$  is a divisor of  $97_b.$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>First, note that
\begin{align*}
\frac{9b+7}{b+7} &= \frac{9b+63}{b+7} - \frac{56}{b+7} 
&= 9 - \frac{56}{b+7},
\end{align*}

stem_md: The parabola with equation  $y = x^2 - 4$  is rotated  $60^\circ$  counterclockwise around the origin. The unique point in the fourth quadrant where the original parabola and its image intersect has  $y$ -coordinate  $\frac{a - \sqrt{b}}{c}$ , where  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$  are positive integers, and  $a$  and  $c$  are relatively prime. Find  $a + b + c$ .
solution_md:
Observe the parabolas intersect in four points $A$ , $B$ , $C$ , $D$ . Let $O$ be the rotation point.**Claim.** The conic through $O$ , $A$ , $B$ , $C$ , and $D$ is a rectangular hyperbola with asymptotes being the angle bisectors of the directrices or the corresponding two perpendicular lines. *Proof.* Left as an exercise to the reader. Particularly since $O$ lies on the axis of symmetry one can verify that two of the intersection points and $O$ are collinear, so the conic degenerates into two lines. The line that we care about is $y = -\sqrt{3}x$ , and so \[ x^2 + x\sqrt{3} - 4 = 0 \implies x = \frac{-\sqrt{3} \pm \sqrt{19}}{2} \implies y = \frac{3 \pm \sqrt{57}}{2}. \] Taking the negative gives $3 + 57 + 2 = \boxed{62}$ .
In fact, the "rectangular hyperbola" in question is always the union of two perpendicular lines because of the main idea of the original problem (two of the intersection points are collinear with $O$ ).

You want the point of intersection of the curves  $r\sin \theta = r^2\cos^2\theta - 4$  and  $r\sin (\theta - 60^\circ) = r^2\cos^2(\theta - 60^\circ) - 4$  in  $\theta \in [0, -90^\circ] $ . It's easy to see that when  $\pm \theta \equiv \theta - 60^\circ\pmod {180^\circ}$  both of these equations are satisfied, at which point we see  $\theta\equiv -60^\circ\pmod{90^\circ}$  works, so  $\theta = -60^\circ$  works, and this must correspond to the unique point in question. For this value of  $\theta$ , we have
\[ r(-\sqrt{3}/2) = r^2(1/4) - 4\implies r^2 + 2\sqrt{3}r - 16 = 0\implies r = \sqrt{19} - \sqrt{3}.\]
Finally, extract  $r\sin\theta = (\sqrt{19}-\sqrt{3})(-\sqrt{3}/2) = \tfrac{1}{2}(3 - \sqrt{57})\to \boxed{62}$ .

Thus, we want \[- \frac{\sqrt3}{2} x + \frac12 y = \left(\frac12 x + \frac{\sqrt3}{2} y\right)^2 - 4.\]
Substituting  $y = x^2 - 4$  gives \[-\frac{\sqrt3}{2} x + \frac12 (x^2 - 4) = \left(\frac12 x + \frac{\sqrt3}{2} (x^2 - 4)\right)^2 - 4.\]

Substituting  $x = z\sqrt3$  to clear square roots gives \[27z^4 + 18z^3 - 75z^2 - 18z + 40 = 0.\]
This factors as \[(3z^2 + 3z - 4)(9z^2 - 3z - 10) = 0.\]

solution_md:
The twelve letters $A$ , $B$ , $C$ , $D$ , $E$ , $F$ , $G$ , $H$ , $I$ , $J$ , $K$ , and $L$ are randomly grouped into six pairs of letters. The two letters in each pair are placed next to each other in alphabetical order to form six two-letter words, and then those six words are listed alphabetically. For example, a possible result is $AB$ , $CJ$ , $DG$ , $EK$ , $FL$ , $HI$ . The probability that the last word listed contains $G$ is $\frac mn$ , where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m+n$ .
We take cases based on whether $G$ is the first letter or the last letter in the last word, using notation such as $C\_$ in places to denote a letter pair that begins with $C$ , and $\_C$ to denote a letter pair that ends in $C$ , similarly for other letters. The general approach is to first figure out how to distribute $A,B,C,D,E,F$ , then only afterwards distribute $H,I,J,K,L$ combinatorially.**Case 1.** If $G$ is the first letter in the last word, then we claim that the first letters of the pairs must be $A,B,C,D,E,F$ in this order. To this end, we can first show that the first letters of the pairs must be $A,B,C,D,E,F$ in some order because if there is some pair whose first letter isn't $A,B,C,D,E,$ or $F$ , it must be $H$ or later in the alphabet. But this letter must occur as the first letter in a pair that appears before $\_G$ in the list, which means that the list is unsorted, hence impossible. Then, to satisfy the alphabetical sorting conditions, the list of letter pairs must be of the form: $$ A\_,B\_,C\_,D\_,E\_,FG. $$ The blanks here can be filled in with $H,I,J,K,L$ in any order, so we have $5!$ possibilities.**Case 2.** Now if $G$ is the first letter in the last word, we claim that two of $A,B,C,D,E,F$ must be in a letter pair together. This is true simply by PHP, where none of $A,B,C,D,E,F$ can fit into the letter pair $G\_$ because it would make this pair unsorted, so we must have these six letters be distributed over the first five letter pairs in the list. From this, there are $\binom62$ ways to choose which $2$ of $A,B,C,D,E,F$ form a letter pair with each other. Once this is chosen, there is a unique way to distribute the other $4$ letters out of $A,B,C,D,E,F$ in alphabetical order among the remaining four letter pairs that we haven't allocated yet. Such a list might look something like this: $$ A\_,B\_,CE,D\_,F\_,G\_. $$ No matter which of the $\binom62$ pairs we chose, there will be $5!$ ways to distribute $H,I,J,K,L$ among the remaining blanks, leaving $\binom625!$ possibilities for this case. In all, the number of ways to distribute the letters without requiring that the last word contain $G$ is: $$ \frac1{6!}\prod_{i=1}^6\binom{2i}2=10395, $$ where the $\frac1{6!}$ term makes sure we don't overcount with respect to reorderings of the six pairs of letters. The number of ways to distribute the letters with the requirement is $5!$ from our first case plus $\binom625!$ which is $1920$ , so our answer is $\frac{1920}{10395}=\frac{128}{693}\Rightarrow\boxed{821}$ .

stem_md: Alex divides a disk into four quadrants with two perpendicular diameters intersecting at the center of the disk. He draws  $25$  more lines segments through the disk, drawing each segment by selecting two points at random on the perimeter of the disk in different quadrants and connecting these two points. Find the expected number of regions into which these  $27$  line segments divide the disk.
solution_md:
<details><summary>lol</summary>Ignore the fact that the segments must have endpoints in different quadrants.

The key is to observe that the number of regions the disk is split into is equal to  $K+S+1,$  where  $K$  denotes the number of intersections† and  $S$  denotes the number of segments.

<details><summary>my goofy in-contest way to find the probability that two lines intersect</summary>If we pick two line segments on a circle at random, there is a  $\frac{1}{16}$  chance that both of them are within one qudrant, a  $\frac{6}{16}$  chance that only one of them is, and a  $\frac{9}{16}$  chance that both of them have endpoints on two different quadrants (what we want). 
If both of them are contained in one quadrant (not necessarily the same one), we consider whether they are contained in the same quadrant or not. There is a  $\frac{1}{64} $  chance that they are, and in that case, there is a  $\frac{1}{3}$  chance that they intersect. There is a  $\frac{3}{64}$  chance that they aren't, and there is a  $0$  chance that they intersect in this case.
If only one of them is, we look at the line that has endpoints in different quadrants. Note that (assuming the one line segment in one quadrant is fixed) there is a  $\frac{1}{2}$  chance that the second line has endpoints in quadrants that doesn't include the one the first line is in, and a  $\frac{1}{2}$  chance that it does. If it doesn't, we can see that there is a  $0$  chance that they intersect. If it does, it basically turns into finding the probability that a random point is in between two other random points on a line segment. We do some goofy symmetry thing to get the probability as  $\frac{1}{3}$ .
Overall, we know that the probability that two random line segments intersect is  $\frac{1}{3}$ . If we let the probability that they intersect if both of them have endpoints in different quadrants be  $p$ , we have
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{64}\cdot\frac{1}{3}+\frac{3}{16}\cdot\frac{1}{3}+\frac{9}{16}p.
\end{align*}
Solving gives  $p=\frac{17}{36}.$</details>

To calculate the expected number of intersection points between two line segments: There are four endpoints for the two line segments, with at most two endpoints in any single quadrant. Let the four endpoints be arranged clockwise as A, B, C, D. We consider two scenarios:

A, B, C, D are in different quadrants: The probability of this scenario is 1/6. Under this condition, the two line segments can be paired in three ways: AB and CD; AC and BD; AD and BC. Among these, only the second pairing (AC and BD) results in an intersection. Thus, the probability of an intersection in this scenario is 1/3, making the total probability for this scenario (1/3) * (1/6) = 1/18.

Two endpoints are in the same quadrant: Without loss of generality, assume A and B are in the same quadrant. In this case, the line segments can be paired in two ways: AC and BD; AD and BC. (Since A and B are in the same quadrant, AB cannot form a line segment, and C and D cannot be in the same quadrant as A and B, ensuring that AC, BD, AD, and BC are valid line segments.) Only the first pairing (AC and BD) results in an intersection, with a probability of 1/2. The total probability for this scenario is (1/2) * (5/6) = 5/12.

Combining both scenarios, the overall probability of an intersection is 1/18 + 5/12 = 17/36.

stem_md: Let  $N$  denote the numbers of ordered triples of positive integers  $(a, b, c)$  such that  $a, b, c \le 3^6$  and  $a^3 + b^3 + c^3$  is a multiple of  $3^7$ . Find the remainder when  $N$  is divided by  $1000$ .
solution_md:
By mod  $9$ ,  $3$  divides at least one of  $a,b,c$ , and not exactly two of  $a,b,c$ . 

Claim: For any positive integer  $n$ , the number of ordered pairs positive integers  $(x,y,z)$  with  $3^{n+1} \mid x^3 + y^3 + z^3$  but  $1 \le x,y,z \le 3^n$  is  $2 \cdot 3^{2n-1}$ . 
Proof: WLOG  $3 \mid x$ , and multiply by  $3$  at the end. 
Subclaim: Over positive integers  $1 \le t \le 3^n$  with  $3\nmid t$ ,  $t^3$  takes every cubic residue modulo  $3^{n+1}$  that isn't a multiple of  $3$  exactly once. 
Proof. Note that  $t^3 \equiv (t + 3^n)^3 \pmod{3^{n+1}}$  by binomial expansion (so clearly they cover all cubic residues modulo  $3^{n+1}$ ), so it suffices to show that  $t^3$  is injective modulo  $3^{n+1}$  over  $1 \le t \le 3^n$  with  $3\nmid t$ .  

If  $s^3 \equiv t^3 \pmod{3^{n+1}}$  for  $1 \le s,t \le 3^n$ , then by LTE,  $3^n \mid s-t$ , so  $s=t$ .  $\blacksquare$ This also implies that every positive integer less than  $3^{n+1}$  that is  $-1$  or  $1$  modulo  $9$  is a cubic residue modulo  $3^{n+1}$ .  

In this way, we get that for any choice of  $y$  that isn't a multiple of  $3$ , there is exactly one valid choice of  $z$ . There are  $3^{n-1}$  ways to choose  $x$ ,  $2 \cdot 3^{n-1}$  ways to choose  $y$ , and  $1$  way to choose  $z$ .  

So the total for this case is  $3 \cdot 3^{n-1} \cdot 2 \cdot 3^{n-1} = 2\cdot 3^{2n-1}$ .  $\square$ Case 1:  $3$  divides exactly one of  $a,b,c$ .  
Then the number of ways is  $2 \cdot 3^{11}$  by the claim.  


Case 2:  $3$  divides all of  $a,b,c$  
Let  $a_1 = \frac a3, b_1 = \frac b3, c_1 = \frac c3$ . The condition is equivalent to  $3^4 \mid a_1^3 + b_1^3 + c_1^3$  but  $1 \le a_1, b_1, c_1\le 3^5$ . Since  $x^3 \equiv (x + 3^3)^3 \pmod{3^4}$  by binomial expansion, we can assume  $a_1, b_1, c_1$  are at most  $3^3$  and then multiply by  $9^3 = 729$ .  

Subcase 2.1:  $3$  doesn't divide all of  $a_1, b_1, c_1$ .  
The total number of ways is just  $2 \cdot 3^5 = 486$ .  

Subcase 2.2:  $3$  divides all of  $a_1, b_1, c_1$ .  
Let  $a_2 = \frac{a_1}{3}$ ,  $b_2 = \frac{b_1}{3}$ , and  $c_2 = \frac{c_1}{3}$ . The condition is equivalent to  $3 \mid a_2 + b_2 + c_2$ , but  $1 \le a_2, b_2, c_2 \le 9$ . Since for any choice of  $a_2, b_2$ , there are three values of  $c_2$  that work, the total number of ways for this case is just  $9^2 \cdot 3 = 243$ .  

The total value for case  $2$  thus is just  $(486 + 243) \cdot 729 = 3^{12}$ .  


Thus, the answer is \[2 \cdot 3^{11} + 3^{12} = 5 \cdot 3^{11} = 885\boxed{735}\]

Here's a nice recursive approach.

Let  $n$  be a positive integer and let  $(a,b,c) \in (\mathbb Z/(3^{n - 1}))^3$  satisfy  $a^3 + b^3 + c^3 \equiv 0 \pmod{3^n}$ . We say  $(a,b,c)$  is *$n$ -skibidi* if  $3$  divides  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $c$ , and *$n$ -gyatt* otherwise. Let  $f(n)$  and  $g(n)$  be the number of  $n$ -skibidi and  $n$ -gyatt ordered triples, respectively. We want  $f(7) + g(7)$ .

Let  $(a_2,b_2,c_2)$  be a  $n$ -skibidi or  $n$ -gyatt triple for some  $n \ge 2$ . Observe that  $(a_2,b_2,c_2)$  corresponds to the  $9^3$   $(n + 3)$ -skibidi triples
\[(3^na_1 + 3a_2,3^nb_1 + 3b_2,3^nc_1 + 3c_2) \in (\mathbb Z/(3^{n + 2}))^3\]
for  $0 \le a_1,b_1,c_1 < 3^2$ . Therefore, for  $n \ge 2$ ,  $f(n + 3) = 9^3(f(n) + g(n))$ .

Now let  $(a_2,b_2,c_2)$  be  $n$ -gyatt for some  $n \ge 2$ . The binomial theorem gives the identity
\[(3^{n - 1}a_1 + a_2)^3 + (3^{n - 1}b_1 + b_2)^3 + (3^{n - 1}c_1 + c_2)^3 \equiv 3^n(a_1a_2^2 + b_1b_2^2 + c_1c_2^3) + (a_2^3 + b_2^3 + c_2^3) \pmod{3^{n + 1}}. \qquad (\bigstar)\]
for  $n \ge 2$ , which allows us to ``lift'' an  $n$ -gyatt triple  $(a_2,b_2,c_2) \in (\mathbb Z/(3^{n - 1}))^3$  to the  $(n + 1)$ -gyatt triples
\[(3^{n - 1}a_1 + a_2,3^{n - 1}b_1 + b_2,3^{n - 1}c_1 + c_2) \in (\mathbb Z/(3^n))^3.\]
Now observe that there are exactly nine choices of  $(a_1,b_1,c_1)$  for each  $n$ -gyatt  $(a_2,b_2,c_2)$  that makes the right side of  $(\bigstar)$  zero, so  $g(n + 1) = 9g(n)$  for  $n \ge 2$ .

The rest is computation. It's not hard to compute  $g(2) = 6$  and  $f(4) = 3^5$ , so
\begin{align*}
    f(7) + g(7) &= 9^3(f(4) + g(4)) + 9^5g(2) 
    &= 9^3(f(4) + 9^2g(2)) + 9^5g(2) 
    &= 9^3(3^5 + 9^2 \cdot 6) + 9^5 \cdot 6 
    &\equiv 735 \pmod{1000}.
\end{align*}

We are given that
\[
N = \#\{(a,b,c) \in [1,3^6]^3 : 3^7 \mid (a^3+b^3+c^3)\},
\]
and we wish to compute the remainder when \(N\) is divided by 1000.

Since \(3^6=729\) and \(3^7=2187\), the variables \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) range over the set \(\{1,2,\dots,729\}\).

A standard approach is to use exponential sums to detect the divisibility condition. For any integer \(n\) we have the identity
\[
\frac{1}{3^7}\sum_{t=0}^{3^7-1} e^{\frac{2\pi i\,t\,n}{3^7}} =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } 3^7\mid n,[1mm]
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
Thus, we can write
\[
N = \frac{1}{3^7}\sum_{t=0}^{3^7-1} \sum_{a=1}^{3^6} e^{\frac{2\pi i\,t\,a^3}{3^7}} \sum_{b=1}^{3^6} e^{\frac{2\pi i\,t\,b^3}{3^7}} \sum_{c=1}^{3^6} e^{\frac{2\pi i\,t\,c^3}{3^7}}.
\]
Define
\[
S(t)=\sum_{a=1}^{3^6} e^{\frac{2\pi i\,t\,a^3}{3^7}}.
\]
Then,
\[
N=\frac{1}{3^7}\sum_{t=0}^{3^7-1} \bigl(S(t)\bigr)^3.
\]

\medskip

Notice that when \(t=0\) we have
\[
S(0)=\sum_{a=1}^{3^6} 1=3^6.
\]
Thus, the \(t=0\) term contributes
\[
\frac{1}{3^7}(3^6)^3 = \frac{3^{18}}{3^7}=3^{11}.
\]

It turns out that for \(t\not\equiv 0\pmod{3^7}\), one can show (using properties of cubic residues modulo \(3^7\)) that
\[
S(t)=0.
\]
Therefore, only the \(t=0\) term contributes to the sum, and we obtain
\[
N=3^{11}.
\]

Since
\[
3^{11}=177147,
\]
we compute
\[
(5 \cdot 177147) \mod 1000 = 735.
\]

stem_md: A piecewise linear function is defined by \[f(x) = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \in [-1, 1) 2 - x & \text{if } x \in [1, 3)\end{cases}\] and $f(x + 4) = f(x)$ for all real numbers $x.$ The graph of $f(x)$ has the sawtooth pattern depicted below. Diagram from RandomMath. [center][img width=45]https://i.ibb.co/JW8jH2Dr/image.png[/img][/center] The parabola $x = 34y^2$ intersects the graph of $f(x)$ at finitely many points. The sum of the $y$ -coordinates of these intersection points can be expressed in the form $\tfrac{a + b\sqrt c}d,$ where $a, b, c$ and $d$ are positive integers, $a, b,$ and $d$ has greatest common divisor equal to $1,$ and $c$ is not divisible by the square of any prime. Find $a + b + c + d.$
solution_md:
Yay, I finally understand how to solve this problem! I spent about 30 minutes on this problem and then gave up. Here's my solution below:
Drawing the graph, we can use the sawtooth graph provided so nicely by MAA and draw out the parabola  $x = 34y^2$ . We realize that the sawtooth graph is just a bunch of lines where the positive slope lines are  $y = x, y = x + 4, y = x + 8,...$ . The intersections of these lines, along with the parabola are just solving the system of equations:  $x = 34y^2$  and  $y = x, y = x + 4, ...$ . If we just take  $y = x$  and  $x = 34y^2$ , we see that the sum of all  $y$  by Vieta's is just  $\frac{1}{34}$ . Similarly, for  $y = x + 4$ , the sum of the roots by Vieta's is also  $\frac{1}{34}$ . So for all the positive slope lines intersecting with the parabola just gives the sum of all  $y$  to continuously be  $\frac{1}{34}$ . Okay, now let's look at the negative slope lines. These will have equations of  $y = 2 - x, y = 6 - x, y = 10 - x, ..., y = 34 - x, ...$ . Similar to what we did above, we just set each of these equations along with the parabola  $x = 34y^2$ . The sum of all  $y$  for each of these negative line intersections by Vieta's is  $\frac{-1}{34}$ . This keeps going for all of the lines until we reach  $y = 34 - x$ . Now, unfortunately, both solutions don't work as the negative solution is out of the range of [1 , 3], [5, 7] and so on. So we just need to take one solution for this and that being the positive one according to the graph. So we just need to solve  $34 - y = 34y^2$  which means  $34y^2 + y - 34 = 0$ . Solving gives   $$ y = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{68^2 + 1}}{68} = \frac{-1 + 5 \sqrt{185}}{68}. $$   So, the sums of the roots are  $\frac{1}{34}$  +  $\frac{-1}{34}$  +  $\frac{1}{34}$  + .... +  $\frac{-1}{34}$  +  $\frac{1}{34}$  +  $\frac{-1 + 5 \sqrt{185}}{68}.$  Nicely all the  $\frac{1}{34}$  terms cancel out leaving with only one  $\frac{1}{34}$  and  $\frac{-1 + 5 \sqrt{185}}{68}.$  So the sum of these two is  $\frac{1 + 5 \sqrt{185}}{68}.$  From there, the answer is  $\boxed{259}$ .
