stem_md:
There are  $2025$  positive integers  $a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_{2025}$  are placed around a circle. For any  $k = 1, 2, \cdots, 2025$ ,  $a_k \mid a_{k-1} + a_{k+1}$  where indices are considered modulo  $n$ . Prove that there exists a positive integer  $N$  such that satisfies the following condition. 


- **(Condition)** For any positive integer  $n > N$ , when  $a_1 = n^n$ ,  $a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_{2025}$  are all multiples of  $n$ .
solution_md:
Such arrangements are very interesting. To solve this problem we need a new property of these arrangements.**Lemma:** Define a sequence  $T(3),T(4), \dots$  by  $T(2)=2$  and  $T(k+1)=(2T(k))!$  for all  $k \geq 2$ . For  $m \geq 2$ , let  $a_1,a_2, \dots, a_m$  be positive integers arranged on a circle such that  $a_i \mid a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$  for all  $i$ . Then  $a_i \mid T(m) a_{i \pm 1}$  for all  $i$ . (Indices modulo  $m$  in both cases).**Proof:** We will use induction. For  $m=2$  the given conditions imply  $a_1 \mid 2a_2$  and  $a_2 \mid 2a_1$ , so  $T(2)=2$  works. Now assume the statement is true up to  $m-1 \geq 2$ .

Let  $a_1,a_2, \dots, a_m$  be the given arrangement. Suppose  $a_i=\max\{a_1,a_2, \dots, a_m\}$ . If  $a_i=a_{i+1}$ , then  $a_{i+1} \mid a_i + a_{i+2}$   $\implies$   $a_{i+1}|a_{i+2}$   $\implies$   $a_{i+2}=a_{i+1}$  because of maximality. Thus, propagating this, all the  $a_i$  are equal, so the divisibility is trivially satisfied.

Now assume  $a_i>a_{i+1}$ , and similarly  $a_i>a_{i-1}$ . Then,  $a_i \mid a_{i-1}+a_{i+1} < 2a_i$   $\implies$   $a_i=a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}$ . Now, delete  $a_i$  from the circle. Then,  $a_{i-1} \mid a_i+a_{i-2}=a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}+a_{i-2}$   $\implies$   $a_{i-1} \mid a_{i+1}+a_{i-2}$ , and similarly  $a_{i-1} \mid a_{i-1}+a_{i+2}$ . Thus this new arrangement of  $m-1$  numbers also satisfies the condition. Hence  $a_j \mid T(m-1) a_{j+1} \mid T(m)a_{j+1}$  for all  $j \neq i,i-1$  and  $a_j \mid T(m-1) a_{j-1} \mid T(m)a_{j-1}$  for all  $j \neq i,i+1$ . Further,  $a_{i \pm 1} \mid T(m-1) a_{i \mp 1}$ . In particular,   $$ a_{i \pm 1} \mid T(m-1)(a_{i \pm 1} + a_{i \mp 1}) = T(m-1)a_i \mid T(m)a_i. $$  Hence it is enough to prove that  $a_i \mid T(m)a_{i \pm 1}$ . Let  $a_{i-1}=db$  and  $a_{i+1}=dc$  where  $d$  is their  $\gcd$  and  $b,c$  are coprime. So  $db \mid T(m-1)dc$   $\implies$   $b \mid T(m-1)c$   $\implies$   $b \mid T(m-1)$  since  $b,c$  are coprime. Similarly  $c \mid T(m-1)$ . Hence,  $b+c \leq 2T(m-1)$   $\implies$   $b+c \mid (2T(m-1))!=T(m)$ . Therefore,  $$ a_i=db+dc \mid T(m)d \mid T(m) a_{i \pm 1}, $$  which completes the induction.  $\blacksquare$ Now we come back to the main problem. We claim that  $N=2024T(2025)+1$  works. Indeed, suppose  $n>N$ , and the  $a_i$  are arranged as in the question with  $a_1=n^n$ . The above lemma implies  $a_1 \mid T(2025)^{k-1} a_k \mid T(2025)^{2024} a_k$  for all  $k=1,2,3, \dots, 2025$ . Now for any prime  $p \mid n$ ,   $$ nv_p(n)=v_p(a_1) \leq 2024v_p(T(2025))+v_p(a_k), $$  and so  $$ v_p(a_k)=v_p(n)+(n-1)v_p(n)-2024v_p(T(2025)) \geq v_p(n)+n-1-2024v_p(T(2025)) > v_p(n), $$  where the last inequality holds because  $n>N=1+2024T(2025) \geq 1+2024v_p(T(2025))$ . Since this holds for all  $p \mid n$ , we get  $n \mid a_k$  for all  $k$ , as required.

<details><summary>solution sketch</summary>Call such arrangements with  $m(\ge 3)$  positive integers “ $m$ -reengs”. Call a reeng ‘monic’ if gcd of all elements of that reeng is  $1$ .

Step 1) There are exactly three monic  $3$ -reengs, namely  $(1,1,1),\,(1,1,2),\,(1,2,3).$ Step 2) If the gcd of some two adjacent elements of a reeng is  $d$ , then  $d$  is a divisor of all elements of that ring. Also, dividing all elements of a reeng by the common gcd of all elements results in a monic reeng.

Step 3) Removing a maximal element from a  $m$ -reeng produces a  $m-1$  reeng. If the original reeng was monic, then so is the new one. Use the result of Step 2 to simplify the proof.

Step 4) The maximum element of a monic  $m$ -reeng is bounded for a fixed  $m$ . To prove this use the result of Step 1 and 3 appropriately.

Step 5) Use induction to prove that the problem statement holds for general  $m$ -reengs. (The problem becomes the case when  $m=2025.$ ) Base case  $m=3$  is proved using the result of Step 1 and 2.
Inducting can be done as follows: first, if  $n^n$  is not the maximal value of the reeng, deleting the maximal value will not remove it from the reeng. Then we get a reeng with one less element that contains  $n^n$ , so apply induction hypothesis.
If  $n^n$  is the maximal value of the reeng, the gcd of all elements  $d$  must be multiple of  $n$ , finishing the induction. For if it were not true, then  $frac{n^n}{d}$  would be the maximal value of a monic reeng which is impossible when  $n$  gets sufficiently large.</details>

stem_md: Determine all triplets of positive integers  $(p,m,n)$  such that  $p$  is a prime,  $m \neq n < 2p$  and  $2 \nmid n$ . Also, the following polynomial is reducible in  $\mathbb{Z}[x]$   $$ x^{2p} - 2px^m - p^2x^n - 1 $$
solution_md:
Proposed by me ;)

The basic idea is to switch between  $\mathbb{Z}[x]$  and  $\mathbb{Z}_p[x]$ . Suppose  $p>3$ .**1.**Let  $f(x):=x^{2p}-2px^m-p^2x^n-1$  and assume  $f(x)=g(x)h(x)$  for nonconstant monic polynomials  $g,h\in\mathbb Z[x]$ , and let  $\tilde{g},\tilde{h}$  be the image of  $g,h$  by the natural map  $\mathbb{Z}[x]\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_p[x]$ , respectively. We have   $$ (x^2-1)^p=x^{2p}-1=\tilde{g}(x)\tilde{h}(x) $$   and since  $p^2\nmid f(\pm 1)$ , our only choice is  $\{ \tilde{g},\tilde{h}\}=\{(x-1)^p,(x+1)^p\}$ .**2.**There exist  $A(x),B(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$  such that  $\{g(x),h(x)\}=\{x^p-1+pA(x),x^p+1+pB(x)\}$ . Rewrite the factorization as $x^{2p}-2px^m-p^2x^n-1=(x^p-1+pA(x))(x^p+1+pB(x))$ , then we get   $$ x^p(A(x)+B(x))+(A(x)-B(x))+pA(x)B(x)=-2x^m-px^n. $$  We go back to  $\mathbb{Z}_p[x]$ . The equation becomes  $$ x^p(\tilde A(x)+\tilde B(x))+(\tilde A(x)-\tilde B(x))=-2x^m. $$  The **key observation** is that since  $g,h$  were monic, the degree of  $A,B$  has to be at most  $p-1$ . Thus  $x^p(\tilde A(x)+\tilde B(x))$  and  $(\tilde A(x)-\tilde B(x))$  are precisely the  $\ge p$  and  $<p$ -degree parts of  $-2x^m$ . This motivates us to divide cases.**3-1.**  $m\ge p$ . This implies  $\tilde A(x)=\tilde B(x)=-x^{m-p}$ , so we let  $A(x)=-x^{m-p}+pQ(x), B(x)=-x^{m-p}+pR(x)$ . We have  $$ x^{2p}-2px^m-p^2x^n-1=(x^p-px^{m-p}-1+p^2Q(x))(x^p-px^{m-p}+1+p^2R(x)), $$   but substituting  $x=1$  gives  $-2-p=(pQ(1)-1)(p^2R(1)-p+2)$ , which is impossible for  $p>3$ .**3-2.**  $m<p$ . This time  $\tilde A(x)=-x^m-pQ(x), \tilde B(x)=x^{m}+pR(x)$  for some  $Q,R$ . Plugging in  $x=-1$  in  $$ x^{2p}-2px^m-p^2x^n-1=(x^p-px^m-1-p^2Q(x))(x^p+px^{m}+1+p^2R(x)) $$  yields   $$ 2(-1)^m-p=(2+p(-1)^m+p^2 Q(-1))((-1)^m+pR(-1)). $$  This is again a contradiction for  $p>3$ .**4-1.**  $p=2$ :  $(m,n)=(2,1),(3,1),(1,3),(2,3)$  all work.**4-2.**  $p=3$ : <details><summary>It can be verified</summary>, with some pain(but hopefully our TAs found this process salvageable under test conditions :P ),</details> that no such  $(m,n)$  exist.

Hence all possible triples are  $\boxed{(2,2,1), (2,3,1), (2,1,3), (2,2,3)}$ .

Remark.  $2\nmid n$  is necessary, otherwise all triples in the form  $(p,m,2m)$  are solutions. We figured the problem was already getting too hard, so we resolved to odd  $n$ . The problem for general  $n$  is open.

stem_md:
In the Faculty of Cybernetics football championship, \( n \geq 3 \) teams participated. The competition was held in a round-robin format, meaning that each team played against every other team exactly once. For a win, a team earns 3 points, for a loss no points are awarded, and for a draw, both teams receive 1 point each.

It turned out that the winning team scored strictly more points than any other team and had at most as many wins as losses. What is the smallest \( n \) for which this could happen?

*Proposed by Bogdan Rublov*
solution_md:
If  $n = 3$ , assume the teams are  $A, B, C$ , with  $A$  being the winner. Then  $A$  must have  $1$  win and  $1$  loss, in which case, the team that beat  $A$  has as many points as  $A$ , contradiction; or  $2$  draws, in which the winner of the match between  $B$  and  $C$  (or any of them in case of a draw) would have at least  $2$  points, contradiction. So  $n = 3$  is not possible.

If  $n = 4$ , assume the teams are  $A, B, C, D$ , with  $A$  being the winner. Then  $6$  matches are played, and each match adds at least  $2$  points combined to both teams. So at the end, the sum of points of all teams must be at least  $12$ , hence, the winning team must have at least  $4$  points. This implies the winning team has  $1$  win,  $1$  draw,  $1$  loss. WLOG assume  $A$  lost to  $B$ , drew to  $C$ , and won against  $D$ . Then  $B$  must have lost to both  $C$  and  $D$  to stay under  $4$  points. However, this means  $C$  reaches  $4$  points, contradiction. Hence,  $n= 4$  is impossible too.

Now we show  $n = 5$  is possible. Let  $A, B, C, D, E$  be the teams. If  $A$  wins against  $B$  and  $C$  but loses to  $D$  and  $E$ ,  $B$  draws  $C$  and  $E$  but wins against  $D$ ,  $C$  draws  $D$  and wins against  $E$ , and  $D$  draws  $E$ , then  $A$  has  $6$  points with  $2$  wins and  $2$  losses, while all other teams have  $5$  points.

Therefore, the smallest  $n$  is  $\boxed{n = 5}$ .

stem_md:
Oleksii wrote some \( 2n \) (\( n > 1 \)) consecutive positive integers on the board. After that, he grouped these numbers into pairs in some way, and within each pair, he multiplied the two numbers together. He then wrote the resulting \( n \) products on the board instead of the original numbers.

Afterward, Anton wrote down the difference between the largest and the smallest of the numbers Oleksii wrote. Oleksii wants Anton to write the smallest possible number. What is the smallest number that can be written?

*Proposed by Oleksii Masalitin, Anton Trygub*
solution_md: Let  $a, a + 1, \dots, a + 2n - 1$  be the numbers on the board. We see the product containing  $a$  after any pairing is at most  $a(a + 2n - 1) = a^2 + 2an - a$ , and by pigeonhole, two of  $a + n - 1, a + n, \dots, a + 2n - 1$  must be paired. So there exists a pair with product at least  $(a + n - 1)(a + n) = a^2 + 2an + n^2- a - n$ . Hence, the difference between max and min products is at least  $a^2 + 2an + n^2- a - n - (a^2 + 2an - a) = n^2 - n$ . By pairing  $(a, a + 2n - 1), (a + 1, a + 2n - 2), \dots, (a + n - 1, a + n)$ , Anton will write  $\boxed{n^2- n}$ , and we are done.  $\Box$

stem_md:
Find all quadruples of positive integers \( (a, p, q, r) \), where \( p, q, r \) are prime numbers, such that the following equation holds:
\[
p^2q^2 + q^2r^2 + r^2p^2 + 3 = 4 \cdot 13^a.
\]

*Proposed by Oleksii Masalitin*
solution_md:
The answer is  $a = 2$ , and  $(p,q,r)$  is a permutation of  $(2,3,7)$ . These clearly work. Now we show they are the only ones. 

Taking modulo  $3$  and  $4$  gives that one of the primes is  $2$  and another is  $3$ . WLOG  $q = 3, r =  2$ . 

We have  $13p^2 + 39 = 4 \cdot 13^a$ . 

Thus,  $p^2 + 3 = 4 \cdot 13^{a - 1}$ . 

Now assume  $p \ne 7$ . If  $a - 1$  is odd, then taking modulo  $7$  gives that  $p^2 \equiv 0 \pmod 7$ , absurd. Therefore,  $a - 1$  is even. 

Hene \[ 3 = 4 \cdot 13^{a - 1}  - p^2 = \left( 2 \cdot 13^{ \frac{a - 1}{2}}  - p \right) \left(2 \cdot 13^{\frac{a-1}{2}} + p  \right) \] Both factors are positive integers, so must be at most  $3$ , meaning  $p < 3$ , so  $p = 2$ , which obviously does not work. 

Thus,  $p = 7$  and we are done.

stem_md:
Point \( H \) is the orthocenter of the acute triangle \( ABC \), and \( AD \) is its altitude. Tangents are drawn from points \( B \) and \( C \) to the circle with center \( A \) and radius \( AD \), which do not coincide with the line \( BC \). These tangents intersect at point \( P \). Prove that the radius of the incircle of \( \triangle BCP \) is equal to \( HD \).

*Proposed by Danylo Khilko*
solution_md: Let  $I$  be the incenter of  $\triangle BCP$ . stem_md: You are given \( 11 \) numbers with an arithmetic mean of \( 10 \). Each of the first \( 4 \) numbers is increased by \( 20 \), and each of the last \( 7 \) numbers is decreased by \( 24 \). What is the arithmetic mean of the new \( 11 \) numbers?
solution_md:
You are given \( 11 \) numbers with an arithmetic mean of \( 10 \). Each of the first \( 4 \) numbers is increased by \( 20 \), and each of the last \( 7 \) numbers is decreased by \( 24 \). What is the arithmetic mean of the new \( 11 \) numbers?
The sum of the old numbers is $11\cdot10=110$ . After the modifications, this sum will increase by $20\cdot4-7\cdot24=-88$ , hence a new sum of $110-88=22$ . Therefore the new average is $\frac{22}{11}=\boxed2$ .

Find all functions \( f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \) that satisfy the following condition: for any positive integers \( m \) and \( n \) such that \( m > n \) and \( m \) is not divisible by \( n \), if we denote by \( r \) the remainder of the division of \( m \) by \( n \), then the remainder of the division of \( f(m) \) by \( n \) is \( f(r) \).

*Proposed by Mykyta Kharin*
solution_md:
Find all functions \( f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \) that satisfy the following condition: for any positive integers \( m \) and \( n \) such that \( m > n \) and \( m \) is not divisible by \( n \), if we denote by \( r \) the remainder of the division of \( m \) by \( n \), then the remainder of the division of \( f(m) \) by \( n \) is \( f(r) \).
1) $f(x)\le x$ $\forall x\ge 1$
Proof$2x+1>x+1$ and is not divisible by $x+1$ . Remainder of division of $2x+1$ by $x+1$ is $x$ and so remainder of division of $f(2x+1)$ by $x+1$ is $f(x)$ and so $f(x) 2) $\forall x\ge 1$ , either $f(x)=1$ , either $f(x)=x$
ProofSo $f(1)=1$ and $f(2)\in\{1,2\}$ Let $x\ge 3$ : $x>x-1$ and is not divisible by $x-1$ . Remainder of division of $x$ by $x-1$ is $1$ and so remainder of division of $f(x)$ by $x-1$ is $f(1)=1$ and so, since $f(x)\le x\le 2(x-1)+1$ : either $f(x)=0\times (x-1)+1=1$ , either $f(x)=1\times(x-1)+1=x$ Q.E.D.
3) If $f(x)=1$ for some $x>1$ , then $\boxed{\text{S1 : }f(x)=1\quad\forall x\in\mathbb Z_{>0}}$
ProofIf $f(x)=1$ for some $x>1$ , then : $2x+1>x+1$ and is not divisible by $x+1$ and so : Remainder of division of $2x+1$ by $x+1$ is $x$ and so remainder of division of $f(2x+1)$ by $x+1$ is $f(x)=1$ But if $f(2x+1)=2x+1$ , then its remainder when divided by $x+1$ is $x$ . So $f(2x+1)=1$ And so we can find such $x$ as great as we want. If $f(x)=1$ for some $x>4$ , then let $2\le y<\frac x2$ : $x>x-y$ and $x-y$ does not divide $x$ . So : Remainder of division of $x$ by $x-y$ is $y$ and so remainder of division of $f(x)=1$ by $x-y$ is $f(y)$ and so $f(y)=1$ So $f(y)=1$ $\forall y\in[2,\frac x2)$ And since we can find such $x$ as great as we want, $f(y)=1$ $\forall y$ , which indeed fits Q.E.D.
4) If $f(x)\ne 1$ $\forall x>1$ , then $\boxed{\text{S2 : }f(x)=x\quad\forall x\in\mathbb Z_{>0}}$
ProofThis is an immediate consequence of 2) above and $f\equiv Id$ indeed fits. Q.E.D.

stem_md:
Real numbers \( a, b, c \) satisfy the following conditions:
\[
1000 < |a| < 2000, \quad 1000 < |b| < 2000, \quad 1000 < |c| < 2000,
\]
and
\[
\frac{ab^2}{a+b} + \frac{bc^2}{b+c} + \frac{ca^2}{c+a} = 0.
\]
What are the possible values of the expression
\[
\frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{a}?
\]

*Proposed by Vadym Solomka*
solution_md:
First, we show that  $ab + bc + ca \ne 0$ . 
Note that if all three of  $a, b, c$  have the same sign, then  $ab + bc + ca > 0$ .
WLOG assume that  $a, b > 0$  and  $c < 0$ , and  $ab + bc + ca = 0$ .
Then  $-c = \frac{ab}{a+b} \le \frac{a + b}{4} < 1000$ , contradiction. Hence,  $ab + bc + ca \ne 0$ .
So  $\frac{ab^2}{a+b} + \frac{bc^2}{b+c} + \frac{ca^2}{c + a} = 0 \Leftrightarrow \frac{b(ab + bc + ca)}{a+b} - bc + \frac{c(ab + bc + ca)}{b+c} - ca + \frac{c(ab + bc + ca)}{c+a} - ab = 0 \Leftrightarrow \frac{b}{a + b} + \frac{c}{b + c} + \frac{c}{c + a} = 1$ .
Next, let  $x = \frac{a}{b}, y = \frac{b}{c}, z = \frac{c}{a}$ . Then  $\frac{b}{a + b} + \frac{c}{b + c} + \frac{c}{c + a} = 1 \Leftrightarrow \frac{1}{\frac{a}{b} + 1} + \frac{1}{\frac{b}{c} + 1} + \frac{1}{\frac{c}{a} + 1} = 1 \Leftrightarrow \frac{1}{x+1} + \frac{1}{y+1} + \frac{1}{z+1} = 1$ ,
which implies  $xy + yz + zx + 2x + 2y + 2z + 3 = xyz + xy + yz + zx + x + y + z + 1 \Leftrightarrow x + y + z = xyz - 2 = -1$ .
Therefore, the only possible value of  $\frac{a}{b} + \frac{b}{c} + \frac{c}{a}$  is  $\boxed{-1}$ .  $\Box$

stem_md: Find all three-digit numbers that are \( 5 \) times greater than the product of their digits.
solution_md:
Find all three-digit numbers that are \( 5 \) times greater than the product of their digits.
$100a+10b+c=5abc$ with $a\in\{1,2,...,9\}$ and $b,c\in\{0,1,...,9\}$ So $c\equiv 0\pmod 5$ and so $c=0$ or $c=5$ $c=0$ implies $100a+10b=0$ , impossible $c=5$ implies $20a+2b+1=5ab$ , which is $(5a-2)(b-4)=9$ and so, since $5a-2\ge 3$ : Either $5a-2=3$ and $b-4=3$ and solution $\boxed{175}$ Either $5a-2=9$ and $b-4=1$ , which does not fit

The answer is  $175$ , which obviously works. Nowe show it's the only one.

stem_md:
Inside a convex quadrilateral \( ABCD \), a point \( P \) is chosen such that
\[
\angle PAD = \angle PAB = \angle PBC = \angle PCB = \angle PDA = 30^\circ.
\]
Prove that \( \angle CDP = 30^\circ \).

*Proposed by Vadym Solomka*
solution_md: Let  $\omega$  be the third root of unity. Consider the diagram in the complex plane, then WLOG  $p = 0$  and  $a = 1$ . Then  $d = \omega$  since it is a 120 degree rotation of  $A$  about  $P$ . Since  $\bar{b}$  lies on  $AD$  we have  $b = t(\bar \omega - 1) + 1 = t(\omega^2 - 1) + 1$  for some real number  $t$ , so  $c = \omega^2 b = t\omega^4 - t\omega^2 + \omega^2 = t\omega - t\omega^2 + \omega^2$ . Since  $\omega$  and  $\omega^2$  have the same real part,  $d$  and  $c$  have the same real part, hence  $DC \perp AP$  and so  $\angle CDP = 180 - \angle PDA - \angle DAP - 90 = 30$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/2025 Contests/2025 Kyiv City MO Round 2/3488985.json

candidates: Let  $(ABP) \cap AD = Q \ne A$ . Then  $\angle QPB = 180^{\circ} - \angle QAB = 180^\circ - \angle PAB - \angle PAD = 120^\circ$ , so  $\angle QPB$  is an external angle bisector of  $\angle BPC$ , implying  $QB = QC$ . Since  $\angle QBC = \angle PBC + \angle QBP = \angle PBC + \angle QAP = 60^\circ$ ,  $\triangle QBC$  is equilateral with  $P$  as its center. Note that  $\angle PCQ = 30^\circ = \angle PDQ$ , hence,  $PCDQ$  is cyclic. Therefore,  $\angle CDP = \angle CQP = 30^\circ$ .  $\Box$

stem_md:
A positive integer \( n \) satisfies the following conditions:
 

 
- The number \( n \) has exactly \( 60 \) divisors: \( 1 = a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_{60} = n \);
- The number \( n+1 \) also has exactly \( 60 \) divisors: \( 1 = b_1 < b_2 < \cdots < b_{60} = n+1 \).

Let \( k \) be the number of indices \( i \) such that \( a_i < b_i \). Find all possible values of \( k \).

*Note: Such numbers exist, for example, the numbers \( 4388175 \) and \( 4388176 \) both have \( 60 \) divisors.*

*Proposed by Anton Trygub*
solution_md:
We call an index  $i$   $\textit{good}$  iff  $a_i < b_i$ .
Note that  $gcd(n, n + 1) = 1$ , so  $a_i \ne b_i$  for all indices  $i > 1$ .
Let  $i \in [2, 59]$ . 
If  $a_i < b_i$  and  $a_{61-i} < b_{61-i}$ , then  $n = a_ia_{61-i} < (b_i - 1)b_{61-i} = n + 1 - b_{61-i} < n$ , contradiction.
If  $a_i > b_i$  and  $a_{61-i} > b_{61-i}$ , then  $n = a_ia_{61-i} > (b_i + 1)b_{61-i} = n + 1 + b_{61-i} > n$ , contradiction.
Hence, for each  $i \in [2, 59]$ , exactly one of  $i$  or  $61 - i$  must be good, giving us  $58/2 = 29$  good indices.
Since  $1$  is not good and  $60$  is good, the only possible value of  $k$  is  $\boxed{30}$ .

stem_md:
Does there exist a sequence of positive integers \( a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{100} \) such that every number from \( 1 \) to \( 100 \) appears exactly once, and for each \( 1 \leq i \leq 100 \), the condition
\[
a_{a_i + i} = i
\]
holds? Here it is assumed that \( a_{k+100} = a_k \) for each \( 1 \leq k \leq 100 \).

*Proposed by Mykhailo Shtandenko*
solution_md:
The answer is  $\boxed{\text{No}}$ . Replace  $a_i$  with  $f(i)$ , then we have \[f(f(i)+i) = i.\]
Subbing in  $i \to f(i)$ , we get \[f(f(i))+f(i) = i.\]
But summing this over all  $i$  gives us  $50 \times 101 \equiv 0 \pmod{100}$ , contradiction.  $\square$ (Note: In the above, we work  $\pmod{100}$ , always, so that  $f$  is a bijection.)
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/2025 Contests/2025 Kyiv City MO Round 2/3488994.json

candidates: Assume such a sequence exists. For each  $i \in \{1, 2, \dots, 100\}$ , let  $n_i$  be the unique index such that  $a_{n_i} = i$ . So  $a_i + i \equiv n_i \pmod{100}$ . Summing both sides from  $i = 1$  to  $100$ , we have  $\sum_{i = 1}^{100} a_i + 5050 \equiv \sum_{i = 1}^{100} n_i \pmod{100} \Leftrightarrow 5050 + 5050 \equiv 5050 \pmod{100}$ , contradiction. Therefore, no such sequence exists.  $\Box$

stem_md:
Point \( A_1 \) inside the acute-angled triangle \( ABC \) is such that 
\[
\angle ACB = 2\angle A_1BC \quad \text{and} \quad \angle ABC = 2\angle A_1CB.
\]
Point \( A_2 \) is chosen so that points \( A \) and \( A_2 \) lie on opposite sides of line \( BC \), \( AA_2 \perp BC \), and the perpendicular bisector of \( AA_2 \) is tangent to the circumcircle of \( \triangle ABC \). Define points \( B_1, B_2, C_1, C_2 \) analogously. Prove that the circumcircles of \( \triangle AA_1A_2 \), \( \triangle BB_1B_2 \), and \( \triangle CC_1C_2 \) intersect at exactly two common points.

*Proposed by Vadym Solomka*
solution_md:
Let  $M$  be the midpoint of the minor arc  $\widehat{BC}$  of the circle  $(ABC)$ . 
Clearly,  $M$  lies on the perpendicular bisector of  $AA_2$ . Angle chasing gives:
  $\angle A_1MA=\angle B- \angle C$  and  $\angle A_2MA = 2\angle C + \angle A$  so  $\overline{A_1-M-A_2}$  are collinear.
Let  $I$  be the incenter and  $E_a$  the  $A$ -excenter. Then  $AA_1E_aA_2$  is an isoscelles trapezoid(from the fact that  $BIA_1C$  is an isoscelles trapezoid and the incenter-excenter lemma). It is clear now that  $I$  has equal power wrt the circles  $(AA_1A_2), (BB_1B_2),(CC_1C_2)$ .
Let  $D$  be the  $A$ -extouch point and  $E$  the second intersection of  $AD$  with the circumcircle. Clearly,  $D$  lies on  $A_1E_a$  so, by PoP we have: $A_1D \cdot DE_a=BD \cdot DC= AD\cdot DE$  so  $E$  lies on  $(AA_1A_2)$ . The fact that the Nagel point has equal powers wrt the three circles follows immediately from the above. 
Therefore we have found two points with equal powers wrt  $(AA_1A_2), (BB_1B_2),(CC_1C_2)$  so the above circles are coaxial, as desired.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
On sides \( AB \) and \( AC \) of an acute-angled, non-isosceles triangle \( ABC \), points \( P \) and \( Q \) are chosen such that the center \( O_9 \) of the nine-point circle of \( \triangle ABC \) is the midpoint of segment \( PQ \). Let \( O \) be the circumcenter of \( \triangle ABC \). On the ray \( OP \) beyond \( P \), segment \( PX \) is marked such that \( PX = AQ \). On the ray \( OQ \) beyond \( Q \), segment \( QY \) is marked such that \( QY = AP \). Prove that the midpoint of side \( BC \), the midpoint of segment \( XY \), and the point \( O_9 \) are collinear.

*The nine-point circle or the Euler circle* of \( \triangle ABC \) is the circle passing through nine significant points of the triangle — the midpoints of the three sides, the feet of the three altitudes, and the midpoints of the segments connecting the orthocenter with the vertices of \( \triangle ABC \).

*Proposed by Danylo Khilko*
solution_md:
Nice problem.

<details><summary>solution</summary>Let  $AHKO$  be a parallelogram. Then  $APKQ$  is also a parallelogram. Notably, let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $BC$ , and  $M_B$  the midpoint of  $AB$ ; then  $MM_B$  is parallel to  $KP$ . If  $P'$  is the reflection of  $P$  across  $M_B$ , then  $OP'$  is parallel to  $KP$ ; thus  $\angle{OPA} = \angle{OP'B} = \angle{A}$ . Now, since  $AQ = PK$ , we find that  $X$  is just the reflection of  $K$  across  $AB$ .

After this, the problem is just some vector calculations. Note that  $K$  is the circumcenter of  $(BHC)$ ; suppose  $(BHC)$  intersects  $AB$  again at  $B'$ ,  $AC$  again at  $C'$ . Then we want to show  $H, K, X + Y - O$  are collinear. Since  $X = B + B' - K$ ,  $Y = C + C' - K$ , we find that it suffices to show that  $H, K, B' + C' - K$  are collinear. But  $HB' = HA = HC'$  and  $KB' = KC'$ , so all three points are on the perpendicular bisector of  $B'C'$  as desired.</details>

stem_md:
A square \( K = 2025 \times 2025 \) is given. We define a *stick* as a rectangle where one of its sides is \( 1 \), and the other side is a positive integer from \( 1 \) to \( 2025 \). Find the largest positive integer \( C \) such that the following condition holds:



- If several sticks with a total area not exceeding \( C \) are taken, it is always possible to place them inside the square \( K \) so that each stick fully completely covers an integer number of \( 1 \times 1 \) squares, and no \( 1 \times 1 \) square is covered by more than one stick.

*(Basically, you can rotate sticks, but they have to be aligned by lines of the grid)*

*Proposed by Anton Trygub*
solution_md: The answer is  $\boxed{3077493}$ To prove that  $C\le 3077493$  you can take  $1013$  sticks of  $1\times 2025$  and  $1013$  sticks of  $1\times 1013$ . FTSOC assume that all the  $1\times 2025$  sticks are placed vertically. Note that the other sticks should also be vertically and it's a contradiction since we have  $2025$  columns and each column has at most one stick in it. Thus  $C<1013\times 2025+1013\times 1013=3077494$ Now for the algorithm, we can assume that all sticks have length  $\ge 1013$  (except for one maybe). Because we can turn two  $1\times r$  and  $1\times s$  sticks (where  $r,s\le 1012$ ) into one stick of length  $r+s$ . Now start from the top-right corner and place the sticks horizontally in decreasing order till you reach the bottom row, now go to the bottom-left corner and place the remaining sticks vertically in decreasing order till we can't place another stick which means the stick that we've placed has a common cell with one of those horizontal sticks. Let this cell be the cell  $(a,b)$ . You can easily notice that so far we have placed  $2025-b$  sticks of length at least  $2025-a$  and  $a+b+1$  sticks of length at least  $b+1$  and now we have a problem. So if we run into a problem, then  $C\ge (2025-a)(2025-b)+(a+b+1)(b+1)=2025^2+b+1-(a+b)(2024-b)+ab$  so  $C\ge b+1+(2025^2-1012^2)+(a+b-1012)^2-a^2\ge 2025^2-1012^2+1013+(b-1012)(b+2a-1012)\ge 3077494$ . Hence if we run into a problem in this algorithm, then  $C\ge 3077494$ . But we have assumed that  $C<3077494$  for the algorithm. Thus the answer is  $3077493$  and we are done

stem_md:
Let \( n > 2 \) be an integer, \( k > 1 \) a real number, and \( x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \) be positive real numbers such that \( x_1 \cdot x_2 \cdots x_n = 1 \). Prove that:

\[
\frac{1 + x_1^k}{1 + x_2} + \frac{1 + x_2^k}{1 + x_3} + \cdots + \frac{1 + x_n^k}{1 + x_1} \geq n.
\]

When does equality hold?
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/2025 Contests/2025 Macedonian Mathematical Olympiad/3567784.json

candidates:
By generalized power mean, we have  $1+x^k\ge 2^{1-k}(1+x)^k$ . So,
\[
\sum_{{\rm cyc}}\frac{1+x_i^k}{1+x_{i+1}}\ge 2^{1-k}\sum_{{\rm cyc}}\frac{(1+x_i)^k}{1+x_{i+1}}.
\]
Next, by AM-GM inequality
\[
\sum_{{\rm cyc}}\frac{(1+x_i)^k}{1+x_{i+1}}\ge n\sqrt[n]{\prod_{1\le i\le n}(1+x_i)^{k-1}}\ge n\sqrt[n]{\prod_{1\le i\le n}2^{k-1}x_i^{\frac{k-1}{2}}} = n\cdot 2^{k-1}

stem_md: On a horizontally placed number line, a pile of \( t_i > 0 \) tokens is placed on each number \( i \in \{1, 2, \ldots, s\} \). As long as at least one pile contains at least two tokens, we repeat the following procedure: we choose such a pile (say, it consists of \( k \geq 2 \) tokens), and move the top token from the selected pile \( k - 1 \) unit positions to the right along the number line. What is the largest natural number \( N \) on which a token can be placed? (Express \( N \) as a function of \( (t_i;\ i = 1, \ldots, s) \).)
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/2025 Contests/2025 Macedonian Mathematical Olympiad/3567785.json

candidates:
First of all, we note that if we want to get the maximum number \(N\), then we should do the operation as much as possible, because after we get our purpose, doing extra operations does not create a problem for us. So after we are done, in any place there can be at most one token.  

Claim: If we get our maximum  N, then there should be exactly one token at every number from 1 to \(N\).


Proof: Let’s assume that is not true. Then there exists some position \(n\) such that there is a token on \(n\), but not on \(n-1\).  

Let’s assume that the last token came to \(n\) from some position \(m\). Then after this operation, there will be \(n-m\) tokens in the position \m\. It means we could also reach position \(n-1\) by using \(m+(n-m-1)=n-1\).  

By this way, after we get our maximum number \(N\), there is exactly one token at each position. So we will need \(N\) tokens in total. But initially we have 
\[
t_1 + t_2 + \cdots + t_s
\]
tokens.  

Therefore,
\[
N = t_1 + t_2 + \cdots + t_s.
\]

stem_md:
Find all functions  $f:\mathbb{N}_0\to\mathbb{N}$  such that**1)** \(f(a)\) divides \(a\) for every \(a\in\mathbb{N}_0\), and**2)** for all \(a,b,k\in\mathbb{N}_0\) we have
  \[
    f\bigl(f(a)+kb\bigr)\;=\;f\bigl(a + k\,f(b)\bigr).
  \]
solution_md:
I claim the only solutions are: (1)  $f(n)=n$  for all  $n$ , (b)  $f(n) = 1$  for  $n$  odd and  $f(n)=2$  for  $n$  even, or (c)  $f(n)=1$  for all  $n\ge 1$  with  $f(0)\ne 0$  arbitrary. (I'm a bit sloppy with  $f(0)$ .)

To that end, we have  $f(1)=1$ . Suppose first that  $f(2)=1$ . Taking  $a=2$  and  $b=1$ , we find  $f(2+k)=f(1+k)$  for all  $k\ge 0$ , forcing  $f(x)=1$  for all  $x$  positive. In this case,  $f(0)$  can take any value. Next, suppose  $f(2)=2$ . Clearly  $f(n)=n$  for all  $n$  works, so we now inspect the other solutions. Let  $a_0\ge 3$  be the smallest positive integer for which  $f(a_0)<a_0$ . Clearly  $a_0\ge 3$ . Further, we have  $f(f(a)+kb)\mid f(a)+kb$  and  $f(f(a)+kb)=f(a+kb)\mid a+kf(b)$ . So,
\[
f(f(a)+kb)\mid a-f(a) + k(f(b)-b) \Rightarrow f(f(a_0)+k) \mid a_0-f(a_0),
\]
by taking  $b=1$ . The key is that the expression above holds for all  $k$ . Suppose now that  $a_0-f(a_0)\ge 3$ . Taking  $k=a_0-f(a_0)-1$  and  $a_0-f(a_0)-2$ , we find that  $f(a_0-1)\mid a_0-f(a_0)$  and  $f(a_0-2)\mid a_0-f(a_0)$ . As  $f(a_0-1)=a_0-1$  and  $f(a_0-2)=a_0-2$ , we have  $(a_0-1)(a_0-2)\mid a_0-f(a_0)\le a_0-1$ , forcing  $a_0\le 3$ , which contradicts with  $a_0-f(a_0)\ge 3$ . So,  $a_0-f(a_0)\in\{1,2\}$ .**Case 1:  $a_0-f(a_0)=1$ .** Since  $a_0\mid f(a_0)$ , we find by modulo  $f(a_0)$  that  $f(a_0)=1$  and  $a_0=2$ , not possible.**Case 2:  $a_0-f(a_0)=2$ .** Once again, modulo  $f(a_0)$  gives  $f(a_0)\mid 2$ . If  $f(a_0)=2$  then  $a_0=4$ . In this case,  $f(2+k)\mid 2$ , a contradiction by taking  $k=1$  as  $f(3)=3$  in this case. So,  $f(a_0)=1$  and  $a_0=3$ . This clearly gives  $f(k+1)\mid 2$ . As  $f(k+1)\mid k+1$ , this immediately yields  $f(c)=1$  for all  $c$  odd and  $f(c)\mid 2$  for all  $c$  even. Taking  $a=3$  we find  $f(1+kb)=f(3+kf(b))$ . For  $b=1$ , this gives  $f(k+1)=f(k+3)$ . So,  $f$  is constant along even numbers, forcing  $f(c)=2$  for all  $c$  even.

stem_md:
Find all pairs of distinct primes  $(p,q)$  such that  $p$  and  $q$  are both prime factors of  $p^3+q^2+1$ , and are the only such prime factors.

*Proposed by Takeda Shigenori*
solution_md:
Obviously, both can't be equal.

Case 1:  $p > q$ We have  $p^2 \mid p^3 + q^2 + 1 \implies p^2 \mid q^2 + 1$ , but  $p^2 > q^2 + 1$ , so  $p^2 \nmid p^3 + q^2 + 1$ . Hence,  $v_p(p^3 + q^2 + 1) = 1$ . If  $q^3 \nmid p^3 + q^2 + 1$ ,  $pq^2 \geq p^3 + q^2 + 1$  but  $pq^2 < p^3$ . So,  $q^3 \mid p^3 + q^2 + 1 \implies q^2 \mid p^3 + q^2 + 1 \implies q^2 \mid p^3 + 1 \implies q^2 \mid (p + 1)(p^2 - p + 1)$ .

If  $q = 3$ ,  $p = 5$ , this clearly works. Assume  $q \neq 3$ . If we have  $q \mid p + 1$ ,  $q \nmid p^2 - p + 1$ , so  $q^2 \mid p + 1$ . Let  $q^2 = kp - 1$ . We have  $kp - 1 \mid p + 1$ , but this is a clear contradiction by size. So,  $q \nmid p + 1$ . Hence,  $q^2 \mid p^2 - p + 1$ , and  $p \mid q^2 + 1$ . Note  $kp  - 1 \mid p^2 - p + 1 \implies kp - 1 \mid kp^2 - kp + k \implies kp - 1 \mid kp^2 - kp + k - kp^2 + p \implies kp - 1 \mid kp - k - p$ , which means  $kp = p + k$  by size. This is a contradiction if  $k \geq 2$  since  $p > 2$ , which means  $k = 1$ . So,  $q^2 = p - 1 \implies p = 5, q = 2$ . This fails.

Case 2:  $q > p$  $q \mid p^3 + q^2 + 1 \implies q \mid (p + 1)(p^2 - p + 1)$ . If  $q \mid p + 1$ , we must have  $q = 3, p = 2$  since  $q \geq p + 1, q \leq p + 1 \implies q = p + 1$ . This works.

Assume  $q \nmid p + 1$  now. We have  $q \mid p^2 - p + 1$ . Note that if  $q^2 \mid p^3 + q^2 + 1$ ,  $q^2 \mid p^3 + 1 \implies q^2 \mid p^2 - p + 1$ , this is a contradiction since  $q^2 > p^2$ , so  $v_q(p^3 + q^2 + 1) = 1$ . Observe that if  $p^2 \nmid p^3 + q^2 + 1$ ,  $p^3 + q^2 + 1 = pq$ , but  $pq < p^2$ , a contradiction, so  $p^2 \mid p^3 + q^2 + 1 \implies p^2 \mid q^2 + 1$ .

So,  $p^2 \mid q^2 + 1$ ,  $q^2 \mid (p^2 - p + 1)^2$ . Let  $q^2 = kp^2 - 1$ . We have  $kp^2 - 1 \mid p^4 - 2p^3 + 3p^2 - 2p + 1 \implies kp^2 - 1 \mid kp^4 - 2kp^3 + 3kp^2 - 2kp + k - kp^4 + p^2 \implies kp^2 - 1 \mid 2kp^3 + 2kp - 3kp^2 - k - p^2 \implies kp^2 - 1 \mid 2kp^3 + 2kp - 3kp^2 - k - p^2 - 2kp^3 + 2p \implies kp^2 - 1 \mid 3kp^2 + p^2 + k - 2kp - 2p \implies kp^2 - 1 \mid 3kp^2 + p^2 + k - 2kp - 2p - 3kp^2 + 3 = (p^2 + k + 3) - (2kp + 2p)$ .

Observe that this means  $2kp + 2p = p^2 + k + 3$  due to size. So,  $p \mid p^2 + k + 3 \implies p \mid k + 3$ . Let  $k = xp - 3$ . We have  $p^2 + xp = 2p(k + 1) \implies p + x = 2(k + 1) = 2(xp - 2) = 2xp - 4$ . This means  $x(2p - 1) = p + 4$ . If  $x \ geq 2$ ,  $x(2p - 1) \geq 2(2p - 1) = 4p - 2$  which is greater than  $p + 4$  unless  $p = 2$ . If  $p = 2$ .  $q = 3$  again. Hence,  $x = 1$  so  $p = 5$ . This means  $k = 2$ , so  $q^2 = 2\cdot5^2 - 1 = 49 \implies q = 7$ . This clearly works.

Hence, all our solutions are  $(p, q) = (2, 3), (5, 3), (5, 7)$ .

stem_md:
Fix a positive integer  $n\ge 2$ . For any cyclic  $2n$ -gon  $P_1 P_2\cdots P_{2n}$  in this order, define its score as the maximal possible value of   $$ \angle P_iXP_{i+1} + \angle P_{i+n}XP_{i+n+1} $$   across all  $1\le i\le n$  (indices modulo  $n$ ), and over all points  $X$  inside the  $2n$ -gon including its boundary. 

Prove that there exist a real number  $r$  such that a cyclic  $2n$ -gon is regular if and only if it has score  $r$ . 

*Proposed by Wong Jer Ren*
solution_md:
Great Problem! Here is a sketch of my solution
Sketch of my sol**Claim 1:** The maximum value of $\angle AXB + \angle CXD$ in a quadrilateral can be attained only when $(AXB)$ and $(CXD)$ are tangent to each other
ProofAssume not, then choose any point $Z$ in the region of intersection of the two circles, then we have $\angle AZB + \angle CZD > \angle AXB + \angle CXD$ , which is contradiction to the definition of maxima.
**Claim 2:** $X$ lies on side $AB$ or $CD$ when $\angle AXB + \angle CXD$ is maximised.
ProofDo inequalities
Call the angle not equal to $180$ in the above sum, for each quadrilateral, the sustaining angle.**Claim 3:** The sum of sustaining angles of quadrilaterals $P_iP_{i+1}P_{i+n}P_{i+n+1}$ for a generic polygon is greater than or equal to the sum of sustaining angles of such quadrilaterals for a regular gon.
Rough Idea of the proofEssentially a smoothing argument, start with an arbitrary $2n$ -cyclic gon, we will prove that at each point you can make opposite sides parallel while not increasing the sum of sustaining angles, at the end of which we end up with an affine 2n- cyclic gon (that is, opp sides parallel) which ofcourse implies regular gon. We will choose a sustaining side call it $P_kP_{k+1}$ , and its friend $P_{n+k}P_{n+k+1}$ (indices modulo $2n$ ), if $P_{n+k}P_{n+k+1}$ is not adjacent to sustaining side then choose new $P'_{n+k+1}$ so that $P_{n+k}P'_{n+k+1} \parallel P_kP_{k+1}$ and clearly this reduces the sum of sustaining angles, the above method works if one sustaining side is adjacent to $P_{n+k}P_{n+k+1}$ by constructing the point on the side (halfplane) containing the sustaining side, and if there are sustaining sides adjacent to our side on both ends then draw a parallel through any one and it works, after we get two parallel sides note that we can "translate" them to move over the circle to reduce the sum of sustaining angles and to ensure the process doesnt get stuck.
By the above global claim and using the fact that the maximum is largest amongst all values we get that all sustaining angles are infact equal.**Claim 4:** If the scores for each quadrilateral $P_iP_{i+1}P_{i+n}P_{i+n+1}$ are the same and equal to the scores for a regular polygon then the polygon is regular.
ProofIf the polygon is not already regular, that means it is not affine, which means by the process in the proof of previous claim we can further reduce the sum of angles, contradiction! so we are done!

stem_md: Let  $\mathbb R^+$  be the set of positive real numbers. Let  $f \colon \mathbb{R}^+\to\mathbb{R}^+$  be a function such that for all  $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^+$  it holds that \[ yf^{2025}(x) \geq xf(y)\,. \] Show that there exists a positive integer  $n_0$  such that for all integers  $n\geq n_0$  and for all  $x>0$  it holds that \[f^n(x)\geq x.\] (Here,  $f^n$  means  $n$ -fold composition of  $f.$ )
solution_md: Let  $P(x,y)$  denote the assertion   $$ yf^{2025}(x) \geq xf(y) $$  By substituting we get $P(x,x)\implies f^{2025}(x) \geq f(x)$ Then we easily get  $f^{n+2025}(x)\ge f^{n+1}(x).   (*)$  $P(x, f^{2024}(x))\implies f^{2024}(x)\ge x$ Let's assume there exists  $a$  such that  $f^{2025}(a)<a$ . Then by  $P(a, f^{2023}(a))$  we get  $f^{2023}(a)>a$ . Inductively,  $f^n(a)>a$  for all  $n<2025$ . Then we get  $f^{2025}(a)\ge f(a)>a$ , which is a contradiction. We will prove the next claim. $\text{Claim.}$  If there exists a  $k$ -element set   $$ S=\{f^m(x), f^{m+1}(x),...,f^{m+k-1}(x)\} $$  such that each element is bigger than or equal to  $x$ , then there exists a set with the same properties, but  $k+1$  elements. $\text{Proof.}$  Just notice that   $$ f^{2m+l}(x)\ge f^{m+l}(x)\ge x, 0\le l\le k-1 $$  and  $$ f^{2m+k}(x)\ge f^{m+1}(x)\ge x $$  proving the claim. $\square$ We keep doing this until  $k>>2025$ . Then, by  $(*)$  and induction we are done;  $$ f^{m+k+1}(x)\ge f^{m+k-2023}(x)\ge x $$   $\square$

stem_md:
On an infinite square grid, on which some unit squares are coloured red, a *ruby rook* is a piece which, in one move, can travel any number of squares in one direction parallel to one of the grid lines (either vertically or horizontally), while remaining on red squares at all times throughout the move.

Starting with an uncoloured infinite square grid, Alice performs the following procedure: 
- First, she colours at most 2025 of the unit squares red.
- Afterwards, she places some ruby rooks on distinct red unit squares, such that the following two rules are satisfied:
(i) no ruby rook can reach another ruby rook in one move,
(ii) every ruby rook can reach every other ruby rook in two moves.

Find the maximum possible number of ruby rooks that Alice can place during this procedure.

*Proposed by Mark Neumann, Switzerland.*
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>We claim the answer is  $\boxed{63}$ . For a construction, fill a  $63$  by  $63$  isosceles right triangle with all red squares, and place the ruby rooks on the squares of the hypotenuse. For a bound, suppose there are  $n$  ruby rooks. We first note that no two ruby rooks lie in the same row/column. For any pair of ruby rooks  $A$  and  $B$ , there exists a red square  $S$ , where the path is  $A \rightarrow S \rightarrow B$ . Call  $S$  the shoulder of  $A$  and  $B$ . Now, take a square  $X$  which is a shoulder. Suppose there exists ruby rooks  $P,Q,R$  which all have  $X$  as their shoulder. Note that as we can go from  $P$  to  $X$ ,  $P$  either lies in the same row or column. By similar reasoning, so do  $Q$  and  $R$ . By PHP, two ruby rooks lie in the same row/column, a contradiction. Therefore, any shoulder  $X$  has a unique pair of rooks  $A,B$  which are it's shoulders. Then, there are at least  $\binom{n}{2}$  shoulders (one for each pair of ruby rooks). As no shoulder has a rook on it, there are at least  $n + \binom{n}{2}$  red squares, and so  $n + \binom{n}{2} \le 2025$ , giving  $n \le 63$ .</details>

stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be a triangle. Its incircle  $\omega$  touches the sides  $BC, CA$  and  $AB$  at points  $D, E$  and  $F,$  respectively. Let  $P$  and  $Q$  be points on the line  $BC$  distinct from  $D$  such that  $PB = BD$  and  $QC = CD.$  Prove that the circumcircles of the triangles  $PCE$  and  $QBF$  and the circle  $\omega$  pass through a common point.
solution_md:
WLOG let  $AC > AB$ . Let  $X$  be the center of the spiral similarity that sends  $PF$  to  $QE$ . **Claim 1:**  $X \in (DEF)$ . 
*Proof:*With complex bashing. Take  $(DEF)$  as the unit circle. Then  $|d|=|e|=|f|=1$ .  $b = \frac{2df}{d+f}, \; c = \frac{2ed}{e+d}, \; p = \frac{3df-d^2}{d+f}, \; q = \frac{3ed-d^2}{e+d}.$ By spiral similarity:  $\frac{x-p}{x-f} = \frac{x-q}{x-e} \;\Rightarrow\; x = \frac{ep-fq}{e+p-f-q}.$ Substituting values gives  $x = \frac{3def - d^2e - d^2f - d^3}{3d^2 - de - df - ef}.$ Its conjugate is  $\overline{x} = \frac{\tfrac{3}{def} - \tfrac{1}{d^2e} - \tfrac{1}{d^2f} - \tfrac{1}{d^3}}{\tfrac{3}{d^2} - \tfrac{1}{de} - \tfrac{1}{df} - \tfrac{1}{ef}} = \frac{3d^2 - de - df - ef}{3def - d^2e - d^2f - d^3}.$ Thus  $x \cdot \overline{x} = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; X \in (DEF).$ Let  $\angle ABC = 2\alpha$  and  $\angle ACB = 2\beta$ . By spiral similarity  $\triangle XPF \sim \triangle XQE$ . Hence  $\angle PXF = \angle QXE = \gamma$  and  $\angle XPF = \angle XQE = \theta$ . 

Also  $\frac{XP}{XQ} = \frac{XF}{XE}, \; \angle PXQ = \angle FXE$ , so  $\triangle PXQ \sim \triangle FXE$ .  $(\ast)$ Since  $PB=DB=FB$  and  $DC=QC=EC$ , we have  $\angle FPB = \alpha, \; \angle EQC = \beta, \; \angle PFD = \angle QED = 90^\circ.$ Thus  $\angle XPQ = \alpha + \theta, \; \angle XQP = \beta - \theta.$ From  $(\ast)$  we get  $\angle XFE = \alpha + \theta, \; \angle XEF = \beta - \theta.$ By cyclicity:  $\angle FDX = \angle FEX = \beta - \theta.$ Now  $\angle FPX + \angle PXD + \angle FDX = \angle PFD = 90^\circ,$  so  $\theta + (\beta - \theta) + \angle PXD = 90^\circ \;\Rightarrow\; \angle PXD = 90^\circ - \beta.$ Also  $\angle PXD = \angle PXF + \angle DXF \;\Rightarrow\; 90^\circ - \beta = \gamma + \angle FXD,$  so  $\angle FXD = 90^\circ - \beta - \gamma.$ From tangency of  $AB$  to  $(DEF)$  and cyclicity:  $\angle FXD = \angle FED = 90^\circ - \alpha.$ Thus  $90^\circ - \beta - \gamma = 90^\circ - \alpha \;\Rightarrow\; \gamma = \alpha - \beta.$ By cyclicity:  $\angle FXE = 180^\circ - \alpha - \beta.$ So  $\angle PXE = 180^\circ - \alpha - \beta + \gamma = 180^\circ - 2\beta.$ Hence  $\angle PXE + \angle PCE = 180^\circ \;\Rightarrow\; P,C,E,X \text{ are concyclic}.$ Also  $\angle FXQ = 180^\circ - \alpha - \beta - \gamma = 180^\circ - 2\alpha.$ Thus  $\angle FXQ + \angle FBQ = 180^\circ \;\Rightarrow\; B,F,Q,X \text{ are concyclic}.$ Therefore the intersection of  $(PCE)$  and  $(QBF)$  is  $X \in (DEF)$ .  $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
A subset  $S$  of the integers is called *Saxonian* if for every three pairwise different elements  $a, b, c\in S$  the number  $ab+c$  is a perfect square. Prove that any Saxonian set is finite and determine the largest possible number of elements that a Saxonian set can have.

*Proposed by Lukas Novak, Croatia.*
solution_md:
Note that  $S$  could also have negative elements, in which case the argument has to be modified a little, but idea stays the same (it's just technical details).

Suppose there is a Saxonian set  $S$  with  $|S|=4$ . If all four elements are non-negative, then the solutions above give contradiction. Hence assume  $S$  has a negative element  $c<0$ . If  $0\in S$ , then  $a\cdot 0 + c=c<0$  would have to be square – impossible, so  $0\not\in S$ . If  $S$  had two positive elements  $a>b>0$ , then  $ac+b<0$  has to be a square – again impossible. So  $S$  has at most one positive element, hence at least three negative elements  $a<b<c<0$ . If the last element  $d$  was positive, then  $ad+b<0$  is square – absurd. So all four elements of  $S$  must be negative.

Define a set  $S\subseteq \mathbb{N}$  to be *anti-Saxonian* if for all distinct  $a,b,c\in S$  we have  $ab-c$  is square. Then the problem now becomes equivalent to whether there exists an anti-Saxonian set with four elements (positive by definition). Let the elements be  $a>b>c>d>0$  and let  $ab-d=x^2$ . Then:
\[   x^2=ab-d>ab-b=b(a-1) \geq b^2,  \]
so  $x>b$ . Note that  $c-d<c<b<x$ , hence
\[ x^2 = ab-d > ab-c = (ab-d)  - (c-d) = x^2 - (c-d) > x^2 - x \geq (x-1)^2,   \]
which gives the same contradiction as before.

Note that for example  $S=\{0,1,4\}$  is also Saxonian – an even easier construction.

Further, note that  $S=\{-2,-3,-6\}$  is Saxonian, and so is for example  $S=\{  -2,-6,-11\}$ .

Claim:A Saxonian set S can have at most 3 elements.

Proof: 
Assume for contradiction that \(S\) has more than 3 elements. 
Then there exist four distinct integers \(a > b > c > d\) in \(S\) satisfying the given condition.

Since \(ab + d\) must be a perfect square, write
\[
ab + d = x^2, \quad \text{with } x > b.
\]
Similarly, \(ab + c\) is also a perfect square. But
\[
ab + c = ab + d + (c-d) = x^2 + (c-d).
\]
Because \(c < b < x\), we have
\[
0 < c-d < b-d < b < x,
\]
which implies
\[
x^2 < ab + c < x^2 + x.
\]
But there is no perfect square strictly between \(x^2\) and \(x^2 + x\), 
a contradiction. 

Therefore, \(S\) can have at most 3 elements. 

\[
\text{Example: } S = \{1,7,9\}.
\]

Consider the lowest difference among consecutive elements among the first n-2, (say a_{i+1}-a_i) then considered the squares formed by the largest element along with these elements respectively, and bound n, where the elements are in ascending order.
Same construction as above

Suppose firstly that there are four distinct non-negative integers  $a>b>c>d$  satisfiying the requirement. In particular,  $ab+c$  and  $ab+d$  must be perfect squares. If  $ab + d = x^2$ , then  $ab \leq x^2$  and from here also  $b<x$ , as  $a>b$ . Hence  $x^2 = ab + d < ab + c < ab + b < ab + x < x^2 + x \leq (x+1)^2$ , so in particular  $ab+c$  is between two consecutive squares, hence cannot be a perfect square. (Just realized that this argument should also work if we desired  $k$ -th powers for any fixed  $k$ , not only  $k=2$ .)

Now finding a triple of distinct (positive)  $a,b,c$  such that  $ab+c, bc+a, ca+b$  are squares is easy - bravely set  $c=1$ , so we want  $ab+1$  and  $a+b$  to be squares; now testing small squares for  $a+b$  leads to the (smallest) examples  $a=9, b=7$  and  $a=12, b = 4$ .
Proposed by Lukas Novak, Croatia.

What.
Suppose there was a Saxonian set with at least  $4$  elements, then pick the largest  $4$  to be  $a>b>c>d$ , now notice that  $ab+d=n^2$  satisfies that  $n>b$  as  $ab>b^2$  but also  $ab+c=m^2$  and this means  $n^2+n>n^2+b>n^2+c-d=m^2>n^2$  should happen but there is no integer square between  $\left(n+\frac{1}{2} \right)^2$  and  $n^2$  so we get a contradiction!.
A Saxonian set with  $3$  elements that works would be  $(0,1,4)$  because if  $0$  is either  $a$  or  $b$  we are done and otherwise the perfect square is  $4$  so we are done :D.

stem_md:
Bob has  $n$  coins with integer values   $$ c_1 \ge c_2 \ge \dots \ge c_n > 0\,. $$   He is standing in front of a vending machine that offers  $n$  candy bars with positive integer costs  $b_1, b_2, \dots , b_n.$  Bob notices that for every  $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ , it holds that   $$ b_1 + b_2 + \dots + b_i \ge c_1 + c_2 + \dots + c_i. $$   Furthermore, the total value of Bob's coins equals the sum of the costs of all the candy bars. The candy bars can be purchased in any order. In order to buy the  $i$ -th candy bar, Bob has to insert coins of total value at least  $b_i$ . However, the machine does not give him back any change.

Prove that Bob can buy at least half of the candy bars.
solution_md:
I believe your solution is not correct but it can be corrected. For example, take the following construction: Let  $ n=9 $  and let  $ b_{1}=b_{4}=b_{7}=7 $  while let every other item have a cost of 1. Now if all of our coins have a value of 3 then the conditions of the problem are satisfied. However, we cannot buy  $ b_{7} $  using only two coins which contradicts your assumption.

My solution is the following. Let's start with a rearranging of the items. Let  $ a_{1}=max(b_{1}, ..., b_{n}) $  and let  $ a_{i} $  equal the  $ i$ th largest value of the items. Notice that we can rearrange the items in decreasing order without contradicting the assumptions of the problem. That is, for every  $i\in \{1, ..., n\} $  it holds that  $a_{1}+...+a_{i} \geq b_{1}+...+b_{i} \geq c_{1}+...+c_{i} $  and the sum of the items remained the same. (I think this rearranging corrects your solution too.)

As mentioned previously, the condition rewrites as  $ c_{k}+...+c_{n} \geq a_{k}+...+a_{n} $ . Now we can buy  $a_{n}$  using the coin  $c_{n}$  and we claim that we can buy item  $a_{n-j}$  using the coins  $c_{n-2j+1}$  and  $c_{n-2j}$ . 

FTSOC, suppose  $c_{n-2j+1} + c_{n-2j} < a_{n-j}$ . This gives us  $c_{n} \leq c_{n-1}+c_{n-2} \leq ... \leq c_{n-2j+1} + c_{n-2j} < a_{n-j} \leq a_{n-j-1} \leq ... \leq a_{n-2j}$ . So we get  $c_{n}<a_{n-j}$ , and  $c_{n-1}+c_{n-2}<a_{n-j-1}$ , ..., and  $c_{n-2j+1} + c_{n-2j}<a_{n-2j}$ . However, adding the two sides together we would get  $c_{n}+...+c_{n-2j} < a_{n-j}+...+a_{n-2j} \leq a_{n}+...+a_{n-2j}$  which is a contradiction.

Therefore, we can buy item  $a_{n-j}$  using the coins  $c_{n-2j+1}$  and  $c_{n-2j}$  for every  $j\in \{ 1, 2, ..., \lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor \}$  and we can buy  $a_{n}$  using the coin  $c_{n}$ . That gives us  $\lceil \frac{n}{2} \rceil$  items that we can purchase.

stem_md: Let  $\mathbb R^+$  be the set of positive real numbers. Determine all functions  $f\colon\mathbb  R^+ \rightarrow\mathbb R^+$  such that for all numbers  $x, y\in\mathbb R^+,$  we have   $$ f(xy) + f(x) = f(y)f\bigl(xf(y)\bigr) + f(x)f(y) $$   and there exists at most one number  $a\in\mathbb R^+$  such that  $f(a) = 1.$ *Proposed by Mykhailo Shtandenko and Serhii Mytsyk, Ukraine .*
solution_md:
$$ f(xy) + f(x) = f(y)f\bigl(xf(y)\bigr) + f(x)f(y) $$  Let  $f(1)=a$ ;  $k= \frac{f(a)}{a}$  $\textbf{Claim 1}: f(xa)=f(x).k$  $P(1,1): f(a)=2-a$  $P(x,1): 2f(x)=af(xa)+af(x) \rightarrow f(xa).a=f(x)(2-a)=f(x)f(a)=> f(xa)=f(x).k \blacksquare$  $\textbf{Claim 2}: f(xk)f(a)=f(x)f(f(a))$  $P(x,ya):$    $$ kf(xy)+f(x)=kf(y)f(xkf(y))+kf(x)f(y) $$    $$ \rightarrow kf(xy)+f(x)-kf(x)f(y)=kf(y)f(xkf(y))=kf(xyk)+kf(xk)-kf(xk)f(y) $$    $$  \Leftrightarrow kf(xy)+f(x)-kf(x)f(y)=kf(xyk)+kf(xk)-kf(xk)f(y) (1) $$  Put  $y=1$  in (1), we have:  $kf(x)+f(x)-akf(x)=kf(xk)+kf(xk)-akf(xk) \rightarrow kf(xk)f(a)=f(x)(k+1-ka)$  $P(1,a): f(f(a))=1+\frac{a}{f(a)}-a=\frac{k+1-ka}{k}$ This give  $f(xk)f(a)=f(x)f(f(a))$  or  $f(xk)=f(x).\dfrac{f(f(a))}{f(a)}(2)$  $\textbf{Claim 3}: f(1)=1$ Put (2) in (1):   $$ kf(xy)+f(x)-kf(x)f(y)=k\dfrac{f(f(a))}{f(a)}\left(f(xy)+f(x)-f(x)f(y)\right)(3) $$  Put  $x=1$  in (3):  $$ kf(y)+a-kaf(y)=\dfrac{f(f(a))}{a}\left(f(y)+a-af(y)\right) $$  Thus, easy to see that  $f$  is not constant then  $k-ka=\dfrac{f(f(a))}{a}(1-a)$  and  $a=f(f(a))$ If  $a \ne 1$  then  $k=1$ . 
Thus,  $\dfrac{1+1-a.1}{1}=f(f(a))=a$  or  $a=1(contradiction)$ So,  $f(1)=1$  $\textbf{Claim 4}: f$  is injective
Suppose there exist  $u<v$  such that  $f(u)=f(v)$  then  $P(x,u)+P(x,v)$  give contradiction $\textbf{Claim 5}: f((f(x)^2)=f(f(x))^2$   $P(1,x): f(x)f(f(x))=1$   $P(f(x),f(x)): 1=f(f(x)^2)+f(f(x))=f(f(x)).1+f(f(x))^2\rightarrow f((f(x)^2)=f(f(x))^2$  $\textbf{Claim 6}: f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$  $P(f(y),y): f(yf(y))+f(f(y))=f(y)f(f(y)^2)+1=f(y)f(f(y))^2+1=f(f(y))+1$ Thus,  $f(yf(y))=1$  then  $\boxed{f(x)=\frac{1}{x}, \forall x \in \mathbb{R^+}}$

stem_md:
Let  $n$  be a positive integer. In the province of Laplandia there are  $100n$  cities, each two connected by a direct road and each of these roads has a toll station collecting a positive amount of toll revenue. For each road, the revenue of its toll station is split equally between the two cities at the ends of the road (meaning that each of the two cities receives half of the income). For each city, the total toll revenue is given by the sum of the revenues it receives from the  $100n-1$  toll stations on its roads.

According to a new law, the revenues of some of the toll stations will be collected by the federal government instead of by the adjacent cities. The governor of Laplandia is allowed to choose those toll stations. The mayors of the cities demand that for each city, the sum of the remaining revenues it receives from the other toll stations after this change is at least  $99\%$  of its former total toll revenue.

Find the largest positive integer  $k,$  depending on  $n,$  such that the governor can always choose  $k$  toll stations for the federal government to collect the toll revenue, while satisfying the demand of the city mayors.

*Proposed by Paulius Aleknavičius, Lithuania.*
solution_md:
Here is a lower bound, that may not be the sharpest, but is very close to it.

Let  $G(V,E)$  be the corresponding complete graph. For each edge  $e\in E$  let  $a_e$  be it's toll tax. The idea is that to assign a variable to each edge that has the value  $1$  if this edge is chosen and the value  $0$  if it is not. But to avoid some of the difficulties that this discrete configuration requires, we allow the variables to have values between  $0$  and  $1$ . We'll see that it can be arranged so that most of the variables have the value  $1$  and only a small portion of them be positive but less than  $1$ . 
To each edge we assign a variable  $x_e$ . The conditions these variable must satisfy are  $$ \sum_{e: v\in e}a_e x_e= \frac{1}{100}\sum_{e: v\in e} a_e\,,\, \forall v\in V\,;\, x_e\in [0,1], \forall e\in E \qquad(1). $$  We want to maximize  $f(x_e):=\sum_{e\in E} x_e.$  

Note that  $x_e:=1/100$  satisfy (1) and for these values,  $f=|E|/100=n(50n-\frac{1}{2})$ . This means  $\max f\ge n(50n-\frac{1}{2})$ . 
Let  $x'_e\in[0,1], e\in E$  be the values that maximize  $f(x_e)$  and for which  $m:=\#\{e\in E : x'_e\in (0,1)\}$  is minimal. We will prove  $m\le |V|=100n$ Suppose on the contrary  $m>|V|$  and let  $E':=\{e\in E: x'_e\in (0,1)\}$ . Consider the system of equations with respect to  $y_e,e\in E'$ :  $$ \sum_{e:v\in e\in E'}a_e y_e=0\,;\, \forall v\in V. $$  We have a system with at most  $|V|$  equations and at least  $|V|+1$  variables. So, it has non-zero solution  $y_e, e\in E'$ . Let us set  $y_e:=0, \forall e\in E\setminus E'$ . Consider the values  $x_e:=x'_e+\varepsilon y_e,e\in E$ . These values satisfy  $(1)$  for small  $\varepsilon$ . Since  $f(x_e)$  is a linear function, it will be non-decreasing either for  $\varepsilon >0$  or for  $\varepsilon <0$ . Therefore, putting appropriate  $\varepsilon$  we can make at least one  $x_e, e\in E'$  either  $0$  or  $1$ . In this way  $f(x_e)\ge f(x'_e)$  but  $\#\{e\in E : x_e\in (0,1)\}$  will decrease, which contradicts the extremality of  $x'_e$ .

Now, since  $f(x'_e)\ge n(50n-\frac{1}{2})$  and the number of non-zero values  $x'_e$  which are less than  $1$  is at most  $100n$ , we obtain  $$ \#\{e\in E : x'_e=1\}\ge n\left(50n-\frac{1}{2}\right)-100n. $$  So, we can chose the edges corresponding to  $x'_e=1$  and satisfy the demands of the mayors.

stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be an acute triangle with  $AB<AC.$  Denote by  $D$  the foot of the perpendicular from  $A$  to  $BC.$  Let  $E$  be the point such that  $ABEC$  is a parallelogram. Let  $M$  be a point inside triangle  $ABC$  such that  $MB=MC.$  Let  $F$  be the reflection of point  $D$  across the tangent to the circumcircle of triangle  $ADM$  at point  $M.$  Prove that  $AF=DE.$
solution_md:
Complex bash: Define  $(ADM)$  to be the unit circle in the complex plane, and denote complex numbers corresponding to points as usual with their lowercase letters. So  $a \bar a = d \bar d = m \bar m = 1$ . Let  $D'$  be the reflection of  $D$  across the midpoint of  $BC$ ; as  $AD' = DE$  for symmetry, it suffices to prove  $AD' = AF$ .

We first need to express  $d'$  in terms of  $a$ ,  $d$ ,  $m$ . If we denote the midpoint of  $BC$  by  $N$ , we have  $d' = 2n - d$ . Let  $A'$  be the point diametrically opposite to  $A$  on  $(ADM)$ , so  $a' = -a$ , which lies on  $BC$  as  $AD \perp A'D$ . Now  $N$  is the projection of  $M$  onto  $BC = A'D$ , which is well known to be \[
  n = \frac{1}{2}(m + a' + d - a'd \bar m)
\] and therefore \[
  d' = 2n - d = m + a' - a'd \bar m = m - a + ad \bar m.
\]

Similarly, the reflection of  $D$  across the tangent at  $M$  is well known to be \[
  f = 2m - m^2 \bar d.
\] The claim  $AD' = AF$  is now equivalent to  $(a - d')(\bar a - \overline{d'}) = (a - f)(\bar a - \bar f)$ . As \[
  a - d' = 2a - m - ad \bar m = \bar m (2am - m^2 - ad)
\] and \[
  \bar a - \bar f = \bar a - 2 \bar m + \bar m^2 d = \bar a \bar m^2 (m^2 - 2am + ad),
\] we obtain indeed that \[
  (a - d')(a - \overline{d'}) = (a - f)(\bar a - \bar f) = (m^2 - 2am + ad) \overline{(m^2 - 2am + ad)},
\] so the problem statement is proved.

solution_md:
Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with an interior point $D$ such that $\angle BDC+\angle BAC=180^\circ.$ The lines $BD$ and $AC$ intersect at the point $E,$ and the lines $CD$ and $AB$ intersect at the point $F.$ The points ${P \neq E}$ and ${Q \neq F}$ lie on the line $EF$ so that $BP=BE$ and $CQ=CF.$ Assume that the segments $AP$ and $AQ$ intersect the circumcircle $\omega$ of $ABC$ at the points $R \neq A$ and $S \neq A,$ respectively. Prove that the lines $RF$ and $SE$ intersect on $\omega.$
Let $X:=BP\cap CQ$ . By angle chasing $X$ lies on $\omega$ . Let $Y:=BS\cap CR$ . By Pascal's theorem applied to $BSARCX$ , $Y$ lies on the line $PQ=EF$ . Let $Z\neq S$ be the second intersection of $SE$ with $\omega$ . Using Pascal's theorem applied to $BSZRCA$ , $Z$ must lie on $RF$ .

stem_md: Let  $n$  be a positive integer such that the *sum* of positive divisors of  $n^2+n+1$  is divisible by 3. Prove that it is possible to partition the set of positive divisors of  $n^2+n+1$  into three sets such that the *product* of all elements in each set is the same.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>First of all, by considering orders,  $n^2+n+1$  has no prime factors  $\equiv 2 \pmod{3}$ .
Then by considering the formula for  $\sigma(m)$ , we see that  $\sigma(n^2+n+1)$  is divisible by  $3$  iff some  $p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$  has  $v_p(n^2+n+1) \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$ .
If  $v_p$  is odd, i.e.  $6k+5$ , we can group the powers of  $p$  into groups of  $3$  with the same product (e.g.  $(1,p^5), (p,p^4), (p^2,p^3)$ ) and just multiply all the remaining divisors of  $n^2+n+1$  to them.
If  $v_p$  is even, since clearly  $n^2+n+1$  is not a pefect square (lying between  $n^2$  and  $(n+1)^2$ ), we must have another prime  $q$  appearing an odd number of times. But then we can still put divisors having at least  $p^3$  as before in groups of six.
Finally, with those having  $1,p$  or  $p^2$  we make groups  $(q,p^2), (pq, p), (p^2q,1)$  and just multiply with all the remaining divisors (and potentially higher powers of  $q$ ). Done!</details>

We now claim that  $n^2+n+1$  is not a perfect square; we indeed have that \[n^2+n+1=m^2\iff (2m)^2-(2n+1)^2=3\] has no solutions with  $n\geq 1$ . Now divide the divisors of  $n^2+n+1$  into  $\frac{1}{2}\tau(n^2+n+1)$  pairs multiplying to  $n^2+n+1$ , and divide these pairs into  $3$  groups containing  $\frac{1}{6}\tau(n^2+n+1)$  pairs each. Then the product within each group is  $(n^2+n+1)^{\frac{1}{6}\tau(n^2+n+1)}$ .

stem_md:
Determine whether the following statement is true for every polynomial  $P$  of degree at least 2 with nonnegative integer coefficients: *there exists a positive integer  $m$  such that for infinitely many positive integers  $n$  the number  $P^{n}(m)$  has more than  $n$  distinct positive divisors*. (Here,  $P^n$  denotes  $P$  applied  $n$  times.)

*Proposed by Paulius Aleknavičius, Lithuania.*
solution_md:
Good problem. The answer is <details><summary>answer.</summary>yes.</details>
<details><summary>Proof</summary>We consider two cases:

1.  $P(0)=0$ .
It suffices to take  $m=2$ . We have  $P^{n}(2)\mid P^{n+1}(2)$  (since  $x\mid P(x)$  because  $P(0)=0$ ) and  $P^{n}(2)<P^{n+1}(2)$  (since  $P(x)>x$  for  $x\geq2$ ). These facts together imply  $d(P^{n}(m))<d(P^{n+1}(m))$ , which completes this case.

2.  $P(0)\neq 0$ .
Here we take  $m=P(0)>0$ . We will prove that the statement of the problem holds for  $n=2^k-1$  for arbitrary nonnegative integer  $k$  by induction on  $k$ . (Base case of  $k=0$  is trivial)
First, notice that  $P^{2^k}(0)-0\mid P^{2^k}(P^{2^k}(0))-P^{2^k}(0)$ , so  $P^{2^k}(0)\mid P^{2^{k+1}}(0)$ . Next, since  $P^{2^k}(x)>x^2$  for nonnegative integers  $x$ , we also have  $\left(P^{2^k}(0)\right)^2<P^{2^{k+1}}(0)$ . Therefore the divisors  $d_1<d_2<\cdots<d_l$  of  $P^{2^k}(0)$  are distinct from the numbers  $\frac{P^{2^{k+1}}(0)}{d_i}$ . Both these numbers and the  $d_i$  divide  $P^{2^{k+1}}(0)$ , which proves that  $d(P^{2^{k+1}}(0))\geq 2d(P^{2^k}(0))$ , which is the induction step that completes the proof.</details>

solution_md:
Let $n$ be a positive integer greater than $2$ . Find all functions $f: \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ satisfying: $(f(x+y))^{n} = f(x^{n})+f(y^{n}),$ for all integers $x,y$
Let $P(x,y)$ be the assertion $f(x+y)^n=f(x^n)+f(y^n)$ $P(0,0)$ $\implies$ $f(0)^n=2f(0)$ and so $f(0)=0$ $P(x,0)$ $\implies$ $f(x)^n=f(x^n)$ and so $P(x,y)$ may be written $f(x+y)^n=f(x)^n+f(y)^n$ And so $f(2x)^n=2f(x)^n$ and so $\boxed{f(x)=0\quad\forall x\in\mathbb Z}$ , which indeed fits

stem_md: Let $p$ be a prime and suppose $2^{2p} \equiv 1 (\text{mod}$ $ 2p+1)$ is prime. Prove that $2p+1$ is prime $^{1}$ $^{1}$ This is a special case of Pocklington's theorem. A proof of this special case is required.
solution_md:
If  $p=2$  this is clear since  $2\cdot 2 + 1 = 5$ . Let the order of  $2$  modulo  $2p+1$  be  $g$ . This exists by the given congruence. We have  $g\mid 2p\implies g \in \{1,2,p,2p\}$ .  $g=1$  and  $g=2$  obviously fail, and if  $g=2p$ , then  $2p\mid \varphi(2p+1)\implies \varphi(2p+1)=2p$ , so  $2p+1$  is prime. So suppose  $g=p$ . Let  $2p+1 = p_1^{\alpha_1}\dots p_{k}^{\alpha_k}$  be the canonical factorization of  $2p+1$  so that
\[\varphi\left(2p+1\right)=p_1^{\alpha_1-1}\left(p_1-1\right)\dots p_k^{\alpha_k-1}\left(p_k-1\right)\]
Since  $p$  divides this and  $p\nmid 2p+1$ , we have  $p\mid p_i-1$  for some  $i\in\{1,2,\dots,k\}$  so that  $p<p_i$ . Let  $2p+1=mp_i$ . If  $m\ge 2$ , then
\[2p+1 = mp_i\ge m\left(p+1\right)\ge 2p+2\]
contradiction. So  $m=1$ . So  $2p+1=p_i$ , as desired.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be an acute triangle with orthocenter  $H$  and circumcenter  $O$ . Let  $E$  and  $F$  be points on the line segments  $AC$  and  $AB$  respectively such that  $AEHF$  is a parallelogram. Prove that  $\vert OE \vert = \vert OF \vert$ .
solution_md:
Call  $M$  the midpoint of  $AH$ . Since  $AFHE$  is a parallelogram,  $M$  is also the midpoint of  $EF$ . Define  $X$  as the  $A$ -antipode in  $(ABC)$ . It is well known that  $HBXC$  is a parallelogram, and since  $\angle BHC = \angle BXC = \pi - \angle A$   $\Longrightarrow$  parallelogram  $AFHE$  is similar to  $HBXC$ . 
In particular this implies  $\Delta HXC \sim \Delta AEF$ , and since  $\angle CHE = \pi - (\angle A) - (\frac{\pi}{2} - \angle A) = \frac{\pi}{2} $ , there is a rotation by  $\frac{\pi}{2}$  centered at  $H$  that sends  $X\mapsto X’$  and  $C\mapsto C’$ . Thus,  $HX’ \parallel EF$  and rotating back gives  $HX \perp EF$ . A homothety cantered at  $A$  with factor  $\frac{1}{2}$  sends  $H\mapsto M$  and  $X\mapsto O$ . Since  $HX\perp EF\Longrightarrow OM\perp EF$ . Thus  $O$  is on the perpendicular bisector of  $EF$  which implies  $\vert OE \vert = \vert OF \vert$ , as required.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Denote by  $S_{n}$  the set of all permutations of the set  $\{1,2,\dots, n\}$ . Let  $\sigma \in S_{n}$  be a permutation. We define the  $\textit{displacement}$  of  $\sigma$  to be the number  $d(\sigma)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \vert \sigma(i)-i \vert$ . We saw that  $\sigma$  is  $\textit{maximally}$   $\textit{displacing}$  if  $d(\sigma)$  is the largest possible, i.e. if  $d(\sigma) \geq d({\pi})$ , for all  $\pi \in S_{n}$ . $\text{a)}$     Suppose  $\sigma$  is a maximally displacing permutation of  $\{1,2, \dots, 2024\}$ . Yes.

{1,2,5,6,10,11,14,15,19,20,23,24,...,2017,2018,2021,2022} which has a total of 2025*4/9=900 numbers.

To prove it is optimal, it can simply be checked that for any set of 9 consecutive integers, taking any 5 of them will create a gap of 2 or 7.
So assume by contradiction there is some 5-number subset of 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 that works. In each pair of {1,3}, {2,4}, {5,7}, and {6,8}, only one can be included. Thus 9 must be in the set. On the other hand, in each pair of {1,8}, {3,5}, {4,6}, and {7,9}, only one can be included. So 2 must be in the set as well. But 9-2=7 contradiction. So only 4 numbers can be included in {9k+1,...9k+9} for each k from 0 to 224, implying at most 4*225=900 numbers.

stem_md: A positive integer is written on a blackboard. Carmela can perform the following operation as many times as she wants: replace the current integer  $x$  with another positive integer  $y$ , as long as  $|x^2 - y^2|$  is a perfect square. For example, if the number on the blackboard is  $17$ , Carmela can replace it with  $15$ , because  $|17^2 - 15^2| = 8^2$ , then replace it with  $9$ , because  $|15^2 - 9^2| = 12^2$ . If the number on the blackboard is initially  $3$ , determine all integers that Carmela can write on the blackboard after finitely many operations.
solution_md:
Firstly, it is obvious that all numbers from  $3$  to  $7$  can be written after finitely many operations. $4:3\rightarrow5\rightarrow4;5:3\rightarrow5;6:3\rightarrow5\rightarrow13\rightarrow12\rightarrow20\rightarrow25\rightarrow24\rightarrow26\rightarrow10\rightarrow6;7:3\rightarrow5\rightarrow13\rightarrow12\rightarrow20\rightarrow25\rightarrow7.$ Nextly, we prove that for all  $n$  is a positive integer, if  $n$  can be constructed then  $n+2$  can.
Induction: If for all  $n\leq 2k-1(k\geq5)$ , the lemma is true, then it shall be true for  $n=2k$  and  $n=2k+1$ .
Using induction, we first prove the lemma for odd  $n$ . Let's say that  $n=2k+1$ , then  $n^2=(2k^2+2k+1)^2-(2k^2+2k)^2$ , so we have  $n\rightarrow2k^2+2k+1\rightarrow2k^2+2k$ . To replace  $2k^2+2k$  with  $2k^2+6k+4$ , since  $\frac{2k^2+6k+4}{2k^2+2k}=\frac{k+3}{k+1}$ , then it can obviously be constructed by the process of  $k+1\rightarrow k+3$ . Clearly  $k+1<2k-1$ , so it can be constructed.
We then prove the lemma for all even  $n$ . Say  $n=2k$ , then  $n^2=(k^2+1)^2-(k^2-1)^2$ . If  $2k-4$  can be written, then since  $\frac{(k^2-1)}{(k-2)^2-1}=\frac{k+1}{k-3}$ , and obiously if  $k-3$  can be written then  $k+1$  can be written.
Therefore, all positive integers  $n$  that satisfies  $n\geq3$  can be written at some point.

stem_md: Let  $d$  be a positive integer. Define the sequence  $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$  such that \[\begin{cases} a_1 = 1  a_{n+1} = n\left\lfloor\frac{a_n}{n}\right\rfloor + d, \quad n \ge 1.\end{cases}\] Prove that there exists a positive integer  $M$  such that  $a_M, a_{M+1}, a_{M+2}, \dots$  is an arithmetic sequence.
solution_md:
Let  $b_n = \frac{a_n}{n}$ We have   $$ b_{n+1} = \frac{n}{n+1} \lfloor b_n \rfloor + \frac{d}{n+1} $$  Hence, for large enough  $n+1 >d$ ,  $\lfloor b_{n+1} \rfloor= \lfloor b_n \rfloor -1$ , if  $d \leqslant \lfloor b_n \rfloor$  and  $\lfloor b_{n+1} \rfloor= \lfloor b_n \rfloor$  otherwise.
Thus, for some  $N > d$ , we have   $$  x = \lfloor b_N \rfloor = \lfloor b_{N+1} \rfloor \leqslant d $$  That is the sequence  $\lfloor b_n \rfloor$  is eventually constant. Thus, we have   $$ a_{N+1} = Nx + d $$   for  $N >M$  for some positive integer  $M$ .

stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be a triangle with incenter  $I$ , and let  $D$  be a point on side  $BC$ . Points  $X$  and  $Y$  are chosen on lines  $BI$  and  $CI$  respectively such that  $DXIY$  is a parallelogram. Points  $E$  and  $F$  are chosen on side  $BC$  such that  $AX$  and  $AY$  are the angle bisectors of angles  $\angle BAE$  and  $\angle CAF$  respectively. Let  $\omega$  be the circle tangent to segment  $EF$ , the extension of  $AE$  past  $E$ , and the extension of  $AF$  past  $F$ . Prove that  $\omega$  is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle  $ABC$ .
solution_md:
Well this geo is really amazing I have to say...solved in around 30 mins but I think this could even be around 30-35 MOHS because the way to find things on this problem requires deep intuition.
Let  $BI \cap (ABC)=M_B$  and  $CI \cap (ABC)=M_C$ , also let  $N_A$  be midpoint of arc  $BAC$  on  $(ABC)$ , now let reflections of  $D$  over  $EX, FY, BI, CI, Y \infty_{\perp CI}, X \infty_{\perp BI}$  be  $D_B, D_C, L', K', K, L$  respectively now let reflection of  $D_B$  over  $AX$  be  $L_1$  and reflection of  $D_C$  over  $AY$  be  $K_1$ .
Using the paralelogram we can easly see from the direction of the reflections that  $KK'$  and  $LL'$  are diameters on  $(Y, YD), (X, XD)$  respectively, now let  $I_B, I_C$  be the  $B,C$  excenters of  $\triangle ABC$  then notice we have  $\measuredangle II_CA=\measuredangle CBI=\measuredangle CDY=\measuredangle YK'C$  which implies  $I_CAK'Y$  cyclic and similarily  $I_BAL'X$  is cyclic however since  $\measuredangle CDY=\measuredangle YD_CF$  we also get that  $I_CAK'YD_C$  is cyclic and similarily  $I_BAL'XD_B$  is cyclic, however it doesn't end here...
Now notice that  $YK'=YD_C$  so  $Y$  is midpoint of arc  $K'D_C$  on  $(I_CAK')$  however  $D, K'$  are symetric in  $CI$  which means both  $I_CD, I_CD'$  are reflections of  $I_CK'$  over  $CI$  and thus  $I_C, D, D_C$  are colinear, and similarily  $I_B, D, D_B$  are colinear.
Now  $\measuredangle CDY=\measuredangle YD_CA=\measuredangle AK_1Y$  which means  $CK_1YD$  is cyclic and similarily we have  $L_1BXD$  cyclic, but also note that  $\measuredangle L_1DL=\measuredangle L_1L'L=\measuredangle AI_BX=\measuredangle ACI=\measuredangle K_1DY$  which means that  $L_1, D, K_1$  are colinear.
Now from here notice that  $\measuredangle DL_1A=\measuredangle DXI=\measuredangle IYD=\measuredangle AK_1D$  which does in fact show that  $\triangle L_1AK_1$  is isosceles and therefore  $AK_1=AL_1$ , and from reflections this gives  $AD_B=AD_C$ , but notice from other reflections we have  $D_BG=DG=D_CG$  where  $EX \cap FY=G$  (clearly then  $G$  is A-excenter of  $\triangle EAF$ ), but now also note that we have  $\measuredangle AD_BG=\measuredangle GDE=\measuredangle AD_CG$  which means that  $AD_BGD_C$  is cyclic but by summing arcs we end up realising  $AG$  is diameter and in fact now this means  $(D_BDD_C)$  is  $\omega$  from the tangencies.
To finish let  $J$  be the miquelpoint of  $L_1BCK_1$  then  $J$  lies on  $(ABC)$  but also from Reim's we get  $N_A, D, J$  colinear and then Reim's twice gives  $M_CX \cap M_BY=J$  and from double Reim's once again we have that  $(AL'X) \cap (AK'Y)=J$  and this is excellent news because now we can note that  $\measuredangle D_CJD_B=\measuredangle D_CJA+\measuredangle AJD_B=\measuredangle D_CI_CA+\measuredangle AI_BD_B=\measuredangle D_CDD_B$  which shows that  $J$  lies on  $\omega$  as well, but since  $N_A, D, J$  are colinear from the converse of Archiemedes Lemma (or just shooting Lemma/homothety) we have that  $\omega, (ABC)$  are tangent at  $J$  as desired thus we are done :cool:

stem_md: Find the largest real constant  $k$  for which the inequality \[(a^2 + 3)(b^2 + 3)(c^2 + 3)(d^2 + 3) + k(a - 1)(b - 1)(c - 1)(d - 1) \ge 0\] holds for all real numbers  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$ , and  $d$ .
solution_md:
Find the largest real constant $k$ for which the inequality \[(a^2 + 3)(b^2 + 3)(c^2 + 3)(d^2 + 3) + k(a - 1)(b - 1)(c - 1)(d - 1) \ge 0\] holds for all real numbers $a$ , $b$ , $c$ , and $d$ .
For $d=3$ and $a=b=c=-1$ we obtain: $$ 4^3\cdot12-16k\geq0, $$ which gives $k\leq48.$ We'll prove that the value $48$ is valid. 1. $(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)\leq0.$ We obtain: $$ (d^2+3)\prod_{cyc}(a^2+3)\geq(d^2+3)\prod_{cyc}\left(2|a-1|\right)=-8(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)(d^2+3) $$ and it's enough to prove that: $$ -8(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)(d^2+3)+48(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)(d-1)\geq0 $$ or $$ -8(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)(d-3)^2\geq0. $$ 2. $(a-1)(b-1)(c-1)\geq0.$ Thus, it's enough to assume $d\leq1$ and since $d^2+3\geq2(1-d)$ it's enough to prove that: $$ (a^2+3)(b^2+3)(c^2+3)\geq24(a-1)(b-1)(c-1). $$ Now, let $c\geq1$ . Thus, since $c^2+3\geq6(c-1),$ it's enough to prove that: $$ (a^2+3)(b^2+3)\geq4(a-1)(b-1) $$ or after flipping of signs $$ (a^2+3)(b^2+3)\geq4(a+1)(b+1), $$ which says that it's enough to prove the last inequality for non-negatives $a$ and $b$ , which follows from C-S and AM-GM: $$ (a^2+3)(b^2+3)=(a^2+1+2)(1+b^2+2)\geq(a+b+2)^2\geq\left(2\sqrt{(a+1)(b+1)}\right)^2=4(a+1)(b+1). $$

stem_md:
An ant is on the Cartesian plane. In a single move, the ant selects a positive integer  $k$ , then either travels 

- $k$  units vertically (up or down) and  $2k$  units horizontally (left or right); or
- $k$  units horizontally (left or right) and  $2k$  units vertically (up or down).

Thus, for any  $k$ , the ant can choose to go to one of eight possible points.  Prove that, for any integers  $a$  and  $b$ , the ant can travel from  $(0, 0)$  to  $(a, b)$  using at most  $3$  moves.
solution_md:
**Lemma 1:** The ant can get to any point  $(x, y)$  in two moves if  $2x - y$  is divisible by  $3$ .**Proof:**
Observe that  $2y - x$  is also divisible by  $3$ , since  $-2(2x - y) = -4x + 2y \equiv 2y - x \pmod 3$ . Now, the ant should make the following moves:
1. Move  $\frac23 (2x - y)$  horizontally and  $\frac13 (2x - y)$  vertically.
2. Move  $\frac13 (2y - x)$  horizontally and  $\frac23 (2y - x)$  vertically.
These are valid knight moves, and the ant ends up at  $(x, y)$ .  $\square$ If  $2a - b$  is divisible by  $3$ , then by Lemma 1 the ant can get there in two moves. Otherwise, observe that one of  $(a', b') \in \{(a - 1, b + 2), (a - 2, b + 1)\}$  is reachable in two moves, since the values for  $2a' - b'$  are  $2a - b - 4$  and  $2a - b - 5$ , and one of these must be divisible by  $3$ . These points are a single knight move away from  $(a, b)$ , so the ant can take one more step from whichever of these points is reachable to end up at  $(a, b)$  in  $3$  moves.

candidates: Revive this!

Define the eight vectors
\[
U=\{(\pm2,\pm1),(\pm1,\pm2)\}
\]
as *unit moves*. Note that a general allowed move must be a positive integer multiple of one of these unit moves.

If \(a\equiv b\pmod 3\), then
\[
x=\frac{2a-b}{3},\qquad y=\frac{2b-a}{3}
\]
are integers and
\[
(2x,x)+(y,2y)=(a,b).
\]
Hence, \((a,b)\) is obtainable in at most two moves (obtainable with one move only if either \(x \text{ or } y\) is \(0\)).

One the other hand, if \(a\not\equiv b\pmod 3\) choose \(u=(u_x,u_y)\in U\) with \(u_x-u_y\equiv a-b\pmod3\) (such a \(u\) exists since the residues \(0,1,2\) occur among the values \(u_x-u_y\)). Put \((a',b')=(a,b)-u\). Then \(a'\equiv b'\pmod3\), so by our previous case
\[
(a',b')=(2x,x)+(y,2y)
\]
for some integers \(x,y\). Hence,
\[
(a,b)=u+(2x,x)+(y,2y),
\]
which is a sum of at most three allowed moves.

Thus, every integer point \((a,b)\) is reachable from \((0,0)\) in at most three moves.

stem_md:
In acute triangle  $ABC$  with circumcenter  $O$  and orthocenter  $H$ , let  $D$  be an arbitrary point on the circumcircle of triangle  $ABC$  such that  $D$  does not lie on line  $OB$  and that line  $OD$  is not parallel to line  $BC$ . Let  $E$  be the point on the circumcircle of triangle  $ABC$  such that  $DE$  is perpendicular to  $BC$ , and let  $F$  be the point on line  $AC$  such that  $FA = FE$ . Let  $P$  and  $R$  be the points on the circumcircle of triangle  $ABC$  such that  $PE$  is a diameter, and  $BH$  and  $DR$  are parallel. Let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $DH$ .
(a) Show that  $AP$  and  $BR$  are perpendicular. 
(b) Show that  $FM$  and  $BM$  are perpendicular.
solution_md:
Complex bash with  $\triangle ABC$  inscribed in the unit circle, so that  $$ |a|=|b|=|c|=|d|=1 $$    $$ o=0 $$    $$ h=a+b+c $$    $$ e = -\frac{bc}d $$    $$ \overline{f} = \frac{f}{ae} = \frac{a+c-f}{ac} \implies f = \frac{e(a+c)}{c+e} = \frac{b(a+c)}{b-d} $$    $$ p = -e = \frac{bc}d $$    $$ r = \frac{b\left(-\frac{ac}b\right)}{d} = -\frac{ac}d $$    $$ m = \frac{d+h}2 = \frac{a+b+c+d}2 $$  Then for part (a), we have  $ap = \frac{abc}d$  and  $br = -\frac{abc}d$ , so  $ap = -br$  and  $AP\perp BR$ .

For part (b), we have  $$ f-m = \frac{2b(a+c) - (b-d)(a+b+c+d)}{2(b-d)} = \frac{ab+ad-b^2+bc+cd+d^2}{2(b-d)} = \frac{(b+d)(a-b+c+d)}{2(b-d)} $$    $$ m-b = \frac{a-b+c+d}2 $$  Thus,  $$ \frac{f-m}{m-b} = \frac{b+d}{b-d} \in i\mathbb{R} $$  so  $FM\perp MB$ .  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $\mathbb{N}$  be the set of positive integers. Find all functions  $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$  such that for all  $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ , \[m^2f(m) + n^2f(n) + 3mn(m + n)\] is a perfect cube.
solution_md:
For any prime number  $p$ , the  $m^2f(m) + p(pf(p) + 3m(m+p))$  is a perfect cube. This means that for fixed  $m$ , the polynomial  $X^3 - m^2f(m)$  has a root in  $\mathbb{F}_p$  for any prime  $p$ . It is known that this implies that  $m^2f(m)$  is a perfect cube. Let  $m^2f(m) = g(m)^3$  for any positive integer  $m$ . For any prime  $p$ ,  $p \mid g(p)$ , so  $g(p) \ge p$ . 

Now, since  $g(p)^3 + 3p^2 + 3p + f(1)$  is a perfect cube for all prime  $p$ , we have that   $$ 3g(p)^2 + 3g(p) + 1 = (g(p) + 1)^3 - g(p)^3 \le 3p^2 + 3p + f(1) $$  When  $p$  is large enough, this can only hold when  $g(p) \le p$ . This implies that  $g(p) = p$  for all sufficiently large prime  $p$ . 

Fix  $m$ , and plug in  $n = p$ , so that  $m^2(f(m) - m) + (m+p)^3$  is a perfect cube for any prime  $p$ . When  $p$  is large enough, the gap between consecutive cubes becomes larger than  $|m^2(f(m) - m)|$ , which implies that  $f(m) = m$ . Therefore, the only possible solution is  $f(m) = m$  for all positive integer  $m$ , which obviously satisfies the condition.

stem_md: Let  $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c$  be a quadratic function, the graph of which doesn't intersect the x-axis. Prove that  $$ a(2a+3b+6c)>0. $$
solution_md:
WLOG let  $a \ge 0$ , else swap all the signs. Then note that the graph not intersecting the x-axis implies  $b^2 < 4ac$  so  $c > 0$ , and we can WLOG  $b < 0$ . We want to show that for  $b > -\sqrt{4ac}$ , that 
\[
2a + 3b + 6c > 0 \iff 2a + 6c \ge 3\sqrt{4ac} \iff \frac{2a + 6c}{2} \ge \sqrt{9ac}
\]
which follows by AM-GM.
