candidates: used up a lot of time on this to no avail, this is prolly a troll :(

Let  $M_{IJ}$  be the midpoint of  $I$ ,  $J$ . Let  $P = (M_{AD}M_{BD}M_{CD}) \cap (M_{AB}M_{BD}M_{BC})$  so
\[
\measuredangle M_{AD}E - \measuredangle EM_{AB} = \measuredangle M_{AD}E - \measuredangle EM_{BD} + \measuredangle EM_{BD} - \measuredangle EM_{AB} = \measuredangle M_{AD}M_{CD} - \measuredangle M_{CD}M_{BD} + \measuredangle M_{BD}M_{BC} - \measuredangle M_{AB}M_{BC} = \measuredangle AC - \measuredangle BC + \measuredangle CD - \measuredangle AC = \measuredangle DCB = \measuredangle M_{AD}M_{AC}M_{AB}
\]
so  $P$  lies on  $(M_{AD}M_{AC}M_{AB})$  and we are done by symmetry.
Z is simply the Gergonne-Steiner Point.

Suppose the four given points are 
\(
A,\; B,\; C,\; D,
\)
with no three collinear and not all four concyclic. (Thus, for each vertex the circle through the other three is well–defined.) We shall now define for each vertex \(X\) the “vertex–circle”
\(
\omega_X=(\text{three points other than }X);
\)
in other words,
\[
\omega_A=(BCD),\quad \omega_B=(ACD),\quad \omega_C=(ABD),\quad \omega_D=(ABC).
\]
Next, for each vertex \(X\) we perform the homothety (dilation) \(h_X\) with center \(X\) and ratio \(1/2\). (A homothety with ratio \(1/2\) sends every point \(Y\) to the midpoint of \(XY\).) Denote
\[
\omega'_X = h_X(\omega_X).
\]
Thus, for example, 
\[
\omega'_A \text{ is the circle through } M_{AB},\; M_{AC},\; M_{AD},
\]
where \(M_{AB}\) is the midpoint of \(AB\), etc. (Similarly, \(\omega'_B\) passes through \(M_{BA},M_{BC},M_{BD}\); note that \(M_{BA}=M_{AB}\).)



Observe that if \(X\) and \(Y\) are two distinct vertices then by construction the circle \(\omega'_X\) contains the midpoint \(M_{XY}\) (since \(M_{XY}=h_X(Y)\)) and similarly \(\omega'_Y\) contains \(M_{XY}\) (since \(M_{XY}=h_Y(X)\)). Hence for any two vertices \(X\) and \(Y\) the circles \(\omega'_X\) and \(\omega'_Y\) have the point \(M_{XY}\) in common.

For each vertex \(X\), note that the homothety \(h_X\) with center \(X\) and ratio 2 sends \(\omega'_X\) back to the circumcircle \(\omega_X\). (Indeed, if a point \(P\) lies on \(\omega'_X\) then by definition \(P=h_X(Q)\) for some \(Q\in\omega_X\); applying the inverse homothety of ratio 2 shows that \(2P-X=Q\in\omega_X\).) In particular, if a point \(Z\) lies on \(\omega'_X\) then the point
\[
X' = 2Z-X
\]
lies on \(\omega_X\). (This is the same as saying that reflecting \(X\) in \(Z\) lands on \(\omega_X\).)

Thus, if we can show that there exists a point \(Z\) lying simultaneously on all four circles \(\omega'_A,\omega'_B,\omega'_C,\omega'_D\) then for each vertex \(X\) the reflection of \(X\) in \(Z\) lies on \(\omega_X\) (that is, on the circle through the three vertices other than \(X\)). This is exactly the property desired in the original problem.



We now prove that the four circles \(\omega'_A,\omega'_B,\omega'_C,\omega'_D\) have a common point. The proof will use two key facts:

1. Common “side–midpoints”: As we have shown earlier, for any two vertices \(X\) and \(Y\) the circles \(\omega'_X\) and \(\omega'_Y\) meet at the midpoint \(M_{XY}\).

2. The Miquel configuration for the complete quadrilateral:  
   In any quadrilateral 
   \(ABCD\) 
   the four circles 
   \(\omega_A,\omega_B,\omega_C,\omega_D\) 
   (i.e. the circumcircles of the triangles determined by three of the four vertices) have a well‐known associated configuration: The three circles determined by the triangles 
   \(ABC\), \(BCD\), 
   and 
   \(CDA\) 
   have a common “Miquel point”. (In our situation the four points are not concyclic so these circles are distinct and their “Miquel point” is defined by three of them.)  

Now, fix two vertices, say \(A\) and \(B\). The circles \(\omega'_A\) and \(\omega'_B\) meet in \(M_{AB}=H\) and in a second point, say \(Z_{AB}\). (Because two distinct circles have two intersections unless they are tangent, and in our configuration tangency is avoided by the general‐position hypothesis.) Next, consider the circles \(\omega'_A\) and \(\omega'_C\); they meet in \(M_{AC}=I\) and in a second point \(Z_{AC}\). One now shows by using the homothetic relationships
\[
h_A(\omega'_A)=\omega_A,\quad h_B(\omega'_B)=\omega_B,\quad h_C(\omega'_C)=\omega_C,
\]
and the standard fact about Miquel points in the complete quadrilateral \(ABCD\) (namely, that the circles \(\omega_A,\omega_B,\omega_C,\omega_D\) “rotate” about a unique Miquel point when three are taken at a time) that the second intersections \(Z_{AB}\) and \(Z_{AC}\) must in fact coincide  $=Z.$  (One way to see this is to “lift” the configuration via the homothety of ratio 2 from each vertex. For example, applying the homothety with center \(A\) sends the pair \(\omega'_A\) and \(\omega'_B\) to \(\omega_A\) and a circle through the image of \(M_{AB}=H\); the unique intersection point of the corresponding circumcircles coming from the Miquel configuration forces the corresponding “half‐points” to agree.)  

A similar argument shows that the second intersection of \(\omega'_B\) and \(\omega'_C\) agrees with these, and then by symmetry the same point \(Z\) lies on all four circles.

Thus, we obtain a unique point \(Z\) such that
\[
Z\in\omega'_A\cap\omega'_B\cap\omega'_C\cap\omega'_D.
\]



Because the homothety with center \(X\) (and ratio 2) sends \(\omega'_X\) to \(\omega_X\), the fact that
\[
Z\in\omega'_X
\]
implies that the point
\[
X' = 2Z - X,
\]
i.e. the reflection of \(X\) in \(Z\), lies on \(\omega_X\). Since this holds for every vertex \(X\in\{A,B,C,D\}\), the point \(Z\) is exactly the desired point with the property that reflecting any one of \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), \(D\) in \(Z\) lands on the circle determined by the three remaining vertices.

This completes the proof of the concurrency of the four circles.

Hence, such a unique point  $Z$  that satisfies the question conditions surely exists and is constructed as said in the solution.

An excircle centered at  $I_{A}$  touches the side  $BC$  of a triangle  $ABC$  at point  $D$ . Prove that the pedal circles of  $D$  with respect to the triangles  $ABI_{A}$  and  $ACI_{A}$  are congruent.
Proposed by:K.Belsky
solution_md:
Let \( F, G, H, I, J \) be the projections of \( D \) on \( AB, AI_A, BI_A, CI_A, CA \) respectively.

[Image](https://www.geogebra.org/m/sczwgchz)

Claim 1: \( FG=GJ \)
Proof:
\( \measuredangle AGD = \measuredangle AFD = \measuredangle AJD = 90^\circ \implies A, D, F, G, J \) are cyclic
\( \implies \measuredangle FJG = \measuredangle FAG = \measuredangle GAJ = \measuredangle GFJ \)
\( \implies FG=GJ \quad \blacksquare \)

Due to the right angles, we also get:
	\( FBHD \) is cyclic
	\( DGHII_A \) is cyclic

Claim 2:  \( \measuredangle GHF= \measuredangle JIG \)
Proof: \( 90^\circ= \measuredangle BDI_A \)                                            (excircle is tangent to BC at D)
\( = \measuredangle BDH+\measuredangle HDI_A \)
\( = \measuredangle BFH+ \measuredangle HGI_A \)                                              (using i & ii)
\( =  \measuredangle AFH+ \measuredangle HGA \)
\( = \measuredangle GHF+\measuredangle FAG \)                                                   (Quadrilateral AFGH)
\( \implies \measuredangle GHF=90^\circ-\measuredangle FAG \)
Similarly, \( \measuredangle JIG=90^\circ-\measuredangle GAJ \quad \blacksquare \)
\( \implies \sin GHF=\sin JIG \) (Note that we can take sine on these directed angles, as \(\sin(x) = \sin(180-x)\), and both are between 0 and 180).

Hence, radius of D-pedal circle of \( ABI_A= \) radius of \( (FGH) =\frac{FG}{2 \sin GHF} =\frac{GJ}{2 \sin JIG }= \) radius of \( (GIJ) = \) radius of D-pedal circle of \( ACI_A \).

stem_md:
One bisector of a given triangle is parallel to one sideline of its Nagel triangle. Prove that one of two remaining bisectors is parallel to another sideline of the Nagel triangle.
Proposed by:L.Emelyanov
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>Let  $D$ ,  $E$ ,  $F$  be the touchpoints of the incircle of  $\triangle ABC$  on sides  $BC$ ,  $CA$ ,  $AB$  respectively. Let  $X$ ,  $Y$ ,  $Z$  be the feet of the  $A$ ,  $B$ ,  $C$  angle bisectors in  $\triangle ABC$  onto sides  $BC$ ,  $CA$ ,  $AB$  respectively. Let  $D'$ ,  $E'$ ,  $F'$  be the points of the Nagel triangle on sides  $BC$ ,  $CA$ ,  $AB$ . Finally, let  $s = (a + b + c)/2$  be the semiperimeter of  $\triangle ABC$  and remember that  $AD = AE = s - a$  and so on. Note also that  $D'$  is the reflection of  $D$  about the midpoint of  $BC$ ,  $E'$  is the reflection of  $E$  about the midpoint of  $AC$ , and so on.

We now assume without loss of generality that  $D'E' \parallel AX$ . We can calculate the lengths of  $BX$  and  $CX$  using the angle bisector theorem which says  $BX : CX = AB : AC$ , so  $BX = ac/b + c$ ,  $CX = ab/b+c$ . Using parallel lines and ratios, we get
\begin{align*}
D'E' \parallel AX &\iff \frac{AE'}{AC} = \frac{XD'}{XC}
&\iff \frac{CE}{AC} = \frac{BD' - BX}{XC} = \frac{CD - BX}{XC}
&\iff \frac{s - c}{b} = \frac{s - c - \frac{ac}{b+c}}{\frac{ab}{b+c}}
&\iff \frac{a(s - c)}{ab} = \frac{(b + c)(s - c) - ac}{ab}
&\iff ac = (b + c - a)(s - c)
&\iff 2ac = (b + c - a)(a + b - c) \iff a^2 + c^2 = b^2
\end{align*}
This means that the original condition of  $D'E' \parallel AX$  is symmetric with respect to side  $AC$  (and the triangle is in fact a right triangle at  $\angle B = 90^{\circ}$ ). Thus we get that  $E'F' \parallel CZ$  as well, and we are done.</details>

stem_md:
Let  $I$ ,  $I_{a}$  be the incenter and the  $A$ -excenter of a triangle  $ABC$ ;  $E$ ,  $F$  be the touching points of the incircle with  $AC$ ,  $AB$  respectively;  $G$  be the common point of  $BE$  and  $CF$ . The perpendicular to  $BC$  from  $G$  meets  $AI$  at point  $J$ . Prove that  $E$ ,  $F$ ,  $J$ ,  $I_{a}$  are concyclic.
Proposed by:Y.Shcherbatov
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>Let  $D$  be the touching point of the incircle of  $\triangle ABC$  with  $BC$  and  $X = AI \cap EF$ . Note that by Ceva's theorem, the lines  $AD$ ,  $BE$ ,  $CF$  must concur at  $G$  (the Gergonne point). We know  $ID \perp BC$  and  $JG \perp BC$ , so we have  $ID \parallel JG$ , which gives  $$ \frac{AG}{AD} = \frac{AJ}{AI} \iff AJ = \frac{AI \cdot AG}{AD} = \frac{AI \cdot a \cdot (s - a)}{(s - b)(s - c) + a(s - a)} $$   
We want to prove from Power of a Point that  $$ (AX - AJ)(AI_a - AX)	= XE \cdot XF = XE^2 = AE^2 - AX^2 $$  since  $\triangle AXE$  is a right triangle. By similarity  $\triangle XAE \sim \triangle EAI$ ,  $$ AX = \frac{(s - a)^2}{AI} $$  and by Ptolemy's theorem and Incenter-Excenter Lemma,  $$ AI_a = II_a + AI = \frac{2 AI \cdot a}{b + c - a} + AI = \frac{AI \cdot (b + c + a)}{b + c - a} $$   
So we want  $$ AX(AI_a + AJ) - AJ \cdot AI_a = AE^2 \iff (s - a)^2 = AX(AI_a + AJ) - AJ \cdot AI_a $$  Now, we simplify this expression by noting that  $AI^2 = AE^2 + r^2$  and  $r^2 = ([\triangle ABC] / s)^2$ , where  $[\triangle ABC]$  is the area of  $\triangle ABC$ . By Heron's formula, we get  $$ AI^2 = (s - a)^2 + \frac{(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}{s} = \frac{(s - a)(s(s - a) + (s-b)(s-c))}{s} $$  \begin{align*}
AJ \cdot AI_a &= AI^2 \left ( \frac{a(s - a)}{(s - b)(s - c) + a(s - a)} \right) \left( \frac{b+c+a}{b+c-a} \right) 
&= \left( \frac{(s - a)(s(s - a) + (s-b)(s-c))}{s} \right) \left( \frac{a(s - a)}{(s - b)(s - c) + a(s - a)} \right)  \left( \frac{b+c+a}{b+c-a} \right) 
&= \frac{2abc(b + c - a)}{-a^2 -b^2 - c^2 + 2ab + 2bc+ 2ca}
\end{align*}
\begin{align*}
AX(AI_a + AJ) &= (s - a)^2 \left(\frac{a(s - a)}{(s - b)(s - c) + a(s - a)} + \frac{b + c + a}{b + c - a}\right) 
&= (s - a)^2 \left(\frac{2a(b + c - a)}{-a^2 - b^2 - c^2 + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca} + \frac{b + c + a}{b + c - a}\right) 
&= (s - a) \left(\frac{a^3 - 3 a^2 b - 3 a^2 c + 3 a b^2 + 10 a b c + 3 a c^2 - b^3 + b^2 c + b c^2 - c^3}{2(-a^2 -b^2 - c^2 + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca)}\right)
\end{align*}
So we now do the final calculation
\begin{align*}
& \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; AX(AI_a + AJ) - AI_a \cdot AJ
&= (s - a) \left(\frac{(a^3 - 3 a^2 b - 3 a^2 c + 3 a b^2 + 10 a b c + 3 a c^2 - b^3 + b^2 c + b c^2 - c^3) - (8abc)}{2(-a^2 -b^2 -c^2 + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca)}\right)
&= (s - a) \left(\frac{a^3 - 3 a^2 b - 3 a^2 c + 3 a b^2 + 2 a b c + 3 a c^2 - b^3 + b^2 c + b c^2 - c^3}{2(-a^2 -b^2 -c^2 + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca)}\right)
&= (s - a)\left(\frac{b + c - a}{2}\right)
&= (s - a)^2
&= AE^2
\end{align*}
and we are done!</details>

stem_md:
The diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral  $ABCD$  meet at point  $P$ . Points  $K$  and  $L$  lie on  $AC$ ,  $BD$  respectively in such a way that  $CK=AP$  and  $DL=BP$ . Prove that the line joining the common points of circles  $ALC$  and  $BKD$  passes through the mass-center of  $ABCD$ .
Proposed by:V.Konyshev
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>Let  $E$  and  $F$  be the midpoints of diagonals  $AC$  and  $BD$  in  $ABCD$ . Note that  $K$  is the reflection of  $P$  about  $E$  and  $L$  is the reflection of  $P$  about  $F$ . **Lemma.** The midpoint of  $EF$ , let it be  $G$ , is the mass-center of  $ABCD$ .**Proof.** Indeed, this can be shown using basic coordinate geometry or complex numbers. Let  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$ ,  $d$  denote the complex coordinates of  $A$ ,  $B$ ,  $C$ ,  $D$  in the complex plane. Then the mass center of  $ABCD$  is  $g = (a + b + c + d)/4$ ,  $E$  is  $(a +c)/2$ ,  $F$  is  $(b + d)/2$ . So the midpoint of  $EF$  becomes  $$ \frac{e + f}{2} = \frac{(a + c)/2 + (b + d)/2}{2} = \frac{a + b + c + d}{4} = g $$   $\blacksquare$ Let  $G'$  be the midpoint of  $KL$ . Since  $E$  is the midpoint of  $PK$ , and  $F$  is the midpoint of  $PL$ ,  $G'$  must be the reflection of  $P$  about  $G$ . Now we claim that  $P$  lies on the line joining the common points of  $(ALC)$  and  $(BKD)$  [the radical axis]. Indeed this is true since
\begin{align*}
\text{power of } P \text{ with respect to } (ALC) &= PA \cdot PC 
&= PB \cdot PD 
&= \text{power of } P \text{ with respect to } (BLD)
\end{align*}
which follows from power of a point in  $(ABCD)$ . Since  $P$  lies on the radical axis, it now suffices to show that  $G'$  lies on the radical axis.
To show this, we use a lemma called Linearity of Power of Point. Define   $$ f(X) = \text{power of } X \text{ with respect to } (ALC) - \text{power of } X \text{ with respect to } (BLD) $$  We know that  $f(X)$  is linear, so 
\begin{align*}
f(G') &= \frac{f(K) + f(L)}{2} 
&= \frac{(KA \cdot KC - 0) + (0 - LB \cdot LD)}{2} 
&= \frac{PC \cdot PA - PD \cdot PB}{2} 
&= 0
\end{align*}
Thus the power of  $G'$  with respect to the two circles is equal, implying that it lies on the radical axis, and we are done.</details>

stem_md: The line  $l$  passing through the orthocenter  $H$  of a triangle  $ABC$   $(BC>AB)$  and parallel to  $AC$  meets  $AB$  and  $BC$  at points  $D$  and  $E$  respectively. The line passing through the circumcenter of the triangle and parallel to the median  $BM$  meets  $l$  at point  $F$ . Prove that the length of segment  $HF$  is three times greater than the difference of  $FE$  and  $DH$ Proposed by: A.Mardanov, K.Mardanova
solution_md:
Let \( K \) be the midpoint of \( DE \).

Claim 1: \( HK = 2KF \)

Proof: \( BM \parallel FO \Rightarrow KG \parallel FO \Rightarrow \angle HKG = \angle HFO \)
\( \angle KHG = \angle FHO \) (since \( F, K, H \) are collinear \& \( O, G, H \) are collinear)
\( \Rightarrow \Delta KHG \sim \Delta FHO \)
\( \Rightarrow \frac{HK}{KF} = \frac{HG}{GO} = 2 \) (Using Euler Line) \(\blacksquare\)

\( HF = HK + KF = 3KF = 3(KH - KF) \)
\( = 3([KE - KD] + [KH - KF]) \)               [ \( KE = KD \) ]
\( = 3([KE - KF] - [KD - KH]) \)
\( = 3(FE - DH) \) \(\blacksquare\)

stem_md:
A point  $X$  is the origin of three rays such that the angle between any two of them equals  $120^{\circ}$ . Let  $\omega$  be an arbitrary circle with radius  $R$  such that  $X$  lies inside it, and  $A$ ,  $B$ ,  $C$  be the common points of the rays with this circle. Find  $max(XA+XB+XC)$ .
Proposed by: F.Nilov
solution_md:
It is clear that  $X$  is the "Fermat point" of  $\Delta ABC$  so we can use it as such to convert  $XA+XB+XC$  into a straight line  $'l'$  . By rotating one of the small triangle by  $60^.$  WLOG ,assume  $\Delta BXC$  is rotated about  $B$ : so let  $C$  be sent to  $C'$   $\implies$   $XA+XB+XC=AC'$ CLAIM:  $max(XA+XB+XC)=3R=T$ PROOF:Its not a very abstract proof rather based on a idea in physics,so first it is clear for it to be maximum the center must be on one of the ray .Notice that the part of the line  $AC'$  contained in circle is < $2R$ ,so to maximize it must lie on one of the ray (Assume it to be  $XC$ .)

Now because if you let your center to be  $X$ (where  $T=3R$ ) and move our point about that ray lets say you move about  $\Delta x$  Then the other two distances would each be reduced by  $\Delta x$  so it would totally be reduced by  $\Delta x$   $\implies$ ( $\Delta T=T-T'=3R-(3R-\Delta x)=\Delta x$ )

Hence the maximum arises at the center point  $X$ . or  $\boxed{XA+XB+XC=T=3R}$

\[
\cos 120^\circ = \frac{-1}{2} = \frac{p^2 + q^2 - c^2}{2pq}
\]

Thus, we obtain the following relations:  

\[
c^2 = p^2 + pq + q^2
\]

\[
a^2 = q^2 + qr + r^2
\]

\[
b^2 = p^2 + pr + r^2
\]

Now, note that:  

\[
a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = p^2 + pq + q^2 + q^2 + qr + r^2 + p^2 + pr + r^2
\]

Since we have the inequality:  

\[
p^2 + q^2 + r^2 \geq pq + qr + rp
\]

we obtain:  

\[
a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 2(p^2 + q^2 + r^2) + pq + qr + rp \geq (p+q+r)^2
\]

Thus,  

\[
\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2} \geq p + q + r
\]

Next, we note that:  

\[
9R^2 \geq (a^2 + b^2 + c^2)
\]

This follows from the identity:  

\[
OH^2 = 9R^2 - (a^2 + b^2 + c^2)
\]

where \( O \) is the circumcenter and \( H \) is the orthocenter. Since \( OH^2 \geq 0 \), it follows that  

\[
9R^2 \geq (a^2 + b^2 + c^2)
\]

which gives:  

\[
\sqrt{9R^2} \geq p + q + r
\]

or  

\[
3R \geq p + q + r
\]**Attainability:**  
Consider an equilateral triangle \( ABC \). Since the angle at the center is twice the angle subtended on the arc, we have \( O \) satisfying the conditions of \( X \) as:  

\[
\angle BOC = 2 \angle BAC = 2(60^\circ) = 120^\circ
\]

By definition,  

\[
OA = OB = OC = R
\]

Thus,  

\[
OA + OB + OC = 3R
\]

as required.  

\(\square\)</details>

Circles  $\omega_{1}$  and  $\omega_{2}$  are given. Let  $M$  be the midpoint of the segment joining their centers,  $X$ ,  $Y$  be arbitrary points on  $\omega_{1}$ ,  $\omega_{2}$  respectively such that  $MX=MY$ . Find the locus of the midpoints of segments  $XY$ .
Proposed by: L Shatunov
solution_md: **Claim: Locus of the midpoints of segments $\color{blue}{XY}$ is the radical axis of circles $\color{blue}{\omega_{1}}$ and $\color{blue}{\omega_{2}}$ .****Proof:** Denote the centers of the circles $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ by $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$ respectively. Toss the figure on the coordinate plane with $O_{1} \equiv (-1,0)$ and $O_{2} \equiv (+1,0)$ . Thus, $M \equiv (0,0)$ . Let the radii of $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ be $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ respectively. Thus, $$ \omega_{1} \equiv (x+1)^2+y^2=r_{1}^2 $$ $$ \omega_{2} \equiv (x-1)^2+y^2=r_{2}^2 $$ Now, let $X \equiv (h_1,k_1),Y \equiv (h_2,k_2)$ and $Z \equiv (h,k) \equiv \left(\frac{h_1+h_2}{2},\frac{k_1+k_2}{2}\right)$ where $Z$ is the midpoint of segment $XY$ . Then, $$ h_{1}^2+k_{1}^2+2h_1+1-r_{1}^2=0 \cdots (1) $$ $$ h_{2}^2+k_{2}^2-2h_2+1-r_{2}^2=0 \cdots (2) $$ As $MX=MY$ , $$ h_{1}^2+h_{2}^2=k_{1}^2+k_{2}^2 \cdots (3) $$ On subtracting $(2)$ from $(1)$ and using $(3)$ we get, $$ 2(h_1+h_2)=(r_{1}^2-r_{2}^2) $$ $$ \implies \boxed{h=\frac{r_{1}^2-r_{2}^2}{4}} $$ Therefore, the locus of $Z$ is $\boxed{x=\frac{r_{1}^2-r_{2}^2}{4}}$ . Now, let $L$ denote the radical axis of $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ . Then, $$ L \equiv \omega_{1}-\omega_{2}=0 \equiv \boxed{4x=(r_{1}^2-r_{2}^2)} $$ Hence, the locus of $Z$ is radical axis of $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ . $\blacksquare$

Let  $O_1$  be the center of  $\omega_1$  and  $O_2$  be the center of  $\omega_2$ . First, we claim that the midpoint  $M'$  of  $XY$  with  $X$  on  $\omega_1$  and  $Y$  on  $\omega_2$  and  $MX = MY$   $\boxed{\text{must lie on the radical axis line of } \omega_1 \text{ and } \omega_2.}$  To show this, we use linearity of power of point with  $f(Z)$  defined as in the above lemma.  $$ f(M') = \frac{f(X) + f(Y)}{2} = \frac{(0 - \text{pow}_{\omega_1}(X)) + (\text{pow}_{\omega_2}(Y) - 0)}{2} $$  We will show  $\text{pow}_{\omega_1}(X) = \text{pow}_{\omega_2}(Y)$ . We have (using Cosine Rule and other trigonometric identities)
\begin{align*}
\text{pow}_{\omega_1}(X) - \text{pow}_{\omega_2}(Y) &= (O_2X^2 - O_2Y^2) - (O_1Y^2 - O_1X^2)
&= (O_2M^2 + MX^2  - 2 \cdot O_2M \cdot MX \cdot \cos(\angle O_2MX) - O_2Y^2)
&- (O_1M^2 + MY^2 - 2 \cdot O_1M \cdot MY \cdot \cos(\angle O_1MY) - O_1X^2) 
&= (- 2 \cdot O_2M \cdot MX \cdot \cos(\angle O_2MX) - O_2Y^2)
&- (- 2 \cdot O_1M \cdot MY \cdot \cos(\angle O_1MY) - O_1X^2) 
&= (2 \cdot O_2M \cdot MY \cdot \cos(\angle O_2MY) - O_2Y^2)
&- (2 \cdot O_1M \cdot MX \cdot \cos(\angle O_1MX) - O_1X^2)
&= (-O_2M^2 - MY^2) - (-O_1M^2 - MX^2)
&= \boxed{\textbf{0}}
\end{align*}
Now, we note that if  $\omega_1$  is completely inside  $\omega_2$  or vice versa, then the shortest distance from  $M$  to  $\omega_2$  is bigger than the longest distance from  $M$  to  $\omega_1$ . This means there are no points  $X$  and  $Y$  on  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2$  with  $MX = MY$ . So we have two scenarios- either  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2$  intersect, or their  areas are completely disjoint from each other. We will deal with these together.

Since  $M'$  lies on the radical axis, letting the point  $X$  move continuously along  $\omega_1$ , there are two choices for  $Y$  (after drawing a circle with center  $M$  and radius  $MX$ ). Both these choices for  $Y$  move continuously along  $\omega_2$ , implying that the segment formed from the midpoints of  $XY$  is continuous. It is left to determine the **endpoints of this segment**.

Note that  $MM_1 \perp XY$  which means that as  $X$  moves, letting the two choices of  $Y$  be  $Y_1$  and  $Y_2$ , the lines  $XY_1$  are all parallel to each other, and the lines  $XY_2$  are all parallel to each other. Thus, the locus is the segment formed by the midpoints of the external common tangents of  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2$ , a subset of the radical axis of  $\omega_1$  and  $\omega_2$ .</details>

Each two opposite sides of a convex  $2n$ -gon are parallel. (Two sides are opposite if one passes  $n-1$  other sides moving from one side to another along the borderline of the  $2n$ -gon.) The pair of opposite sides is called regular if there exists a common perpendicular to them such that its endpoints lie on the sides and not on their extensions. Which is the minimal possible number of regular pairs?
Proposed by: B.Frenkin
solution_md:
<details><summary>For storage ( Transported from MSE ) With a little more ellaboration,</summary>The minimal possible number of regular pairs is \boxed{1}.



We will give a construction for the common perpendicular 

Let \(f(x):=\left(\frac{x-1}{n-1}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\) and note that for \(1\leq x\leq n\) we have \(-\frac{1}{2}\leq f(x)\leq\frac{1}{2}\). Consider a centrally symmetric polygon with vertices \(P_{1},\ldots,P_{2n}\) given by \(P_{x}:=(x,f(x))\) and \(P_{x+n}:=-P_{x}\) for \(1\leq x\leq n\).

To prove the polygon is convex, it suffices to show that the 2D cross product (cross product \(P_{i}P_{i+1}\times P_{i+1}P_{i+2}\) is positive) (i.e., the signed area of the triangle made by any three consecutive vertices) is positive for every set of three consecutive vertices. In other words, if we denote

\[
\vec{A}=P_{i+1}-P_{i}\quad\text{and}\quad\vec{B}=P_{i+2}-P_{i+1},
\]

we must show that

\[
\vec{A}\times\vec{B}>0\quad\text{for all }i,
\]

where the cross product can be computed via the determinant

\[
\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1  f(i+1)-f(i) & f(i+2)-f(i+1) \end{pmatrix}.
\]

For \(1\leq x\leq n\) we have

\[
P_{x}=\left(x,f(x)\right)\quad\text{with}\quad f(x)=\left(\frac{x-1}{n-1}\right)^ {2}-\frac{1}{2}.
\]

Define

\[
g(x):=\left(\frac{x-1}{n-1}\right)^{2},
\]

so that \(f(x)=g(x)-\frac{1}{2}\). For three consecutive vertices \(P_{i},P_{i+1},P_{i+2}\), the vectors corresponding to edges are

\[
\vec{A}=P_{i+1}-P_{i}=\left(1,\;f(i+1)-f(i)\right)
\]

and

\[
\vec{B}=P_{i+2}-P_{i+1}=\left(1,\;f(i+2)-f(i+1)\right).
\]

Then, the signed area (i.e., the cross product) is given by

\[
\vec{A} \times \vec{B} = \det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1  f(i+1)-f(i) & f(i+2)-f(i+1) \end{pmatrix}.
\]

Thus,

\[
\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=f(i+2)-2f(i+1)+f(i).
\]

Because \(f(x)=g(x)-\frac{1}{2}\), the constant \(-\frac{1}{2}\) cancels out in the second difference, so that

\[
\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=g(i+2)-2g(i+1)+g(i).
\]

Since

\[
g(x)=\left(\frac{x-1}{n-1}\right)^{2}=\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{(n-1)^{2}},
\]

this is a quadratic function in \(x\) with leading coefficient

\[
a=\frac{1}{(n-1)^{2}}.
\]

For a quadratic function \(ax^{2}+bx+c\), its second finite difference is constant and equal to \(2a\). In our case,

\[
g(i+2)-2g(i+1)+g(i)=\frac{2}{(n-1)^{2}}.
\]

Thus, we obtain

\[
\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=\frac{2}{(n-1)^{2}}>0.
\]

The polygon is defined to be centrally symmetric by the relation

\[
P_{x+n}=-P_{x}\quad\text{for }1\leq x\leq n.
\]

This symmetry implies that the behavior of the second half of the polygon mirrors first half. In particular, the second differences (which measure the turning of the polygon) are the same by symmetry if the vertices are taken in order along the full polygon. Therefore, the cross product is positive between every set of three consecutive vertices in the entire polygon.

Since the cross product for any three consecutive vertices is given by

\[
P_{t}P_{t+1}\times P_{t+1}P_{t+2}=\frac{2}{(n-1)^{2}}>0,
\]

the polygon consistently turns in one direction, proving that it is convex.

\subsection*{Alternative Proof}

To show that the polygon defined by the vertices \(P_{1},P_{2},\ldots,P_{2n}\) is convex, we will show the 2D cross products \(P_{i}P_{i+1}\times P_{i+1}P_{i+2}\) for \(i=1,2,\ldots,2n-2\) are positive.

\[
P_{i}=(i,f(i))=\left(i,\left(\frac{i-1}{n-1}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\right)
\]

\[
P_{i+1}=(i+1,f(i+1))=\left(i+1,\left(\frac{i}{n-1}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\right)
\]

\[
P_{i+2}=(i+2,f(i+2))=\left(i+2,\left(\frac{i+1}{n-1}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\right)
\]

Next, we compute the vectors \(P_{i}P_{i+1}\) and \(P_{i+1}P_{i+2}\):

\[
P_{i}P_{i+1}=P_{i+1}-P_{i}=((i+1)-i,f(i+1)-f(i))=(1,f(i+1)-f(i))
\]

\[
P_{i+1}P_{i+2}=P_{i+2}-P_{i+1}=((i+2)-(i+1),f(i+2)-f(i+1))=(1,f(i+2)-f(i+1))
\]

Now, we can compute the cross product \(P_{i}P_{i+1}\times P_{i+1}P_{i+2}\).

\[
(a,b)\times(c,d)=ad-bc
\]

Applying it:

\[
P_{i}P_{i+1}\times P_{i+1}P_{i+2} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & f(i+1)-f(i)  1 & f(i+2)-f(i+1) \end{vmatrix} = 1 \cdot (f(i+2)-f(i+1)) - 1 \cdot (f(i+1)-f(i))
\]

This simplifies to:

\[
f(i+2)-2f(i+1)+f(i)
\]

The expression is \(f(i+2)-2f(i+1)+f(i)\). This is the second finite difference of the function \(f\), which indicates the concavity or convexity of \(f\).

To show that this expression is positive, we can compute the second derivative of \(f(x)\):

1. \(f^{\prime}(x)\):
\[
f(x)=\left(\frac{x-1}{n-1}\right)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}
\]
\[
f^{\prime}(x)=2\cdot\frac{x-1}{n-1}\cdot\frac{1}{n-1}=\frac{2(x-1)}{(n-1)^{2}}
\]

2. \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)\):
\[
f^{\prime\prime}(x)=\frac{2}{(n-1)^{2}}
\]

Since \(f^{\prime\prime}(x)>0\) for all \(x\) in the interval \([1,n]\), this means that \(f(x)\) is a convex function on this interval.

Thus, the second finite difference \(f(i+2)-2f(i+1)+f(i)>0\) for \(1\leq i\leq n-2\), which implies that the cross product \(P_{i}P_{i+1}\times P_{i+1}P_{i+2}>0\).

Therefore, the polygon is convex.



The pair of edges \(P_{n}P_{n+1}\parallel P_{2n}P_{1}\) has a common perpendicular: the \(y\)-axis.

\textbf{Claim:} All other pairs \(P_{k}P_{x+1}\parallel P_{n+x}P_{n+1+x}\) (for \(1\leq x<n\)) have no common perpendiculars. It suffices to show that the angle \(\angle P_{n+x}P_{x}P_{x+1}\) is obtuse.

We should compute the dot product, which should be negative:

\[
(P_{n+x}-P_{x})\cdot(P_{x+1}-P_{x})=-2P_{x}\cdot(P_{x+1}-P_{x})
\]
\[
=-2(x,f(x))\cdot(1,f(x+1)-f(x))
\]
\[
=-2x-2f(x)(f(x+1)-f(x))
\]
\[
\leq-2+2|f(x)|(|f(x+1)|+|f(x)|)
\]
\[
\leq-2+2\cdot\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right)=-1.
\]

.</details>

A point  $D$  lies inside a triangle  $ABC$  on the bisector of angle  $B$ . Let  $\omega_{1}$  and  $\omega_{2}$  be the circles touching  $AD$  and  $CD$  at  $D$  and passing through  $B$ ;  $P$  and  $Q$  be the common points of  $\omega_{1}$  and  $\omega_{2}$  with the circumcircle of  $ABC$  distinct from  $B$ . Prove that the circumcircles of the triangles  $PQD$  and  $ACD$  are tangent.
Proposed by: L Shatunov
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>We first state the following well-known lemma:**Lemma.** Given a triangle  $XYZ$ , and points  $Y'$  and  $Z'$  on the circumcircle of  $(XYZ)$ , such that  $XY'$  and  $XZ'$  are isogonal in  $\angle YXZ$  (that is,  $\angle Y'XY = \angle Z'XZ$ ). Then  $Y'Z' \parallel YZ$ . **Proof.** Suppose  $M$  is the midpoint of the minor arc  $YZ$  on circle  $(XYZ)$  and  $N$  is the midpoint of the major arc  $YZ$ . Then since  $M$  lies on the angle bisector of  $\angle YXZ$ , we have  $\angle MXY' = \angle MXZ'$ , implying  $MY' = MZ'$ . This further means that  $Y'Z' \perp MN$ , but since  $YZ \perp MN$  is also true,  $Y'Z' \parallel YZ$  must hold. $\blacksquare$ Now we begin with the problem. We first invert at a circle centered at  $D$  with arbitrary radius. This sends  $A$  to  $A'$  on  $AD$ ,  $B$  to  $B'$  on  $BD$ , and  $C$  to  $C'$  on  $CD$ . Next, since  $\omega_1$  passes through  $B$  and is tangent to  $AD$  at  $D$ , we get that its inverted image  $\ell_1$  is a line through  $B'$  that is parallel to  $A'D$ . Similarly  $\omega_2$  becomes  $\ell_2$ , a line through  $B'$  that is parallel to  $C'D$ .  $P$  goes to  $P'$ , the intersection of  $\ell_1$  and circle  $(A'B'C')$ , and  $Q$  goes to  $Q'$ , the intersection of  $\ell_2$  and circle  $(A'B'C')$ . 

We originally wished to prove that  $(PQD)$  and  $(ACD)$  are tangent at  $D$  - but  $(PQD)$  becomes  $P'Q'$  under inversion,  $(ACD)$  becomes  $A'C'$ , so we wish to prove  $P'Q' \parallel A'C'$ . 

But now note that originally,  $D$  was on the angle bisector of  $\angle ABC$ , that is  $\angle DBA = \angle DBC$ , but after inversion, the angle condition becomes  $\angle DA'B' = \angle DC'B'$ . Since  $DC' \parallel BQ'$  and  $DA' \parallel AQ'$ , we get:  $$ \angle A'B'P' = \angle D'A'B' = \angle D'C'B' = \angle C'B'Q' $$  so  $P'B'$  and  $Q'B'$  are isogonal in  $\angle A'B'C'$ , and using the Lemma at the start of the solution,  $P'Q' \parallel A'C'$  and we are done.</details>

<details><summary>sol</summary>Let  $r_A$  be the radius of the circle with center  $A$  touching  $SB$ , and  $r_B$  be the radius of the circle with center  $B$  touching  $SA$ . We will prove that  $r_A + r_B = AB$ , thus proving the problem. First let  $A'$  be the foot of perpendicular from  $A$  to  $SB$ , and  $B'$  be the foot from  $B$  to  $SA$ . Observe that  $AA'= r_A$  and  $BB' = r_B$  must be true since the circles touch the segments tangentially. So we wish to prove  $AA' + BB' = AB$ . 

Let the angle  $\angle ASB = 2 \theta$ , and  $SC = x$ . Then  $AA' = SA \sin(2 \theta)$  and  $BB' = SB \sin(2 \theta)$ , so we want to show  $(SA + SB) \sin(2 \theta) = AB$ .

Observe that  $XP = XQ = x \sin(\theta)$ . Since  $SPCQ$  must be a cyclic quadrilateral with diameter  $SC$ , we get  $\angle CPQ = \angle CSQ = \theta = \angle CSP = \angle CQP$ . So using the Cosine Rule in  $\triangle CPQ$ , we get
\begin{align*}
PQ^2 &= CP^2 + CQ^2 - 2 \cos(180^{\circ} - 2\theta) \cdot CP \cdot CQ 
&= (x \sin(\theta))^2 + (x \sin(\theta))^2 + 2 \cos(2 \theta) (x \sin(\theta))^2 
&= 2x^2 \sin^2 (\theta) (1 + 2 \cos(2 \theta) )
&= 2x^2 \sin^2(\theta) (2 \cos^2(\theta))
&= 4x^2 \sin^2(\theta) \cos^2(\theta)
\end{align*}
So  $PQ = 2x \sin(\theta) \cos(\theta) = x \sin(2 \theta)$ . We know that  $CA = CB = PQ = x \sin(2 \theta)$ , so using Cosine Rule in triangle  $\triangle SAC$  letting  $y = SA$ :   $$ x^2 + y^2 - 2xy \cos(\theta) = x^2 \sin^2(2 \theta) $$  This is a quadratic in  $y$ ,   $$ y^2 - (2x \cos(\theta)) y + (x^2 \cos^2(2 \theta)) = 0 $$  But note that after using Cosine Rule in triangle  $\triangle SBC$ , letting  $z = SB$ , we get the same equation   $$ x^2 + z^2 - 2xz \cos(\theta) = x^2 \sin^2(2 \theta) $$  Since  $y \neq z$ , we get that  $y$  and  $z$  are the roots of the quadratic equation ( $\alpha$  is a placeholder variable)  $$ \alpha^2 - (2x \cos(\theta)) \alpha + (x^2 \cos^2(2 \theta)) = 0 $$  We wish to only find  $SA + SB = y + z$ , so using Vieta's relations of quadratic equation, we get  $y + z = 2x \cos(\theta)$ . So, we want to prove  $$ AB = (SA + SB) \sin(2 \theta) = 2x \cos(\theta) \sin(2 \theta) $$  Finally, since  $CP = CQ$ ,  $CA = CB$  and  $\angle APC = \angle BQC = 90^{\circ}$ , we get  $\triangle ACP$  is congruent to  $\triangle BCQ$  and  $\angle ACP = \angle BCQ$ . So
\begin{align*}
\angle ACB &= \angle ACS + \angle BCS 
&= (\angle SCP - \angle ACP) + (\angle SCQ + \angle BCQ)
&= \angle SCP + \angle SCQ 
&= \angle PCQ = 180^{\circ} - 2 \theta
\end{align*}
Now, because  $CP = CQ$  and  $\angle PCQ = 180^{\circ} - 2\theta$ , and  $CA = CB$  and  $\angle ACB = 180^{\circ} - 2 \theta$ , we get  $\triangle ACB \sim \triangle PCQ$ :  $$ \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{PQ}{PC} = \frac{2x\sin(\theta)\cos(\theta)}{x\sin(\theta)} = 2 \cos(\theta) $$    $$ AB = AC(2 \cos(\theta)) = 2x \cos(\theta) \sin(2\theta) = (SA + SB) \sin(2 \theta) = AA' + BB' = r_A + r_B $$  which is exactly what we wanted, so we are done.</details>

stem_md:
The Feuerbach point of a scalene triangle lies on one of its bisectors. Prove that it bisects the segment between the corresponding vertex and the incenter.
Proposed by: A.Zaslavsky
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol</summary>Let  $I$  denote the incenter of  $\triangle ABC$ ,  $H$  be the orthocenter,  $N$  be the nine-point center,  $O$  be the circumcenter, and  $F$  be the Feuerbach point.

We know that  $F$  is the point of tangency of the incircle and nine-point circle, which means it lies on the line joining their centers:  $I$ ,  $N$ ,  $F$  are collinear. Without loss of generality, assume  $F$  lies on  $AI$ , this means  $N$  lies on  $AI$  as well. But now note that lines  $AO$  and  $AH$  are reflections in  $AI$  (since  $O$  and  $H$  are isogonal conjugates).  $N$  is the midpoint of  $OH$ , so either  $O$  and  $H$  are reflections in  $AI$  themselves, or  $O$  and  $H$  lie on  $AI$ . 

In the latter scenario, if  $O$ ,  $H$  lie on  $AI$ , the triangle must be isosceles, a contradiction to the given condition that  $\triangle ABC$  is scalene. Thus  $O$  and  $H$  are reflections in  $AI$ , which means  $AO = AH$ .   $$ R = AO = AH = 2R \cdot \cos(\angle BAC) \implies \cos(\angle BAC) = \frac{1}{2} \implies \angle BAC = 60^{\circ} $$  where  $R$  is the circumradius of  $(ABC)$ . Now, finally we want to show  $2IF = IA$ . Since  $IF = r$ , where  $r$  is the inradius of  $\triangle ABC$ , we wish for  $AI = 2r$ . 

Consider  $\triangle AIE$  where  $E$  is the touchpoint of the incircle of  $\triangle ABC$  on  $AC$ . This triangle has  $\angle IAE = 30^{\circ}$  and  $\angle IEA = 90^{\circ}$ , so  $IA = 2IE = 2r$ , and we are done.</details>

<details><summary>sol</summary>We start with the following claim:**Claim.** The circumcenter of  $ABC$  lies on the Euler Line of  $DEF$ .**Proof.** If  $D'$ ,  $E'$ ,  $F'$  are the feet of altitudes from  $D$  to  $EF$ ,  $E$  to  $FD$  and  $F$  to  $DE$ , and  $I_A$  is the circumcenter of  $\triangle DEF$ , then we know  $I_A D \perp BC$ , but due to properties of the orthic triangle,  $I_A D \perp E'F'$  as well. Thus  $BC \parallel E'F'$ , similarly  $CA \parallel F'D'$  and  $AB \parallel D'E'$ . This means  $\triangle ABC$  and  $\triangle D'E'F'$  are homothetic.

Since  $ABC$  is acute-angled, we know  $DEF$  is obtuse-angled at  $D$ . It is well known that the excenter of the orthic triangle corresponding to the obtuse-angled vertex is the orthocenter of the reference triangle (if it is obtuse). Thus we look at the  $D'$ -excenter of  $D'E'F'$  and the  $A$ -excenter of  $ABC$ . The first point is the orthocenter of  $DEF$  and the second is the circumcenter  $I_A$  of  $DEF$ . The center of homothety between  $ABC$  and  $D'E'F'$  must lie on the line joining the corresponding excenters - but this line is the Euler line of  $DEF$ .

Finally, the center of homothety between  $ABC$  and  $D'E'F'$  must also lie on the line joining the corresponding circumcenters - but the circumcenter of  $D'E'F'$  is the nine-point center of  $DEF$  which lies on the Euler line of  $DEF$ . Since we know that the center of homothety also lies on the Euler line of  $DEF$ , this is enough to conclude that the circumcenter of  $ABC$  lies on the Euler line of  $DEF$ .  $\blacksquare$ Let the orthocenter of  $DEF$  be  $H$ , the circumcenter of  $ABC$  be  $O$ , the centroid of  $DEF$  be  $G$ . Let  $N$  be the nine point center of  $DEF$  - the circumcenter of  $D'E'F'$ . We know that  $H$  lies on the circumcircle of  $ABC$ . The Euler Line of  $DEF$  is the line through  $H$ ,  $N$ ,  $G$ ,  $O$ ,  $I_A$ . **Claim.**  $N$ , the nine point center of  $DEF$ , lies on the circumcircle of  $ABC$ . Furthermore,  $HI_A = 2r_A$ , where  $r_A$  is the circumradius of  $DEF$ . **Proof.** We invert about the excircle, and let the inversion of  $H$  be  $H'$ .  $A$  goes to the midpoint of  $EF$  ( $AE$  and  $AF$  are tangent to the excircle),  $B$  goes to the midpoint of  $FD$ ,  $C$  goes to the midpoint of  $DE$ . Let these midpoints be  $A'$ ,  $B'$ ,  $C'$ . But  $(A'B'C')$  is exactly the nine point circle of  $DEF$  - and since  $H$  lies on  $(ABC)$ ,  $H'$  must lie on  $(A'B'C')$ , the nine point circle of  $DEF$ .

This means that  $NH'$  is the radius of the nine point circle of  $DEF$ , which is exactly half the radius of  $(DEF)$ ,  $r_A$ , so  $$ NH' = \frac{r_A}{2} $$  However, if  $N'$  is the inversion of  $N$  about the excircle, then since  $N$  is the midpoint of  $I_A H$ ,  $H'$  must be the midpoint of  $I_A N'$ . If  $N$  is inside circle  $(DEF)$ ,  $N'$  must be outside the circle, but knowing  $NH' = r_A/2$ , it means  $N'H' > r_A/2 > H'I_A$ . Similarly if  $N$  is outside circle  $(DEF)$ , then  $N'$  is inside, but knowing  $NH' = r_A/2$ , it means  $N'H' < r_A/2 < H'I_A$ . Thus  $N$  must be lie on circle  $(DEF)$ , and since  $NI_A = NH = r_A$ ,  $HI_a = 2r_A$ .  $\blacksquare$ **Claim.**  $G$  lies on the circumcircle of  $ABC$ . Furthermore,  $2r_A = 3R$ , where  $R$  is the circumradius of  $ABC$ . **Proof.** We know  $NG : GI_A = 1 : 2$  and  $HG : GI_A = 2 : 1$  by properties of the Euler Line. If  $G'$  is the inversion of  $G$  about the excircle, then since  $I_A G : r_A = 2 : 3$ , we get  $I_A G' : r_A = 4.5 : 3$  (because  $2 \cdot 4.5 = 3^2$ ). This implies that  $NG' : r_A = 1.5 : 3 = 1 : 2$ , thus  $NG' = r_A / 2$ , and  $G'$  lies on the nine point circle of  $DEF$ . This means that before inversion  $G$  lies on the circle  $(ABC)$ .

Since the Euler Line of  $DEF$  has the points  $H$ ,  $O$ ,  $N$ ,  $G$ ,  $I_A$ , and  $H$  and  $G$  lie on  $(ABC)$  - this means  $HG$  is a diameter of  $(ABC)$ , and  $O$  is the midpoint of  $HG$ . Since  $HG = 2R$ , where  $R$  is the circumradius of  $(ABC)$ , we get that  $HI_A = 3R$ . Hence:  $$ 2r_A = 3R $$   $\blacksquare$ Now consider the reflection of  $I_A$  about  $OI$ , and call it  $I_A'$ . Let  $L$  be the minor arc midpoint of  $BC$ , and  $N$  be the major arc midpoint. Let  $L'$  be the reflection of  $L$  about  $OI$ . Note that  $N$  is the reflection of  $L$  about  $O$ , so  $NL' \parallel OI$ . But note also that by the Incenter-Excenter Lemma,  $L'$  is the midpoint of  $II_A'$ . If  $N'$  is the midpoint of  $I_A' O$ , then  $N'$  must lie on the circumcircle of  $(ABC)$  since  $2N'I_A = OI_A' = OI_A = 2R$ . So by the midpoint theorem in  $\triangle I_A' O I$ , we also get  $N'L' \parallel OI$  - since both  $N$  and  $N'$  lie on  $(ABC)$ , we must have  $N = N'$ . This implies that  $I_A'$ ,  $N$ ,  $O$ ,  $L$  are collinear. 

Reflecting the above line about  $OI$ , we get the line  $I_A O$ , which is exactly the Euler Line of  $DEF$  - its intersections with the circumcircle of  $ABC$  are  $H$  and  $G$ . Thus the reflections of  $H$  and  $G$  about  $OI$  must be  $L$  and  $N$  - and we are done.</details>

There exists a (kinda) nice complex bash to this problem:

Take the A-excircle to be the unit circle. So we have the following: $|d|=|e|=|f|=1$ ,  $i_a=0$ ,  $a=\frac{2ef}{e+f}$ ,  $b=\frac{2df}{d+f}$ ,  $c=\frac{2de}{d+e}$ ,  $o=\frac{2def(d+e+f)}{(d+e)(e+f)(f+d)}$ .

Let  $H$  be the orthocenter of the  $\Delta DEF$  triangle. So  $h=d+e+f$ .

Due to Incenter-Excenter Lemma we know that  $L$  - the midpoint of arc  $\widehat{BC}$  on the  $(ABC)$  circle is the center of the  $(IBI_AC)$  circle.

Compute  $L$  using the circumcenter formula for  $\Delta I_ABC$  and we get  $\ell=\frac{2def}{(d+e)(d+f)}$ .

Since  $L$  is the midpoint of  $[II_A]$  we have  $i=2\ell=\frac{4def}{(d+e)(d+f)}$ . $H\in(ABC)\implies \frac{a-h}{b-h}\cdot\frac{b-c}{a-c}\in\mathbb{R}\implies...\implies \frac{d^2(e^2+f^2+de+df)(f-e)}{e^2(d^2+f^2+de+ef)(f-d)}\in\mathbb{R}\implies$  $\implies \frac{d^2(e^2+f^2+de+df)(f-e)}{e^2(d^2+f^2+de+ef)(f-d)}=\frac{(de^2+df^2+ef^2+e^2f)(e-f)}{(d^2e+ef^2+d^2f+df^2)(d-f)}\implies$  $\implies d^2(e^2+f^2+de+df)(d^2e+ef^2+d^2f+df^2)=e^2(d^2+f^2+de+ef)(de^2+df^2+ef^2+e^2f)\implies...\implies$  $\implies (d-e)(d+e)(e+f)(f+d)(d^2e+de^2+e^2f+ef^2+d^2f+df^2-def)=0$ .

Obviously  $(d-e)(d+e)(e+f)(f+d)\neq0\implies d^2e+de^2+e^2f+ef^2+d^2f+df^2-def=0\quad(1)$ .

Now, since  $H, L\in(ABC)$ ,  $L$  will be the reflection of  $H$  through  $OI$  if and only if the midpoint  $M$  of  $[HL]$  belongs to line  $OI$ , which is equivallent to  $\frac{o-i}{\overline{o}-\overline{i}}=\frac{m-i}{\overline{m}-\overline{i}}$ .

We have  $m=\frac{d+e+f}{2}+\frac{def}{(d+e)(d+f)}$ . $o-i=\frac{2def}{(d+e)(d+f)}\left(\frac{d+e+f}{e+f}-2\right)=\frac{2def(d-e-f)}{(d+e)(e+f)(f+d)}$ , so  $\frac{o-i}{\overline{o}-\overline{i}}=\frac{def(d-e-f)}{ef-de-df}$ . $m-i=\frac{3def}{(d+e)(d+f)}-\frac{d+e+f}{2}=\frac{3def-d^3-2d^2e-2d^2f-de^2-df^2-e^2f-ef^2}{2(d+e)(d+f)}$ , so  $\frac{m-i}{\overline{m}-\overline{i}}=\frac{def(d^3+2d^2e+2d^2f+de^2+df^2+e^2f+ef^2-3def)}{d^2e^2+e^2f^2+f^2d^2+2de^2f+2def^2+d^3e+d^3f-3d^2ef}$ So  $M, I, O$  are collinear if and only if  $\frac{d-e-f}{ef-de-df}=\frac{d^3+2d^2e+2d^2f+de^2+df^2+e^2f+ef^2-3def}{d^2e^2+e^2f^2+f^2d^2+2de^2f+2def^2+d^3e+d^3f-3d^2ef}\iff ...\iff$  $\iff 2(d^2-ef)(d^2e+de^2+e^2f+ef^2+d^2f+df^2-def)=0$ , which is true by  $(1)$ , so we're done.

Let \( K \) be the inverse center of homothety of \( \omega_1 \) and \( \omega_2 \).  
Let \( X \) and \( Y \) be the points of tangency of \( \omega_2 \) with \( BD \) and \( CD \), respectively.  
Let \( Z \) and \( W \) be the points of tangency of \( \omega_1 \) with \( AB \) and \( AD \), respectively.  
Note that \( BP = BZ = BX \) and \( CP = CW = CY \).

Let \( \gamma_1 \) be the circle tangent to \( AB \) and \( BD \) at \( Z \) and \( X \), respectively.  
Let \( \gamma_2 \) be the circle tangent to \( CA \) and \( CD \) at \( W \) and \( Y \), respectively.  

By Monge's Theorem on \( \omega_1, \omega_2, \gamma_1 \), we get that \( K, Z, X \) are collinear.  
By Monge's Theorem on \( \omega_1, \omega_2, \gamma_2 \), we get that \( K, W, Y \) are collinear.  

Let \( Z' \) and \( W' \) be the second points of intersection of lines \( XZ \) and \( YW \) with \( \omega_1 \).  
Let \( T \) be the intersection of the tangents from \( Z' \) and \( W' \) to \( \omega_1 \).  

Since \( K \) is the inverse center of homothety of \( \omega_1 \) and \( \omega_2 \),  
we have that \( D, K, T \) are collinear, and the polar of \( Z'W' \cap ZW \) passes through \( T, K, A \),  
so \( D, K, A \) are collinear.

Let \( P' \) be the antipode of \( P \) in \( \omega_1 \).  
Then, since \( K \) is the inverse center of homothety of \( \omega_1 \) and \( \omega_2 \), we have that:  
WLOG, \( S \) and \( D \) lie on different rays with respect to \( K \).  
Then:
\[
PQ \parallel SP' \Rightarrow 90^\circ = \angle SPP' + \angle SP'P = \angle SPK + \angle KPQ = \angle SPQ_\blacksquare

solution_md: <details><summary>sol</summary>We claim that the concurrence point is the Spieker center  $Sp$  of  $\triangle ABC$ , which is the incenter of  $\triangle M_aM_bM_c$ . Let  $I_a$  be the  $A$ -excenter of  $\triangle ABC$  and  $G$  be the centroid of  $\triangle ABC$ . **Claim.**  $AI \parallel M_aSp$ .**Proof.** This is true by considering a homothety with ratio  $-1/2$  at  $G$ , sending  $\triangle ABC$  to  $\triangle M_aM_bM_c$ . $\blacksquare$ **Claim.**  $I_a$  is the reflection of  $A'$  in  $M_a$ .**Proof.** By the Orthocenter Reflection Lemma,  the reflection of  $A'$  in  $M_a$  lies on  $(BIC)$  and is the antipode of  $I$ , which is  $I_a$  by the Incenter-Excenter Lemma. $\blacksquare$ Combining the two claims, a homothety with ratio  $2$  centered at  $A'$  sends  $S_aM_a$  to  $AI_a = AI$  implying  $M_aS_a \parallel AI$ , however  $M_aSp \parallel AI$  as well, so  $Sp$  lies on  $S_aM_a$  and similarly lies on  $S_bM_b$  and  $S_cM_c$ .</details>

\( = \measuredangle ABC - \measuredangle C' BC \)  [Parallel Lines]

Let  $O$  be the circumcenter of  $\triangle ABC$ . **Claim.**  $NHMO$  is a parallelogram. Furthermore,  $A'$  is the point on  $BC$  such that  $NA' \perp NO$ . **Proof.** Note that  $h = a + b + c$ ,  $n = (a + h)/2 = (2a + b + c)/2$ ,  $o = 0$ , and  $m = (b + c)/2$ . Thus  $$ h + o = a + b + c = \frac{2a + b + c}{2} + \frac{b + c}{2} = m + n $$  so  $NHMO$  is indeed a parallelogram with  $MH \parallel NO$ . Since  $NA' \perp MH$ , we get  $NA' \perp NO$ , which gives a unique characterization for point  $A'$  on  $BC$ . $\blacksquare$ Now, we determine the characterization of  $a'$ . Firstly,  $A'$ ,  $B$ ,  $C$  are collinear, so  $$ a' + bc\overline{a'} = b + c \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \cdots\textbf{(1)} $$  Next,  $NA'\perp NO$ , so  $$ \frac{n - a'}{n} \in i\mathbb{R} \iff \frac{n-a'}{n} = -\frac{\overline{n - a'}}{\overline{n}} $$  Since  $n = a + (b + c)/2$ ,   $$ \overline{n} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{\frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c}}{2} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{b + c}{2bc} = \frac{2bc + ab + ac}{2abc} $$    $$ \frac{2a + b + c - 2a'}{2a + b + c} = -\frac{2bc + ab + ac - 2\overline{a'}abc}{2bc + ab + ac} $$     $$ (2bc+ab+ac)a' + abc(2a+b+c)\overline{a'} = (2bc+ab+ac)(2a+b+c) \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \cdots \textbf{(2)} $$  Multiplying equation  $\textbf{(1)}$  by  $a(2a+b+c)$  to eliminate the  $\overline{a'}$  term, we get  $$ a(2a+b+c)a' + abc(2a+b+c)\overline{a'} = a(b+c)(2a + b + c) \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \cdots \textbf{(3)} $$  Subtracting equation  $\textbf{(3)}$  from equation  $\textbf{(2)}$ , we get  $$ (2bc - 2a^2)a' = 2bc(2a + b + c) $$    $$ \boxed{a' = \frac{bc(2a + b + c)}{bc - a^2}} $$  By symmetry, we know that   $$ b' = \frac{ca(2b + c + a)}{ca - b^2} \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; c' = \frac{ab(2c + a + b)}{ab - c^2} $$  Using the collinearity formula we want  $$  \frac{a' - b'}{a' - c'} = \frac{\frac{bc(2a + b +c)}{bc - a^2} -  \frac{ca(2b + c +a)}{ca - b^2} }{ \frac{bc(2a + b +c)}{bc - a^2} -  \frac{ab(2c + a +b)}{ab - c^2} } \in \mathbb{R} $$    $$ b(2a + b + c)(ca - b^2) - a(2b + c + a)(bc - a^2) = (a - b)(a + b)^2 (a + b + c) $$    $$ c(2a + b + c)(ab - c^2) - a(2c + a + b)(bc - a^2) = (a - c)(a + c)^2 (a +  b + c) $$  So we want to show  $$ \frac{\frac{bc(2a + b +c)}{bc - a^2} -  \frac{ca(2b + c +a)}{ca - b^2} }{ \frac{bc(2a + b +c)}{bc - a^2} -  \frac{ab(2c + a +b)}{ab - c^2} } = \frac{c (a + b)^2 (a - b) (a b - c^2)}{b (a + c)^2 (a - c) (a c - b^2)} \in \mathbb{R} $$    $$ \overline{\left(\frac{c (a + b)^2 (a - b) (a b - c^2)}{b (a + c)^2 (a - c) (a c - b^2)}\right)} = \frac{(\frac 1c)(\frac 1a + \frac 1b)^2 (\frac 1a - \frac 1b) (\frac{1}{ab} - \frac{1}{c^2})}{(\frac 1b) (\frac 1a + \frac 1c)^2 (\frac 1a - \frac 1c) (\frac{1}{ac} - \frac{1}{b^2})} $$  Multiplying the numerator and denominator of this fraction by  $a^4b^4c^4$ , we get  $$ \frac{(\frac 1c)(\frac 1a + \frac 1b)^2 (\frac 1a - \frac 1b) (\frac{1}{ab} - \frac{1}{c^2})}{(\frac 1b) (\frac 1a + \frac 1c)^2 (\frac 1a - \frac 1c) (\frac{1}{ac} - \frac{1}{b^2})} = \frac{c (a + b)^2 (b - a) (c^2 - a b)}{b (a + c)^2 (c - a) (b^2 - a c)} $$  So indeed (since if  $x = \overline{x}$ , then  $x \in \mathbb{R}$ ),   $$ \frac{c (a + b)^2 (a - b) (a b - c^2)}{b (a + c)^2 (a - c) (a c - b^2)} \in \mathbb{R} $$  and the problem is proven.</details>

\cdots \textbf{(3)} $$ Subtracting equation $\textbf{(3)}$ from equation $\textbf{(2)}$ , we get $$ (2bc - 2a^2)a' = 2bc(2a + b + c) $$ $$ \boxed{a' = \frac{bc(2a + b + c)}{bc - a^2}} $$ By symmetry, we know that $$ b' = \frac{ca(2b + c + a)}{ca - b^2} \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; c' = \frac{ab(2c + a + b)}{ab - c^2} $$ Using the collinearity formula we want $$ \frac{a' - b'}{a' - c'} = \frac{\frac{bc(2a + b +c)}{bc - a^2} - \frac{ca(2b + c +a)}{ca - b^2} }{ \frac{bc(2a + b +c)}{bc - a^2} - \frac{ab(2c + a +b)}{ab - c^2} } \in \mathbb{R} $$ $$ b(2a + b + c)(ca - b^2) - a(2b + c + a)(bc - a^2) = (a - b)(a + b)^2 (a + b + c) $$ $$ c(2a + b + c)(ab - c^2) - a(2c + a + b)(bc - a^2) = (a - c)(a + c)^2 (a + b + c) $$ So we want to show $$ \frac{\frac{bc(2a + b +c)}{bc - a^2} - \frac{ca(2b + c +a)}{ca - b^2} }{ \frac{bc(2a + b +c)}{bc - a^2} - \frac{ab(2c + a +b)}{ab - c^2} } = \frac{c (a + b)^2 (a - b) (a b - c^2)}{b (a + c)^2 (a - c) (a c - b^2)} \in \mathbb{R} $$ $$ \overline{\left(\frac{c (a + b)^2 (a - b) (a b - c^2)}{b (a + c)^2 (a - c) (a c - b^2)}\right)} = \frac{(\frac 1c)(\frac 1a + \frac 1b)^2 (\frac 1a - \frac 1b) (\frac{1}{ab} - \frac{1}{c^2})}{(\frac 1b) (\frac 1a + \frac 1c)^2 (\frac 1a - \frac 1c) (\frac{1}{ac} - \frac{1}{b^2})} $$ Multiplying the numerator and denominator of this fraction by $a^4b^4c^4$ , we get $$ \frac{(\frac 1c)(\frac 1a + \frac 1b)^2 (\frac 1a - \frac 1b) (\frac{1}{ab} - \frac{1}{c^2})}{(\frac 1b) (\frac 1a + \frac 1c)^2 (\frac 1a - \frac 1c) (\frac{1}{ac} - \frac{1}{b^2})} = \frac{c (a + b)^2 (b - a) (c^2 - a b)}{b (a + c)^2 (c - a) (b^2 - a c)} $$ So indeed (since if $x = \overline{x}$ , then $x \in \mathbb{R}$ ), $$ \frac{c (a + b)^2 (a - b) (a b - c^2)}{b (a + c)^2 (a - c) (a c - b^2)} \in \mathbb{R} $$ and the problem is proven.

Therefore,  $|a|=|b|=|c|=1$   $$ h=a+b+c $$     $$ m_a=\frac{b+c}{2} $$     $$ n_a=\frac{2a+b+c}{2} $$   $(i)\ A',B,C$  collinear:  $$ \frac{c-b}{a'-b}=\overline{\left(\frac{c-b}{a'-b}\right)}=\frac{\frac{1}{c}-\frac{1}{b}}{\overline{a'}-\frac{1}{b}}=-\frac{c-b}{\overline{a'}bc-c} $$     $$ \boxed{\overline{a'}=\frac{b+c-a'}{bc}} $$   $(ii)\ A'N\perp MH$ :  $$ q=\frac{n_a-a'}{h-m_a}\in i\mathbb{R} $$    $$ q=\frac{\frac{2a+b+c}{2}-a'}{a+b+c-\frac{b+c}{2}}=\frac{2a+b+c-2a'}{2a+2b+2c-b-c}=1-\frac{2a'}{2a+b+c} $$    $$ \overline{q}=1-\frac{2\overline{a'}}{\frac{2}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}}=1-\frac{2ab+2ac-2aa'}{2bc+ac+ab} $$    $$ \implies 0=1-\frac{2a'}{2a+b+c}+1-\frac{2ab+2ac-2aa'}{2bc+ac+ab} $$  By solving the equation, we have   $$ \boxed{a'=\frac{(2a+b+c)(ab+ac+bc)}{bc-a^2}} $$    $$ \boxed{b'=\frac{(a+2b+c)(ab+ac+bc)}{ac-b^2}} $$     $$ \boxed{c'=\frac{(a+b+2c)(ab+ac+bc)}{ab-c^2}} $$  From that,  $A',B',C'$  collinear  $\iff \frac{a'-c'}{b'-c'}=\overline{\left(\frac{a'-c'}{b'-c'}\right)}$ Let  $p=\frac{a'-c'}{b'-c'}$ With that,   $$ p=\frac{a'-c'}{b'-c'}=\frac{\frac{2a+b+c}{bc-a^2}-\frac{a+b+2c}{ab-c^2}}{\frac{a+2b+c}{ac-b^2}-\frac{a+b+2c}{ab-c^2}} $$    $$ \overline{p}=\frac{\frac{\frac{2}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}}{\frac{1}{bc}-\frac{1}{a^2}}-\frac{\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{2}{c}}{\frac{1}{ab}-\frac{1}{c^2}}}{\frac{\frac{1}{a}+\frac{2}{b}+\frac{1}{c}}{\frac{1}{ac}-\frac{1}{b^2}}-\frac{\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{2}{c}}{\frac{1}{ab}-\frac{1}{c^2}}}=\frac{\frac{2a+b+c}{bc-a^2}-\frac{a+b+2c}{ab-c^2}}{\frac{a+2b+c}{ac-b^2}-\frac{a+b+2c}{ab-c^2}}=p $$  And with so we are done!

<details><summary>sol</summary>We first state the following well-known lemma that can be found in any text relating to isogonal conjugation in a quadrilateral:**Lemma (Quadrilateral Isogonal Conjugation).** For a point  $O$  inside quadrilateral  $WXYZ$ , a point  $O'$  such that   $$ \measuredangle ZWO = \measuredangle O'WX; \;\; \measuredangle WXO = \measuredangle O'XY; \;\; \measuredangle XYO = \measuredangle O'YZ; \;\; \measuredangle YZO = \measuredangle O'ZW $$   exists if and only if  $\angle WOX + \angle YOZ = 180^{\circ} = \angle WOZ + \angle XOY$ . This point  $O'$  is the isogonal conjugate of  $O$  (and  $O$  is the isogonal conjugate of  $O'$ ) with respect to quadrilateral  $WXYZ$ .

Thus we now define  $P'$  to be the isogonal conjugate of  $P$  with respect to quadrilateral  $ABCD$ , which exists since  $\angle APB + \angle CPD = 180^{\circ}$ , and define  $E$  to be the intersection of diagonals in quadrilateral  $ABCD$ . **Claim.** The lines  $AP_c$ ,  $BP_d$ ,  $CP_a$ ,  $DP_b$  concur at  $P'$ . **Proof.** Note that  $P_c$  is the isogonal conjugate of  $P$  with respect to  $\triangle ABD$ . Thus  $$ \measuredangle DAP = \measuredangle BAP_c $$  But  $P'$  is the isogonal conjugate of  $P$  with respect to  $ABCD$ , so   $$ \measuredangle BAP_c = \measuredangle DAP = \measuredangle BAP' $$  This means that  $AP_c$  and  $AP'$  must be the same line, and  $P'$  lies on  $AP_c$ . Similarly we can obtain that  $P'$  lies on  $BP_d$ ,  $CP_a$ , and  $DP_b$ . $\blacksquare$ **Claim.**  $E$  is the isogonal conjugate of  $P'$  in  $BCP_cP_b$ ,  $CDP_dP_c$ ,  $DAP_aP_d$ ,  $ABP_bP_a$ . **Proof.** Consider quadrilateral  $BCP_cP_b$ . In this quadrilateral,  $P'$  must have an isogonal conjugate since  $\angle P_cP'P_b + \angle CP'B = \angle AP'D + \angle CP'B = 180^{\circ}$  (since  $P'$  has an isogonal conjugate in  $ABCD$ ). Note that  $$ \measuredangle BCP' = \measuredangle PCD = \measuredangle ACP_b = \measuredangle ECP_b $$    $$ \measuredangle CBP' = \measuredangle PBA = \measuredangle DBP_c = \measuredangle EPB_c $$  So the isogonal conjugate lies on both  $AC$  and  $BD$ , and must be exactly the point  $E$ . Symmetrically, we get that  $E$  is the isogonal conjugate of  $P'$  in all the 4 quadrilaterals. $\blacksquare$ Finally, note that since  $E$  has an isogonal conjugate (namely,  $P'$ ) in  $BCP_cP_b$ , we have  $$ \angle BEC + \angle P_bEP_c = 180^{\circ} $$  But  $E$  also has an isogonal conjugate in  $CDP_dP_c$ , which gives  $$ \angle CED + \angle P_dEP_c = 180^{\circ} $$  So, we have  $$ \angle P_bEP_c = 180^{\circ}- \angle BEC = \angle CED = 180^{\circ}- \angle P_dEP_c $$  This means that  $E$  must lie on  $P_bP_d$ , and similarly we obtain that  $E$  must lie on  $P_aP_c$ . Thus, the diagonals of  $ABCD$  and the diagonals of  $P_aP_bP_cP_d$  all concur at  $E$ .</details>

Let us say that a subset  $M$  of the plane contains a hole if there exists a disc not contained in  $M$ , but contained inside some polygon with the boundary lying in  $M$ . Can the plane be presented as a union of  $n$  convex sets such that the union of any  $n-1$  from them contains a hole?
Proposed by: N.Spivak
solution_md:
The answer is yes

for the case  $n=2$  we consider an imaginary line dividing the plane into two halves our subsets will be two planes
one contaning a hole in one half and other containig hole in other (both the holes are symmetrical about the line
dividing the plane in half)


it is easy to see that their union will represent the whole plane and the union of any  $n-1$  in this case 1 contains a
hole


For the case  $n=3$  we consider 3 rays originating from a single point making angles  $120^{\circ}$  with each other in this case
we will have three subsets each contaning  $n-1$  holes, in this case 2 holes 

Taking the definition of union of planes as: The union of two planes is the set of all points that lie in either of the
planes.

If the planes intersect, their union will include all points in both planes, as well as the line of intersection

Now we prove the general case take a plane M take any point in plane M and divide the region from there to 2
sectors (This is a well known construction)

now construct a circle in any one of the sectors completely lying inside it now as there are n axis of symmetry
reflect the circle about each of them, so we have n sectors with each of them having a hole

let the sectors be indexed as  $a_{1},a_{2},........a_{n}$ 1:our subsets is this newly constructed plane only given that we do not reflect the circle about any one of the axis
of symmetry, as there are n axis of symmetry so there are n planes [cite: 29, 30]

2:now next thing we need to prove that union of any n-1 of them contains a hole, to prove this we will use the fact

contained in, will have this hole, as we have n holes we are done

3:now the last thing to prove is that union of all the subsets make the plane, to prove this we can use 2 or we can
make the following argument take any subset it will have one hole missing in some region say  $a_{i}$  all the other
subsets will have a hole in this region when we take the union of all the subsets, the  $a_i$ th region in this subset will
cover the  $a_i$ th region in other subsets, and as we have n subsets we are done..

stem_md:
Let  $ABCD$  be a cyclic quadrilateral. Two lines passing through the orthocenter  $H$  of the triangle  $ABC$  and parallel to  $BD$  and  $CD$  meet  $AC$  and  $AB$  respectively at points  $E$  and  $F$ . Prove that the line segment  $EF$  bisects the segment  $DH$ . 

*Proposed by E. Volokitin*
solution_md: My solution from the contest. We **MMP** bash this problem. **Degree Counting** Vary $D$ projectively with degree $2$ on $(ABC)$ while fixing $(ABC)$ . Due to conic doubling, lines $BD$ and $CD$ both have degree $1$ . Therefore, $E$ and $F$ also have degree $1$ by translation. By considering homogeneous coordinates, we see $(D+H)/2$ has degree $2$ . We need to show $\overline {E-F-\frac{D+H}{2}} \Leftrightarrow (D+H)/2 \cdot (E \times F)=0$ (in homogeneous coordinates), a statement which has degree $4$ . We need to check $5$ cases, but I present $6$ as it shall help with degeneracies. **Cases** Let $X'$ denote the reflection of $X$ over the circumcenter of $(ABC)$ . The cases are $1) D=A$ $2) D=BH \cap (ABC)$ $3) D=CH \cap (ABC)$ $4) D=A'$ $5) D=B'$ $6) D=C'$ . The first case follows after noticing that $DEHF$ forms a parallelogram. The other cases follow from standard orthocenter reflection properties. **Degeneracies** Did you think that the solution was over? You are in for a shock :diablo:. We need to demonstrate that none of the cases are distinct. Observe that the problem is not defined if $H\in\{A, B, C\}$ . We shall denote this fact using $\clubsuit$ . Observe that cases $(1,4,5,6)$ are pairwise distinct due to $\clubsuit$ . By similar reasoning using $\clubsuit$ , $(1,2,3)$ are pairwise distinct, as well as $(2,4,6)$ and $(3,4,5)$ . The only source of degeneracy is if $2,5$ and $3,6$ become the same. We deal with this using further case bash. *a)* When $ABC$ is not equilateral: Observe that if cases $2$ and $5$ become the same, $3$ and $6$ cannot be the same. Since we have demonstrated $5$ cases, we are done. Similar reasoning holds if $3$ and $6$ become the same. *b)* When $ABC$ is equilateral: In this case, $2$ and $5$ as well as $3$ and $6$ overlap. We make up for this by considering $D=B$ and $D=C$ , which works trivially as the triangle is equilateral. Hence, we are done. $\blacksquare$ **Remarks** In the exam, I had to show all the details (wherever I mentioned, "it follows" in this proof). stem_md: Let  $CH$  be an altitude of triangle  $ABC$ ;  $CA', CB'$  be bisectors of triangles  $CBH, CAH$  respectively. Prove that the circumcenter of triangle  $CA'B'$  coincides with the incenter of triangle  $ABC$  if and only if  $\angle ACB = 90 \textdegree .$ *Proposed by **L.Emelyanov***
solution_md:
The case of isosceles triangle is trivial.
Let  $O$  be the circumcenter of triangle  $CA'B'$ ,  $I$  incenter of triangle  $ABC$ , M and M' the projections of  $O,I$  to  $AB$ . Let circumdiameter of  $(ABC)$  be 1. Then the points coincide only if  $AM=AM'$   $$ \iff \frac{AC \cdot AH}{AC+CH} + AB - \frac{BC \cdot BH}{BC+CH} = AB + AC - BC $$    $$ \iff \frac{\cos a \sin b}{1+ \sin a} -\frac{\cos b \sin a}{1+ \sin b} = \sin b - \sin a $$    $$  \iff f(a) = \frac{1+ \sin a -  \cos a}{\sin a(1+ \sin a)} = \frac{1+ \sin b -  \cos b}{\sin b(1+ \sin b)}=f(b) $$    $$ f'(x)= \frac{(\sin x -\cos x)(1-\cos x)}{\sin^2 x(1+\sin x)} $$  Clearly,  $f$  is decreasing in  $[0,\pi/4]$ , increasing in  $[\pi/4,\pi]$ . So  $f(a)=f(b), a \neq b$  has only one solution. However, we know that  $b=\pi/2-a$  works. So, the centers can coincide only if  $\angle ACB = 90$ .

Since we can check  $CO=CI$  in right angled triangle and  $f(a)=f(b)$  we have that the 2 points coincide.

\[PQ=2\frac{O_1P\cdot O_2P\sin\angle O_1PO_2}{O_1O_2}\le2\frac{O_1P\cdot O_2P}{O_1O_2}=\frac{AB\cdot CD}{2O_1O_2}.\tag{1}\]

\[AB\cdot CD\le AB\cdot BD=2[ABD]\le2[AMD]=\frac12AD^2,\]
where  $M$  is the midpoint of arc  $AD$ . Therefore,
\[PQ\le\text{RHS}_{(1)}<\frac{\frac12AD^2}{2\frac{AD}2}=\frac12AD.\]

stem_md: A regular triangle  $ABC$  is inscribed into a circle  $\Omega$  . Circles  $\Omega_A,\Omega_B,\Omega_C$  centered at  $A, B, C$  respectively pass through a point  $P$  lying on  $\Omega$  and have a common tangent. Prove that there exists a line touching two of these circles and passing through some vertex of  $ABC$ *Proposed by K. Belsky*
solution_md:
Invert about $P$ . Then the problem becomes:
A point $P$ outside a triangle $XYZ$ lies on the $X$ -excircle. Suppose the reflections $A, B, C$ of $P$ across $YZ, ZX, XY$ (respectively) are collinear, and suppose that $\angle APB = \angle BPC = 60^\circ$ . Show that there exists a circle passing through $P$ and $A$ tangent to $XY$ and $XZ$ .
By simson lines, $P$ in fact is an intersection of $(XYZ)$ and the $X$ -excircle. The angle condition also implies that $XYZ$ is equilateral, so it suffices to show that the circle centered on $YZ$ tangent to $XY$ and $XZ$ passes through $P$ . In other words if the $X$ -excenter is $T$ , it suffices to show that $(XYZ)$ , the incircle of $XYTZ$ , and the $X$ -excircle are coaxial. But this can be coordinate bashed. Edit: here's a short synthetic solution to the finish. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $YZ$ and let $L$ be the foot from $M$ to $TY$ . Then the power from $T$ to the incircle of $XYTZ$ is $TL^2$ while the power from $T$ to $(XYZ)$ is $TY^2$ . Now $TL \cdot TY = TM^2$ , so the incircle of $XYTZ$ and $(XYZ)$ are inverses with respect to the $X$ -excircle, as desired.

stem_md: Let  $BE$  and  $CF$  be altitudes of traingle  $ABC$ . The internal bisectors of angle B and C meet at point  $I$ , and the external ones meet at point  $J$ . Prove  $IJ>EF$ *Proposed by I.Mikhailov*
solution_md:
Let  $M$  be the midpoint of arc  $BC$  (not containing  $A$ ), then  $AIMJ$  is the internal bisector of  $\angle BAC$ . By the incenter-excenter lemma (simple angle chasing),  $MI=MJ=MB=MC$ . Hence,
\[IJ=IM+MJ=2MB=2\frac{\frac12BC}{\cos\angle CBM}=\frac{BC}{\cos\frac{\angle BAC}2}.\]
Since  $B$ ,  $C$ ,  $E$ ,  $F$  are all on the circle with diameter  $BC$ , then
\begin{align*}
EF&=BC\sin\angle ECF=BC\sin\pm\left(\frac\pi2-\angle BAC\right)
&=BC|\cos\angle BAC|=BC\left|2\cos^2\frac{\angle BAC}2-1\right|.
\end{align*}
Let  $\cos\tfrac{\angle BAC}2=x$ , then it suffices to prove  $\tfrac1x>\left|2x^2-1\right|\Leftrightarrow x\in(0,1)$ .

Let  $I$  be the incenter of a scalene triangle  $ABC$ ; and  $P, Q$  be two isogonal points such that  $AP \parallel \parallel IQ \parallel BC$ . Prove that  $AP=| AB - AC |$ .

solution_md:
Here's a clean bash. Assume that  $b=AC >AB=c$ <details><summary>Step 1</summary>Let's find  $\frac{sin \angle PIB}{sin \angle PIC}$ . Note that by a sine ceva in  $\triangle AIB$ :  $$ \frac{sin \angle QAB}{sin \angle QAI} . \frac{sin \angle QIA}{sin \angle QIB} . \frac{sin \angle QBI}{sin \angle QBA} = 1 $$  Which is also equal to:  $$ \frac{sin \angle QAB}{sin \angle QAI} . \frac{sin \angle QIA}{sin \angle QIB} . \frac{sin \angle QBI}{sin \angle QBA} = \frac{sin \angle C}{sin \angle C+\frac{A}{2}} . \frac{sin \angle C + \frac{A}{2}}{sin \angle \frac{B}{2}}. \frac{sin \angle PBI}{sin \angle PBC} $$  So :  $\frac{sin \angle PBI}{sin \angle PBC} = \frac{sin \angle \frac{\angle B}{2}}{sin \angle C}$  and  $\frac{sin \angle PCI}{sin \angle PCB} = \frac{sin \angle \frac{\angle C}{2}}{sin \angle B}$ .
Finally , By sine ceva in  $\triangle BIC$ :  $$ \frac{sin \angle PIB}{sin \angle PIC} = \frac{\frac{sin \angle \frac{\angle B}{2}}{sin \angle C}  }  {\frac{sin \angle \frac{\angle C}{2}}{sin \angle B}} = \frac{CI}{BI}.\frac{AC}{AB} $$   which implies that ,  by ratio lemma, if  $IP$  intersects  $BC$  at  $R$  ,  $\frac{BR}{CR}=\frac{AC}{AB}$ . But if  $AI$  intersects  $BC$  at  $D$ , by angle bisector theorem  $\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB}{AC}$ . So if we let  $M$  to be the midpoint of  $BC$  ,  $DM=MR$ . That is, we can redefine  $P$  as the intersection of the reflection of  $D$  over  $M$  and intersect  $RI$  with a line through  $A$  parallel to  $BC$ . and we gotta prove that  $AP=b-c$ . This turns to be so easier to prove.</details>

<details><summary>Step 2</summary>Again by angle bisector theorem,  $BD = \frac{ac}{b+c}$  and since  $BM=\frac{a}{2}$  ,  $DR=2DM=\frac{a(b-c)}{b+c}$ . But again, By angle bisector theorem in  $\triangle ABD$ ,  $\frac{AI}{ID}=\frac{c}{BD}=\frac{b+c}{a}$ . And the problem statement follows by Thales in  $\triangle API , \triangle IDR$ .</details>

stem_md:
Do there exist six points  $A_1 \dots A_6$  in general position in the space, such that the triangles  $A_1A_2A_3$  and  $A_4A_5A_6$  are linked, and two triangles corresponding to any other dividing of these points into two triplets are not linked. *Two triangles on the space are linked if the outline of one triangle meets the inside of the second one at a unique point.*

*Proposed by E. Alkin and A. Skopenkov*
solution_md:
Yes, such six points exist. Let  $\ A_1=(-1,-1,0)$ ,  $\ A_2=(0,1,0)$ ,  $\ A_3=(1,-1,0)$ ,  $\ A_4=(0,0,1)$ ,  $\ A_5=(0,0,-1)$ ,  $\ A_6=(0.1, 2, 0.1)$ . Then clearly the triangles  $\ A_1A_2A_3\ $  and  $\ A_4A_5A_6\ $  are linked, but no other two triangles are. Let's elaborate.     

Why are the triangles  $\ A_1A_2A_3\ $  and  $\ A_4A_5A_6\ $  linked? Because the line segment  $\ A_4A_5\ $  passes through the origin, which is inside the triangle  $\ A_1A_2A_3\ $ .  But the segments  $\ A_4A_6\ $  and  $\ A_5A_6\ $  meet the  $xy$ -plane near the point  $A_6$  and thus far away from the triangle   $\ A_1A_2A_3\ $ . 

Now we need to investigate the remaining 9 cases , which is easy to do in practice, once you imagine how these points are located in space, but typing all this is tiresome, so allow me to elaborate only on one, most difficult case of triangles  $\ A_1A_3A_6\ $  and  $\ A_2A_4A_5\ $ . The line segment    $\ A_4A_5\ $  passes through the origin, which is inside the triangle  $\ A_1A_3A_6\ $ , however the line segment  $A_2A_4$  also meets the interior of the  triangle  $\ A_1A_3A_6\ $ , therefore these two triangles are not linked. 

This does not seem like a very interesting problem. Here are two better problems:**1.**  $\ $ Given 6 points in general position, what is the maximum number of partitions of these points into two triples leading to linked triangles?**2.**  $\ $ Is it possible to have zero or two such partitions?

stem_md:
Let  $M, H, L$  be the centroid, the orthocenter, and the Lemoine point respectively of a triangle  $ABC$ . A point  $S$  is such that the circles  $SLH, SML$  touch  $MH$ , and  $L'$  is the reflection of  $L$  about the circumcircle of the triangle. Prove that  $SL' \parallel MH$ .

*Proposed by S. Kuznetsov*
solution_md:
Here is my solution.

Let  $O$  be the circumcenter of triangle  $ABC$ ,  $K$  the midpoint of  $HM$ . Note that  $H, K, M, O$  are collinear.

Let  $X, Y, Z$  be the orthogonal projections of  $M$  onto the  $A$ -altitude,  $B$ -altitude,  $C$ -altitude of triangle  $ABC$  then:
-  $H, M, X, Y, Z$  are concyclic.
-  $\triangle XYZ$  and  $\triangle ABC$  are inversely similar.
- Two triangles  $\triangle XYZ$  and  $\triangle ABC$  have the same symmedian point. Multiple proofs for this result can be found [here](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/q2h1800469p11950998).

From the definition of  $S$ , it follows that  $S$  is the  $L$ -humpty point of triangle  $LHM$ , which means  $S$  is the reflection of  $L$  about the circumcircle of triangle  $XYZ$  (with diameter  $HM$ ).

Hence  $ABCLOL^{\prime}$  and  $XYZLKS$  are similar, which implies that  $\dfrac{\overline{LO}}{\overline{LL^{\prime}}} = \dfrac{\overline{LK}}{\overline{LS}}$ , which means  $SL^{\prime} \parallel MH$  according to Thales' theorem.

*Proposed by M. Vekshin*
solution_md:

<details><summary>random bits and pieces of an epic solution created on an airplane</summary>If the quadrilateral formed is  $PQRS$ , then we know that as  $ABCD$  is fixed, the directions of lines  $PQ$ ,  $QR$ ,  $RS$ ,  $ST$  are all fixed angles by some simple angle chasing. There are a bunch of cases we can exploit - for example when  $PQRS$  concur at a point to form a degenerate quadrilateral. 

The main observation is that the incenter of  $PQRS$  is the circumcenter of  $ABCD$ . Eventually, all we want to show is that  $P$  varies on a line that passes through  $O$  and taking the case where the conic is  $AC \cup BD$ , we note that this line is actually the perpendicular bisector of a side.

By Pascal,  $CC \cap BB$  is collinear with some two fixed points, meaning that the intersection of  $BB$  with the line formed by those two fixed points defines  $CC$ . Thus  $CC$  is degree 1, and similar to  $BB$ , everything obtained after is degree 1 as well, and we can easily check a case.</details>

solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>There are two sequences that only contain  $A$  and  $B$ : the sequence  $ABABAB$ , and the sequence  $BABABA$ . Similarly, there are two sequences that only contain  $C$  and  $D$ . Otherwise, there are  $2^6 - 2$  ways to choose a subset of the positions to contain  $A$ s and  $B$ s. The remaining spots must then contain  $C$ s and  $D$ s. There are two ways to fill the spots containing  $A$ s and  $B$ s: they must alternate between  $A$  and  $B$ , and so their values is completely determined by the value in the first spot containing an  $A$  or a  $B$ . Similarly, there are two ways to fill the spots containing  $C$ s and  $D$ s. We thus find that there are  $4 + 4(2^6 - 2) = 252$  alternating sequences.

This argument can be generalised to show that there are  $4 + 4(2^n - 2) = 2^{n + 2} - 4$  alternating sequences of length  $n$ .</details>

Define the sequence  $a_1,a_2,\dotsc$  of integers by  $a_1 = 2$  and, for  $n\geq 1$ ,
\[ a_{n+1} = \begin{cases*}
    n +a_n & if  $a_n$  is divisible by  $17$  
    n \cdot a_n & if  $a_n-1$  is divisible by  $17$  
    a_n^2 & otherwise.
\end{cases*} \]
Calculate the remainder when  $a_{2025}$  is divided by  $17$ .
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Consider the pairs of values  $P_n = (n \bmod 17, a_n \bmod 17)$ , and note that the problem statement tells us that  $P_{n + 1}$  only depends on  $P_n$ . By explicit calculation, you find that  $P_{19} = P_{36}$ , and so starting from  $n = 19$ , this sequence is periodic with period  $17$ . The same is then true for  $a_n \bmod 17$ , and so we find that  $a_{2025} \equiv a_{19} \equiv 1 \pmod{17}$ .</details>

Show that there are infinitely many functions  $f : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$  such that for all  $x, y, z \in \mathbb{Z}$  satisfying  $xy +yz +zx = -1$  we have that
\[ f(x)^2 +f(y)^2 +f(z)^2 -f(x)f(y)f(z) = 4. \]
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>Let  $k$  be an arbitrary positive integer. We claim that the function  $$ f(n) = \begin{cases}
-1 & \text{if } k\nmid n 
2 & \text{if } k\mid n
\end{cases} $$  works.
If  $k=1$  then  $f(n)=2$  and  $3\cdot2^2-2^3=4$ .
For the case  $k\neq1$ , if two or more among  $x,y,z$  divides  $k$  then  $k\mid xy+yz+zx=-1$ , a contradiction. If exactly one of  $x,y,z$  divides  $k$ , then  $2^2+(-1)^2+(-1)^2-2=4$ . If none divides  $k$ , then  $3\cdot(-1)^2-(-1)^3=4$ .</details>

stem_md: The cyclic quadrilateral  $ABCD$ , inscribed in the circle  $\Gamma$ , satisfies  $AB=BC$  and  $CD=DA$ , and  $E$  is the intersection point of the diagonals  $AC$  and  $BD$ . The circle with center  $A$  and radius  $AE$  intersects  $\Gamma$  in two points  $F$  and  $G$ . Prove that the line  $FG$  is tangent to the circles with diameters  $BE$  and  $DE$ .
solution_md: Complex bash with  $\Gamma$  as the unit circle, so that  $$ |a|=|b|=1 $$    $$ c = \frac{b^2}a $$    $$ d = -b $$    $$ e = \frac{a+c}2 = \frac{a^2+b^2}{2a} $$  Now suppose  $z$  is the coordinate of either  $F$  or  $G$ , so that  $|z|=1$  and  $|a-z| = |a-e|$ . Squaring both sides,  $$ -\frac{(a-z)^2}{az} = -\frac{(a^2-b^2)^2}{4a^2b^2} $$    $$ 4ab^2(a-z)^2 = z(a^2-b^2)^2 $$    $$ 4ab^2z^2 - z(a^4+6a^2b^2+b^4) + 4a^3b^2 = 0 $$  Thus by Vieta's formulas,  $$ f+g = \frac{a^4+6a^2b^2+b^4}{4ab^2} $$    $$ fg = a^2 $$  Now let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $BE$ , so that  $$ m = \frac{b+e}2 = \frac{(a+b)^2}{4a} $$  Then the distance from  $M$  to line  $FG$  is given by  $$ \frac12|m-f-g+fg\overline{m}| = \frac12\left|\frac{(a+b)^2}{4a} - \frac{a^4+6a^2b^2+b^4}{4ab^2} + \frac{a(a+b)^2}{4b^2}\right| = \frac{|2a^3b-4a^2b^2+2ab^3|}8 = \frac{|a-b|^2}4 $$  and this is the same as  $$ |m-b| = \frac{|b-e|}2 = \frac{|a-b|^2}4 $$  So the distance from  $M$  to line  $FG$  is the same as the distance from  $M$  to  $B$ , and thus the circle with diameter  $BE$  (and center  $M$ ) is tangent to line  $FG$ . The proof for the circle with  $DE$  is exactly the same, but with  $b$  replaced by  $-b$  everywhere.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: We write the decimal expressions of  $\sqrt{2}$  and  $\sqrt{3}$  as \[\sqrt{2}=1.a_1a_2a_3\dots\quad\quad\sqrt{3}=1.b_1b_2b_3\dots\] where each  $a_i$  or  $b_i$  is a digit between 0 and 9. Prove that there exist at least 1000 values of  $i$  between  $1$  and  $10^{1000}$  such that  $a_i\neq b_i$ .
solution_md: **Solution.** For all positive integers $mClaim:** Let $k$ be a positive integer. Then there exists an integer $i_k$ , with $kProof:** Assume otherwise that $a_i=b_i$ for all $i$ , with $kA_{1,k}$ , let $C=B_{1,k}-A_{1,k}$ . Then $$ \lambda=\frac{C}{10^k}+\epsilon_3 $$ for some real number $\epsilon_3$ with $|\epsilon_3|<2\cdot 10^{-10k}$ . The key property is that $10\lambda^2-\lambda^4=1$ . Thus $$ 1=10\lambda^2-\lambda^4=\frac{10^{2k+1}C^2-C^4}{10^{4k}}+\epsilon_3\cdot \left( \frac{20C}{10^k}+10\epsilon_{3}-\frac{4C^3}{10^{3k}}-\frac{6C^2\cdot\epsilon_3}{10^{2k}}-\frac{4C\cdot \epsilon_3^2}{10^k}-\epsilon_3^3 \right) $$ Since $C<10^k$ we can easily bound the trailing part by $21\epsilon_3$ . Since $|21\epsilon_3|<10^{-4k}$ it must be that the trailing part is equal to $0$ and $$ 10^{2k+1}C^2-C^4=10^{4k}\Rightarrow \frac{C^2}{10^{2k}}=5\pm2\sqrt{6} $$ but this is absurd. Then to finish we can simply choose $i\in\{i_1,i_{10},i_{10^2},\dots,i_{10^{999}}\}$ , which all must be distinct.**Remark.** Using this approach it is not hard to replace $10^n$ with $\mathcal{O}((4+\epsilon)^n)$ .

stem_md:
Let  $S$  be a finite set of cells in a square grid. On each cell of  $S$  we place a grasshopper. Each grasshopper can face up, down, left or right. A grasshopper arrangement is Asturian if, when each grasshopper moves one cell forward in the direction in which it faces, each cell of  $S$  still contains one grasshopper.
[list]
[*] Prove that, for every set  $S$ , the number of Asturian arrangements is a perfect square.
[*] Compute the number of Asturian arrangements if  $S$  is the following set:


**Attachments:**

![setS.png](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/0/b/577470ded6eb7728b0a4a0a022014c6bd88544.png)
solution_md:
<details><summary>sol for part 1</summary>Label the cells with coordinates in  $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$  and color  $(i, j)$  with  $(-1)^{i+j}$ . We want to show that the number of bijections  $f: S \mapsto S$   such that  $\text{dist}(u, f(u)) = 1$  for all cells  $u \in S$ .

Divide  $S$  into  $S_{+}$  and  $S_{-}$  depending on color, and realise that it is sufficient to find bijections  $f_1 : S_{+} \mapsto S_{-}$  and  $f_2 : S_{-} \mapsto S_{+}$  such that  $\text{dist}(u, f_1(u)) = 1$  for all  $u \in S_{+}$  and  $\text{dist}(v, f_2(v)) = 1$  for all  $v \in S_{-}$ . But  $f_1, f_2$  are essentially the same thing (the inverse of each  $f_2$  is a valid  $f_1$  and similarily for the other way round). As a result, we obtain that if there are  $N$  bijections  $f_1 : S_{+} \mapsto S_{-}$ , there are also  $N$  bijections  $f_2 : S_{-} \mapsto S_{+}$ , which makes the answer  $N^2$ , a perfect square.</details>
<details><summary>note</summary>It's very likely that the above ideas already enable us to count the particular  $N$  in the case given above. I'm a bit lazy about it though. :D</details>

Let $\mathbb{R}_{\neq 0}$ be the set of nonzero real numbers. Find all functions $f:\mathbb{R}_{\neq 0}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\neq 0}$ such that, for all $x,y\in\mathbb{R}_{\neq 0}$ , \[(x-y)f(y^2)+f\left(xy\,f\left(\frac{x^2}{y}\right)\right)=f(y^2f(y)).\]
Let $P(x,y)$ be the assertion $(x-y)f(y^2)+f(xyf(\frac{x^2}y))=f(y^2f(y))$ If $y+\frac{f(y^2f(y))}{f(y^2)}\ne 0$ , then $P(y+\frac{f(y^2f(y))}{f(y^2)},y)$ $\implies$ $f(\text{something})=0$ , impossible So $f(y^2f(y))=-yf(y^2)$ $\forall y\ne 0$ and $P(x,y)$ becomes (replacing RHS) : New assertion $Q(x,y)$ : $f(xyf(\frac{x^2}y))=-xf(y^2)$ $\forall x,y\ne 0$ $Q(xf(x),xf(x)^2)$ $\implies$ $f(x^2f(x)^4)=-xf(x)f(x^2f(x)^4)$ And so $\boxed{f(x)=-\frac 1x\quad\forall x\ne 0}$ , which indeed fits
